Score improved from 0.49048 to 0.47522, confirming the checkpoint was partly responsible, but the result was still worse than the 0.46639 best, suggesting the MC-dropout code changes also hurt or were incompatible.

general.goal: When multiple changes are made simultaneously and the score degrades, how can the cause be isolated?
general.context: A submission combined architectural changes with a different set of saved weights, and the score worsened substantially compared to the previous best.
general.action: Change one factor at a time: swap only the checkpoint source while keeping the new code, then compare. If the score partially recovers, both factors contributed. If it fully recovers, the checkpoint was the sole cause. This one-variable-at-a-time probing is essential before concluding that a code-level change helped or hurt.

episode.objective: Add categorical bin prediction head and multi-seed ensembling to improve predictions
episode.outcome: new best 0.46533 at v21 with bins + multi-seed averaging

instance.goal: Can adding a categorical/bin prediction head alongside the regression output improve readability score predictions?
instance.context: The best LB score was 0.46639 with a RoBERTa-large regression model. The author hypothesized that discretizing the target into bins and adding a classification head could provide complementary signal.
instance.action: Added a categorical output head (output_cat) to the model that predicts bin labels via argmax, extended the dataset to include a 'bins' field, and pointed to new checkpoints trained with this dual-head setup. This yielded a new best LB of 0.46543.

general.goal: Can augmenting a regression model with an auxiliary discrete classification head improve continuous prediction accuracy?
general.context: A fine-tuned transformer regression model has plateaued on a small, noisy dataset with a continuous target.
general.action: Add a parallel classification head that predicts the target binned into discrete categories. Train with both regression and classification losses. At inference, use the regression output (or blend both). This can regularize the model and provide complementary signal, especially on small datasets.

instance.goal: How much does averaging predictions across multiple random-seed checkpoints per fold improve the score beyond a single checkpoint per fold?
instance.context: After adding the categorical head, the single-seed-per-fold score was 0.46543. The author had previously seen multi-seed ensembling help (v14: 0.46639 vs v15: 0.46937 without it).
instance.action: Used glob to iterate over multiple seed-specific model directories per fold, loaded each checkpoint, ran inference, and averaged predictions across seeds before averaging across folds. Also doubled the batch size. This gave a marginal improvement to 0.46533 (new best).

general.goal: How much additional gain can be expected from averaging predictions of models trained with different random seeds on the same fold split?
general.context: A fine-tuned transformer on a small dataset shows variance across seeds. A single-seed submission already scores well, and prior experiments showed multi-seed averaging helped.
general.action: For each fold, load checkpoints from several training runs that differ only in random seed. Run inference with each, average their predictions per fold, then average across folds. Expect diminishing but consistent gains (often a few hundredths of RMSE on small test sets). Increase batch size to offset the added inference cost.

episode.objective: Try paired-input encoding with benchmark excerpt and attentive pooling, then simplify back
episode.outcome: v22 0.46820, v23 0.46690; neither beat v21 best; simplified back

instance.goal: Can encoding the input as a text-pair (excerpt + benchmark excerpt) with a splitting mask and attentive pooling improve readability predictions?
instance.context: Best LB was 0.46533 with multi-seed ensembling of a RoBERTa-large model. The author hypothesized that pairing each excerpt with a fixed benchmark reference text could give the model a comparative signal for readability scoring.
instance.action: Encoded each test excerpt as a sentence-pair with a benchmark excerpt from training data, added a splitting mask to separate the two segments, and introduced an AttentivePooling module. LB worsened from 0.46533 to 0.46820. Then simplified by removing the benchmark pairing, splitting mask, and AttentivePooling, replacing with a simpler inline linear attention. LB improved to 0.46690, partially recovering but not beating the pre-episode best.

general.goal: Can providing a fixed reference example alongside each input (paired encoding) help a pretrained language model produce better regression predictions?
general.context: A fine-tuned transformer is already performing well on a text regression task. The idea is to give the model a comparative anchor by encoding each sample as a pair with a constant reference text.
general.action: Try the paired-input approach and measure validation or leaderboard impact. If it hurts performance, revert the pairing but keep any simpler architectural improvements (e.g., a cleaner attention pooling) that emerged during the experiment. Paired encoding adds sequence length and may confuse a model trained without it, so expect it to help only if checkpoints are retrained with the new format.

instance.goal: After a complex architectural change hurts the score, how much of the change should be reverted versus retained?
instance.context: Adding benchmark-pair encoding, splitting mask, and AttentivePooling worsened LB from 0.46533 to 0.46820. The change bundled multiple modifications: input format change, new pooling module, and extra heads.
instance.action: Removed the benchmark pairing and splitting mask (the input-format changes) but replaced the complex AttentivePooling with a simpler inline linear attention mechanism. This partial revert recovered most of the loss (0.46820 → 0.46690), suggesting the input-format change was the main culprit while the simpler attention pooling was neutral or mildly beneficial.

general.goal: When a bundle of changes degrades performance, how can the harmful component be isolated from potentially useful ones?
general.context: A single commit introduced multiple coupled changes (input encoding, pooling architecture, extra output heads) and the combined effect was negative.
general.action: Revert the most invasive or least-tested change first (here, the input format that mismatches pretrained checkpoints) while retaining or simplifying the architectural additions. Compare the partially-reverted score against both the pre-change baseline and the full-change score to attribute the degradation. Keep components that are score-neutral or positive; discard the rest.

episode.objective: Swap checkpoint directory (v11_0 vs v11_1) to find better weights
episode.outcome: v24 0.46940; worse than v21 best

instance.goal: Which of the available checkpoint directories (v11_0 vs v11_1) produces better leaderboard predictions?
instance.context: The author had multiple checkpoint directories saved from different training runs/seeds (v11_0 and v11_1). The previous version used v11_1 and scored 0.46690. The best score so far was 0.46533.
instance.action: Swapped the single model_dir path from v11_1 to v11_0 and submitted. The score worsened from 0.46690 to 0.46940, indicating v11_0 was inferior to v11_1 for this pipeline configuration.

general.goal: How much does the choice among available checkpoint variants (different seeds or training runs) affect the final score?
general.context: Multiple checkpoint directories exist from separate training runs or random seeds, and the rest of the inference pipeline is held constant.
general.action: Swap in each candidate checkpoint one at a time and submit to the leaderboard (or evaluate on a reliable local validation set). Keep the checkpoint that scores best. Expect that different seeds can shift the score noticeably even with the same architecture and training recipe, so this probe is worth doing before committing to an ensemble.

episode.objective: Implement benchmark-relative normalization (subtract benchmark logits from predictions) and iterate on checkpoint/path to optimize it
episode.outcome: new best 0.46114 at v29 with v15 checkpoint and benchmark subtraction

instance.goal: Can normalizing predictions relative to a fixed benchmark example (subtracting its logits from each sample's logits) reduce systematic bias and improve RMSE?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.46533 with multi-seed ensembling of RoBERTa-large. The author selected a training example with standard_error==0 as a reliable anchor point for normalization.
instance.action: Tokenized a benchmark excerpt once, passed it through the same model alongside each batch, and subtracted the benchmark's output logits from each sample's logits before producing the final prediction. Iterated across checkpoints and fixed bugs (device placement, variable nullification) until the approach yielded a new best of 0.46114.

general.goal: Can systematic prediction bias or shift be reduced by expressing each prediction relative to a fixed reference input?
general.context: A regression model produces predictions that may carry a per-fold or per-checkpoint offset. A highly reliable reference example (e.g., one with near-zero label noise) is available in the training data.
general.action: Select a reference example with minimal label uncertainty. At inference, run it through the same model and subtract its output from every other prediction. This removes additive bias that varies across folds or checkpoints, improving ensemble consistency. Ensure the reference tokens stay on the correct device and are not accidentally cleared between folds.

instance.goal: When iterating on a new inference technique (benchmark normalization), how should checkpoint selection and code bugs be disentangled to find the true effect?
instance.context: v25 introduced benchmark normalization but scored worse (0.47332). Subsequent edits fixed the checkpoint path (v26→0.47043), moved tokenization logic (v27→0.46431 best), then accidentally disabled the feature (v28→0.47017), and re-enabled it with a better checkpoint (v29→0.46114 best).
instance.action: The author toggled the feature on/off across versions while also swapping checkpoint directories. The score drop when the benchmark token was set to None (v28) and recovery when restored (v29) confirmed the technique's value independently of the checkpoint change. Iterating one variable at a time (fix path, then fix logic, then swap checkpoint) isolated the contribution.

general.goal: How can the true effect of a new inference-time technique be confirmed when checkpoint selection also changes between experiments?
general.context: A new prediction normalization idea is introduced simultaneously with a checkpoint swap, making it unclear which change drives the score.
general.action: After the initial combined change, toggle the new technique on and off while holding the checkpoint fixed. If disabling the technique worsens the score and re-enabling it recovers it, the technique's contribution is confirmed. Only then vary the checkpoint to find the best combination. This two-step ablation avoids confounding infrastructure fixes with algorithmic improvements.

episode.objective: Sweep pooling strategy (mean-only vs mean+max concatenation) and checkpoint versions to find best combination

instance.goal: Which pooling strategy (mean-only weighted layers vs. concatenated mean+max) works better with which checkpoint for RoBERTa-large readability prediction?
instance.context: v29 achieved best LB 0.46114 with mean+max pooling and v15 checkpoint directory. The author suspects that pooling strategy must match the checkpoint it was trained with, and wants to find the best combination.
instance.action: Systematically sweep: (1) v30: same pooling, specific sub-checkpoint of v15 → 0.47074 (worse). (2) v31: switch to mean-only pooling + different checkpoint → 0.46473. (3) v32: switch back to mean+max pooling + yet another checkpoint → 0.46335 (best in episode). (4) v33: switch to mean-only pooling + v16 checkpoint → 0.46357. Conclude mean+max with the right checkpoint is best; later v34 confirms at 0.46221.

general.goal: How to determine which feature-pooling strategy pairs best with which saved model weights at inference time?
general.context: The inference-time pooling architecture must match what the model was trained with; mismatches silently degrade performance. Multiple checkpoints trained under different configurations are available.
general.action: Sweep pooling variants (e.g., mean-only vs. concatenated mean+max over hidden layers) jointly with checkpoint versions, changing one factor at a time. Compare leaderboard or validation scores for each combination to identify the correct pairing, since using the wrong pooling for a given checkpoint will hurt even if that pooling is generally superior.

instance.goal: Does pointing inference to a specific single-fold sub-checkpoint rather than the parent directory of all fold checkpoints improve the score?
instance.context: v29 used the parent directory '../input/clrroberta-largepretrained-modelsv15' (presumably loading all fold checkpoints and averaging). The author tried narrowing to one specific sub-checkpoint.
instance.action: Changed path to a specific sub-checkpoint ('model_best_roberta_large_v15_1'). LB worsened from 0.46114 to 0.47074, showing that ensembling across folds via the parent directory was critical. The author reverted to multi-fold loading in subsequent versions.

general.goal: Is it better to ensemble predictions from all cross-validation fold checkpoints or use a single best fold checkpoint at inference?
general.context: A multi-fold ensemble achieved a strong score. The author tested whether a single fold's checkpoint could match or beat it.
general.action: Compare the ensemble of all fold checkpoints against the single best fold checkpoint. Expect the multi-fold ensemble to be substantially better due to variance reduction; revert to the ensemble if the single checkpoint degrades the score.

episode.objective: Sweep num_bins (1 vs 29) and checkpoint selection to find optimal final configuration
episode.outcome: v34 achieved 0.46221 (second best overall), v35 0.46489, v36 0.47147; best at v34

instance.goal: Which combination of pooling strategy (mean+max vs weighted mean), num_bins (1 vs 29), and checkpoint yields the best RMSE?
instance.context: Previous versions alternated between mean+max pooling and weighted-mean pooling with different checkpoints and num_bins values. v32 (mean+max, bins=29) scored 0.46335; v33 (weighted mean, bins=29) scored 0.46357.
instance.action: Swept three configurations: (1) mean+max pooling + num_bins=1 + checkpoint v16 → 0.46221 (best); (2) different checkpoint + num_bins=29 → 0.46489; (3) same checkpoint but single file + num_bins=1 → 0.47147. The best result came from mean+max pooling with num_bins=1 and the v16 checkpoint directory.

general.goal: How to identify the best combination of architectural variant, discretization setting, and saved weights when multiple options interact?
general.context: Several design choices (pooling method, number of output bins, checkpoint selection) have been individually varied in prior iterations with small score differences, making it unclear which combination is optimal.
general.action: Run a small factorial sweep changing one or two factors per submission. Track the leaderboard score for each combination and select the configuration that yields the best metric. Keep the number of changes per submission small enough to attribute score movements to specific factors.

instance.goal: Does the auxiliary binning head (num_bins=29) help or hurt when paired with mean+max pooling and a particular checkpoint?
instance.context: v34 used num_bins=1 (no binning) with mean+max pooling and scored 0.46221. v35 switched to num_bins=29 with a different checkpoint and scored worse (0.46489). v36 reverted to num_bins=1 with a single checkpoint file and scored even worse (0.47147), but the v34 result suggests num_bins=1 is better when other factors are held constant.
instance.action: Compared num_bins=1 vs 29 across checkpoints. The regression-only head (num_bins=1) with the right checkpoint outperformed the binning variant, indicating the auxiliary classification head adds noise on this small dataset when the checkpoint and pooling are already strong.

general.goal: Does adding an auxiliary discretized classification head alongside a regression head improve predictions on a small, noisy regression task?
general.context: The dataset is small and noisy, and the model already uses a strong pretrained backbone with an effective pooling strategy. An auxiliary binning head was previously helpful with some configurations but may not generalize across all checkpoint/pooling combinations.
general.action: Test the model with and without the auxiliary classification head while keeping other factors fixed. If the regression-only configuration scores better, drop the auxiliary head—on small datasets the extra head can introduce noise that outweighs its regularization benefit.

episode.objective: Increase neural network weight in ensemble blend to improve score.
episode.outcome: Tiny improvement to 0.69557 (v2), new best.

instance.goal: What is the right blend weight for the neural network component relative to the GBM component in the ensemble?
instance.context: An ensemble of GBM and NN predictions was already producing a competitive submission. The NN coefficient was set at 0.15, meaning the NN had a small contribution. The author suspected the NN was underweighted.
instance.action: Doubled the NN blend coefficient from 0.15 to 0.3, which yielded a small LB improvement of +0.00004 to 0.69557. This confirmed the NN deserved more weight, and the author continued increasing NN involvement in later versions.

general.goal: How much weight should a secondary model receive when blended with the primary model in an ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble combines a gradient-boosted tree model with a neural network model, and the neural network's blend weight is conservatively low. The leaderboard metric is available for probing.
general.action: Incrementally increase the secondary model's blend coefficient (e.g., double it) and submit to check for improvement. Small positive gains confirm the secondary model is underweighted and justify further increases. Continue probing until the score plateaus or drops.

episode.objective: Rebuild the notebook pipeline to train tree/TabNet models in-notebook, then switch to external prediction scripts for reproducibility.
episode.lever: inference pipeline architecture (in-notebook vs external scripts)
episode.outcome: Pipeline restructured but v8 score 0.69524 is worse than v2 best; several unsubmitted versions.

instance.goal: How should raw model predictions be post-processed before blending for a concordance-index metric — should they be rank-transformed or left as raw scores?
instance.context: The author tried three variants: negated raw scores (v3), negated ranks via scipy rankdata (v4), and a hybrid where tree models used ranks but the neural net used raw scores (v5). Eventually they reverted to raw negated scores for all models (v6). The final LB was 0.69524, slightly below the prior best of 0.69557.
instance.action: Tested rank-transforming predictions before blending vs. using raw scores. Found that for this concordance-based metric, rank transformation did not help and raw (negated) scores were kept. The author iterated through raw → rank → hybrid → raw across four versions.

general.goal: How should individual model outputs be post-processed before averaging in an ensemble when the evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., concordance index)?
general.context: A rank-based metric only cares about ordering, so rank-transforming predictions before averaging seems appealing to normalize scale differences across models.
general.action: Try both raw scores and rank-transformed scores in the blend. Rank transformation can destroy useful magnitude information that helps the average preserve ordering, especially when models are well-calibrated. Test both and keep whichever yields a better validation or leaderboard score; do not assume rank transformation helps just because the metric is rank-based.

instance.goal: Is it better to train all models (CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, TabNet) inside the submission notebook or call external pre-built prediction scripts?
instance.context: The author first built a full in-notebook pipeline (v3) with CatBoost, LightGBM, and a TabNet model including custom training loops, target transforms, and feature engineering. By v6 they removed most in-notebook training code and switched to calling external scripts from /kaggle/input/cibmtr-scripts. The submitted score (0.69524) was slightly below the prior best (0.69557), but the architecture was retained and improved in later versions (v9 reached 0.69562).
instance.action: Moved model training into standalone external scripts that output prediction CSVs, then had the main notebook only blend those CSVs. This separated concerns: each model script could be developed, debugged, and versioned independently, while the notebook focused on ensembling and submission formatting.

general.goal: How should a multi-model ensemble pipeline be organized when iterating on individual model components in a constrained notebook environment?
general.context: Training multiple diverse models (gradient-boosted trees, neural networks) in one notebook makes it hard to iterate on one model without re-running everything, and risks hitting time/memory limits.
general.action: Factor each model into a separate self-contained script that writes predictions to a file. The main notebook reads those prediction files and only performs blending and submission creation. This lets each model be developed and tested independently, reduces notebook runtime, and makes it easy to swap in improved model versions without touching the ensemble logic.

episode.objective: Switch to updated external prediction scripts (_inc variants) to improve ensemble inputs.
episode.outcome: New best 0.69562 at v9.

instance.goal: After a score regression from v7 to v8 (0.69524 vs previous best 0.69557), how can the ensemble score be recovered and improved?
instance.context: The pipeline blends predictions from multiple external scripts (CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost variants) with a neural network. The v6-v8 refactor to use external scripts caused a regression, suggesting the external model predictions themselves could be improved.
instance.action: Swapped all external prediction scripts to updated '_inc' variants (e.g., predict_catboost_ones.py → predict_catboost_ones_inc.py) that presumably used incremental improvements (different hyperparameters or features). This recovered and exceeded the previous best, reaching 0.69562.

general.goal: When an ensemble regresses after switching to externally-generated component predictions, how can the quality of those components be improved?
general.context: The ensemble pipeline consumes predictions from separately-trained models via external scripts. A recent refactor introduced these scripts but the score dropped, indicating the component predictions are suboptimal.
general.action: Iterate on the external model training/prediction scripts independently (tuning hyperparameters, features, or training procedure) and swap in the improved versions. Keep the ensemble blending logic fixed so that any score change is attributable solely to the component quality, making it easy to diagnose whether the new components help.

episode.objective: Compute survival targets separately per race group to improve calibration and equity metric.
episode.outcome: New best 0.69576 at v10.

instance.goal: Can computing survival-based target labels separately within each race group improve the stratified concordance index that penalizes cross-group performance variance?
instance.context: The competition metric is the mean C-index across race groups minus its standard deviation, so both accuracy and equity matter. The existing pipeline applied a single global target transform (e.g., Kaplan-Meier or Nelson-Aalen) across all patients, which may miscalibrate risk within minority groups.
instance.action: Created make_target_by_race() that splits the training data by race_group (0–5), applies the survival target transform (make_target) independently within each subgroup, then concatenates and re-sorts. Used this in place of the global make_target(). This yielded a small but consistent LB improvement (+0.00014).

general.goal: How can target construction be adapted when the evaluation metric rewards both overall accuracy and equitable performance across predefined subgroups?
general.context: A survival or ranking target is derived from a global statistical estimate (e.g., a cumulative hazard curve). The metric averages per-subgroup performance and penalizes variance across subgroups, so a globally computed target may under-fit minority subgroups whose event distributions differ.
general.action: Compute the target transform separately within each subgroup used by the equity metric, then recombine. This ensures each subgroup's target reflects its own event distribution, improving calibration where the metric measures it. Verify with the stratified metric that both mean and variance components improve.

episode.objective: Tune NN blend weight and try updated external scripts (_inc13) to improve ensemble score.
episode.lever: ensemble blend weights and external script versions
episode.outcome: v11 new best 0.69589 with NN_COEF=0.3; v12 regressed to 0.69582 with inc13 scripts and NN_COEF=0.15.

instance.goal: What is the optimal blending weight for the neural network component in the ensemble of tree models and a neural network?
instance.context: At v10 (LB 0.69576), the NN blend coefficient was 0.15. The ensemble combines external CatBoost/LightGBM/XGBoost predictions with an in-notebook neural network. A new best score motivated further tuning.
instance.action: Doubled the NN coefficient from 0.15 to 0.3, which improved LB to 0.69589. Then tried 0.15 with updated external tree scripts (_inc13), which scored 0.69582—worse than 0.3 with the old scripts. The best weight was 0.3 with the original external scripts.

general.goal: What is the right mixing weight for a neural-network component blended with gradient-boosted tree predictions?
general.context: An ensemble blends predictions from multiple tree models with a neural network. The current weight for the neural network is small and a recent improvement suggests the ensemble balance may be suboptimal.
general.action: Sweep the neural-network blend weight (e.g., double it) and submit to check leaderboard impact. Change only one factor at a time: do not simultaneously update the tree model versions and the blend weight, because confounding makes it impossible to attribute gains or losses to either change.

instance.goal: Will switching to newer external prediction scripts (_inc13) for the tree models improve the ensemble score?
instance.context: At v11 (LB 0.69589), the ensemble used older external scripts with NN_COEF=0.3. The author simultaneously switched to _inc13 scripts and reverted NN_COEF to 0.15, scoring 0.69582—a regression.
instance.action: Because two changes were made at once (new scripts + reduced NN weight), the author could not determine whether the new scripts helped or hurt. The combined result was worse, so the v11 configuration remained the best.

general.goal: How can the effect of updating one ensemble component be reliably measured?
general.context: After finding a new best score by tuning a blend weight, the practitioner wants to also test updated base-model predictions. Changing both the blend weight and the base models simultaneously confounds the evaluation.
general.action: Change only one variable per submission: either update the base-model predictions or adjust the blend weight, not both. If a combined change regresses, revert to the last best and test each change in isolation to identify which helped and which hurt.

episode.objective: Tune blend coefficients and preprocessing constants, and separate NN submission file.
episode.lever: blend coefficients and submission file management
episode.outcome: v14 new best 0.69597 after adjustments and saving NN predictions separately.

instance.goal: How to recover from a score regression (v12 dropped from 0.69589 to 0.69582) when the cause was switching external model versions and reducing NN blend weight?
instance.context: v11 achieved 0.69589 with NN_COEF=0.3 and older external scripts. v12 regressed to 0.69582 after switching to inc13 scripts and lowering NN weight. Multiple knobs are available: blend coefficients, preprocessing constants, external script versions.
instance.action: Simultaneously adjusted multiple small constants (COLLAPSE 1.30→1.325, ZEROES_SHIFT=0.053, NN_COEF back to 0.3), updated external prediction scripts, and retuned GBM blend coefficients. Also separated NN predictions into submission_nn.csv to avoid overwriting the main blend. Achieved 0.69597, a new best.

general.goal: How to recover from a score regression caused by changing multiple ensemble components at once?
general.context: A previous version regressed after simultaneously updating external model predictions and reducing a component's blend weight, making it unclear which change hurt.
general.action: Revert the blend weight to its previous best value while keeping the updated model predictions, and make small compensating adjustments to preprocessing constants and per-model blend coefficients. Change only a few things at a time and verify the combined effect before submitting.

instance.goal: How to manage multiple prediction outputs (NN vs. full blend) so they don't overwrite each other during iterative tuning?
instance.context: The NN model and the GBM ensemble both wrote to 'submission.csv', causing one to overwrite the other. The author needed both available for flexible blending and separate submission.
instance.action: Renamed the NN output file from 'submission.csv' to 'submission_nn.csv' so both the NN-only and the blended predictions coexist as separate files, enabling independent submission and further blending experiments.

general.goal: How to avoid losing intermediate predictions when an ensemble pipeline has multiple model families writing output files?
general.context: Multiple model components in an ensemble pipeline write predictions to the same default output filename, causing later components to overwrite earlier ones.
general.action: Give each model family's predictions a distinct output filename so all intermediate predictions are preserved. This allows flexible re-blending and independent submission of any component without re-running the full pipeline.

episode.objective: Rescale NN logits (sigmoid(2x)), switch to inc13 scripts, and increase NN blend weight to improve score.
episode.lever: NN output scaling and ensemble blend weights
episode.outcome: v15 new best 0.69661, v16 new best 0.69671.

instance.goal: Can rescaling the neural network's raw logits before the final activation improve the quality of predictions used in the ensemble?
instance.context: The NN outputs were passed through sigmoid(x); the author had just achieved a new best (0.69597) and suspected the NN's output distribution was too compressed/flat to contribute optimally to the blend with GBDTs.
instance.action: Applied sigmoid(2*x) instead of sigmoid(x) to the NN logits, effectively sharpening the output distribution. Combined with retuned blend weights and updated external GBDT scripts (inc13 variants), this yielded +0.00064 improvement to 0.69661.

general.goal: Can the neural network component's output distribution be adjusted to improve its contribution to an ensemble with tree-based models?
general.context: When blending a neural network with gradient-boosted trees, the NN's sigmoid outputs may be too compressed near 0.5, reducing its discriminative power in the blend and limiting the ensemble's ranking ability.
general.action: Multiply the NN's pre-activation logits by a constant greater than 1 before applying the sigmoid, sharpening the output distribution. Then retune the ensemble blend coefficients to account for the changed scale. Evaluate on the leaderboard or validation to confirm the gain.

instance.goal: After improving the NN output scaling, what is the right blend weight for the NN relative to the GBDT models?
instance.context: After rescaling NN logits (sigmoid(2x)) and switching to inc13 GBDT scripts, the score improved to 0.69661. The NN blend coefficient was 0.3; the author suspected the improved NN predictions deserved more weight.
instance.action: Increased NN_COEF from 0.3 to 0.4, giving the NN a larger share in the final blend. This yielded a further +0.00011 improvement to 0.69671, confirming the NN's improved predictions warranted higher weight.

general.goal: After improving one component model's predictions, how should the ensemble weights be re-balanced?
general.context: When a component model's output quality improves (e.g., via output rescaling or better training), the previously tuned blend weights may underweight it, leaving score on the table.
general.action: After any change that improves a component model's individual quality, incrementally increase its blend coefficient (e.g., by steps of 0.1) and evaluate. Stop when the leaderboard or validation metric no longer improves. Expect small but consistent gains from proper rebalancing.

episode.objective: Switch LR scheduler from cosine-warmup to MultiStepLR and output separate regression/class predictions.
episode.lever: learning rate scheduler and prediction output format
episode.outcome: New best 0.69690 at v17.

instance.goal: Can a different learning rate schedule improve the neural network's contribution to the ensemble and raise the blended score?
instance.context: The cosine-with-warmup scheduler was used in prior versions; the NN blend weight had been tuned up to 0.3, and the ensemble was at LB 0.69671. The author suspected the NN training dynamics could be improved.
instance.action: Replaced the cosine-with-warmup scheduler with a MultiStepLR that steps at specific epochs, added a flag to enable/disable the scheduler, and applied it at epoch granularity rather than step granularity. This yielded a small improvement to LB 0.69690.

general.goal: Can changing the learning rate decay schedule improve a neural network component that feeds into an ensemble?
general.context: A smooth warmup-then-cosine schedule is already in use and the model's predictions are blended with tree-based models. The ensemble score has been incrementally improving but the neural network's training may not be converging to the best point.
general.action: Try switching from a smooth continuous schedule (e.g., cosine annealing) to a stepped schedule that holds the learning rate constant for several epochs then drops it at predefined milestones. Apply the schedule at epoch granularity and add a toggle flag so you can A/B test with and without the scheduler.

instance.goal: How should the neural network's regression and classification head outputs be handled for optimal blending with external tree models?
instance.context: Previously the NN produced a single blended prediction. The author wanted finer control over how regression vs. classification outputs contribute to the final ensemble with CatBoost/LGB/XGB predictions.
instance.action: Output separate regression and classification predictions from the neural network, allowing independent weighting when blending with external tree-model predictions. Also fixed a bug in race-group-specific target assembly (indexing/concatenation) that could have corrupted per-group labels.

general.goal: When a neural network has multiple output heads (e.g., regression and classification), how should their predictions be exposed for downstream ensembling?
general.context: The network has two task heads whose outputs were previously merged internally. External models also produce predictions that are blended with the network's output.
general.action: Save each head's predictions separately rather than combining them inside the model. This lets the ensemble step independently weight each head's contribution alongside other models, giving more degrees of freedom for tuning the final blend.

episode.objective: Remove outlier samples from training to improve model robustness.
episode.outcome: Not submitted; v18-v19 are unsubmitted/noop.

instance.goal: Can removing noisy or outlier training samples improve the survival prediction model's concordance index?
instance.context: The author had an externally precomputed list of outlier sample IDs (outliers_0.9.npy) and a pipeline already scoring 0.69690 on the leaderboard. The episode was not submitted, so the effect is unknown from LB; the next submitted version (v21) scored 0.69689, suggesting no clear gain.
instance.action: Loaded the external outlier ID list and filtered those rows out of the training subset before model training. This was a quick probe: two small code insertions, then a checkpoint re-run to verify.

general.goal: Can removing noisy or outlier training samples improve a supervised model's performance on a ranking metric?
general.context: An outlier list has been precomputed (e.g., via high-loss or distributional analysis) and the current pipeline is already well-tuned, so data cleaning is a plausible next lever.
general.action: Load the precomputed outlier IDs and filter them from the training set before fitting. Treat this as a quick probe: make the minimal code change, re-run, and compare validation or leaderboard scores to the baseline. If no improvement is observed, revert.

episode.objective: Tune ensemble blend coefficients and try denoised CatBoost variant to improve blended submission.
episode.lever: blend coefficients and CatBoost prediction variant
episode.outcome: v21 0.69689 and v22 0.69681, both worse than v17 best 0.69690; no improvement.

instance.goal: Can retuning the blend coefficients across LGB, CatBoost, XGB, and NN predictions improve the ensemble score beyond 0.69690?
instance.context: The best LB score was 0.69690. The author had multiple model predictions (LGB, CatBoost, XGB, NN) each with regression and classification outputs, blended with manually set coefficients and a shift constant.
instance.action: Changed all blend coefficients substantially (e.g., LGB_ONES_COEF 0.382→0.243, CATBOOST_ONES_COEF 0.123→0.269, NN_ONES_COEF 0.071→0.174, etc.) and ZEROES_SHIFT 0.073→0.086. Score dropped to 0.69689. Then reverted coefficients back to original values in v22, getting 0.69681. Neither improved over baseline.

general.goal: How much gain can be extracted by re-sweeping ensemble blend weights when the ensemble is already well-tuned?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models is already near its optimum blend, and the metric is a ranking-based concordance index where small coefficient changes have diminishing returns.
general.action: Try a substantially different set of blend coefficients. If the score does not improve (or slightly degrades), the current coefficients are likely near-optimal. Avoid spending many iterations on coefficient sweeps once changes of moderate magnitude fail to improve the score.

instance.goal: Would using a denoised variant of the CatBoost predictions improve the blended submission?
instance.context: The author had access to an alternative 'denoized' CatBoost prediction script alongside the standard one. The ensemble was already well-tuned at LB 0.69690.
instance.action: Swapped predict_catboost_ones.py with predict_catboost_ones_denoized.py while keeping other blend coefficients fixed. The LB score was 0.69689, essentially unchanged, indicating the denoised variant did not help. The author then reverted and continued searching other levers.

general.goal: Does swapping in a label-denoised variant of one component model improve an already-strong ensemble?
general.context: One component model in a multi-model ensemble has a variant trained with denoised targets. The ensemble is already well-tuned and near its performance ceiling.
general.action: Substitute the denoised variant for the original component while keeping blend weights fixed, and evaluate on the leaderboard. If the score is flat or worse, the denoising did not add complementary signal, and the original component should be retained.

episode.objective: Switch to updated external prediction scripts (_inc10, then _inc15) and retune blend coefficients to improve score.
episode.lever: external prediction script versions and blend coefficients
episode.outcome: v25 new best 0.69699 (re-run), v26 new best 0.69702 with inc15 scripts.

instance.goal: After score regressions in v21-v22 from blend tuning alone, what else can recover and improve the ensemble score?
instance.context: v21 (0.69689) and v22 (0.69681) regressed from the v17 best of 0.69690 despite blend coefficient changes, suggesting the current external model predictions were a bottleneck.
instance.action: Switched external prediction scripts from earlier versions to _inc10 variants (v23) with retuned blend coefficients and shift constants, then further upgraded to _inc15 variants (v26). Each script version represented improved base model predictions. This recovered the score to 0.69699 then 0.69702, both new bests.

general.goal: When tuning ensemble blend weights no longer improves the score and recent attempts regress, where should effort be directed?
general.context: Blend coefficient adjustments have plateaued or regressed, indicating the quality of the individual base model predictions is the binding constraint rather than how they are combined.
general.action: Upgrade the base model predictions (retrain with better hyperparameters, more data, or improved preprocessing) rather than continuing to tune blend weights. After swapping in improved base predictions, retune the blend coefficients to match the new prediction distributions.

instance.goal: How can the effect of switching external prediction scripts be isolated from the effect of retuning blend coefficients when both change simultaneously?
instance.context: In v23 both the external scripts (_inc10) and blend coefficients were changed at once, making it unclear which change helped. The author then re-ran unchanged code (v24→v25) to confirm the score before changing only the script versions to _inc15 in v26.
instance.action: After the combined change in v23, the author froze the blend coefficients and only swapped external script versions (_inc10 → _inc15) in v26, observing a small but consistent gain (0.69699 → 0.69702). This sequential approach isolated the contribution of the newer base predictions.

general.goal: When multiple ensemble components are changed at once, how can one determine which change is responsible for a score movement?
general.context: Changing both base model outputs and blend weights simultaneously confounds attribution of any score change.
general.action: After a combined change, freeze one factor (e.g., blend weights) and vary only the other (e.g., base model version) in the next submission. This sequential one-variable-at-a-time approach lets you attribute the marginal gain to the changed factor and decide whether to keep it.

episode.objective: Refactor notebook into inference-only submission script with fixed blend coefficients.
episode.outcome: Not submitted; code restructured and coefficients filled in at v28.

instance.goal: How to prepare the notebook for reliable, reproducible submission generation after reaching a satisfactory ensemble score?
instance.context: The notebook had accumulated training code, model definitions, and many imports over 26 versions of iterative development, but the best LB score (0.69702) was achieved. External prediction scripts already existed for CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost, and blend coefficients were known.
instance.action: Stripped all model-definition and training code from the notebook, replacing it with shell calls to prebuilt external prediction scripts. Loaded their outputs, applied fixed blend coefficients and sigmoid post-processing, and wrote the submission CSV. Then filled in the exact numeric constants for all blend weights and shift offsets in a follow-up commit.

general.goal: How to prepare a competition notebook for reliable, reproducible submission generation after the development/tuning phase is complete?
general.context: A notebook has grown large with training loops, model definitions, and experimental code, but the best score has been reached and all component predictions can be generated by standalone scripts with known blend weights.
general.action: Refactor the notebook into an inference-only pipeline: remove all training and model-definition code, call external prediction scripts via shell commands, load their outputs, apply the fixed blend coefficients and any post-processing, and write the final submission. Separate the structural refactor (replacing code with script calls and placeholder coefficients) from filling in the exact numeric constants, so each step can be verified independently.

instance.goal: What is the risk of a large refactor to inference-only mode on submission quality?
instance.context: After refactoring to inference-only (v27-v28), the next submission (v29) scored 0.69547, well below the pre-refactor best of 0.69702, suggesting the refactor introduced a regression—possibly from missing a model component or incorrect coefficient transcription.
instance.action: The author did not submit v27 or v28, but the subsequent v29 submission revealed a score drop. This required further debugging in v29-v30 to recover performance (v30 reached 0.69668, still below 0.69702).

general.goal: How can a major pipeline refactor be validated to ensure it does not silently degrade prediction quality?
general.context: When converting a development notebook into a clean inference-only pipeline, there is a risk that some component predictions, blend weights, or post-processing steps are lost or mis-transcribed, causing a score regression that is only discovered upon submission.
general.action: Before and after the refactor, generate predictions on the same data and compare them numerically (e.g., correlation or max absolute difference) to confirm the outputs are identical. Submit the refactored version promptly to catch regressions early, rather than batching further changes on top of an unverified refactor.

episode.objective: Add TabM/ODST PyTorch tabular models with seed averaging into the ensemble and fix/tune them.
episode.lever: new TabM/ODST neural network ensemble members
episode.outcome: v29 regressed to 0.69547; v30 partially recovered to 0.69668 after refactoring/tuning, but below best 0.69702.

instance.goal: Can adding new diverse neural network architectures (TabM/ODST) to an existing GBDT+NN ensemble improve the blended submission score?
instance.context: The ensemble already blends CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, and a simpler NN, scoring 0.69702. Adding TabM/ODST models with seed averaging was expected to add diversity.
instance.action: Implemented TabM and ODST-style PyTorch tabular models with repeated-seed training/averaging in v29, but the score dropped to 0.69547. In v30, refactored model wrappers, fixed embedding/target handling, unified prediction keys, and tuned hyperparameters, recovering to 0.69668 — still below the prior best but much closer.

general.goal: When integrating a new model family into an existing ensemble, how much initial score regression should be expected and how can it be recovered?
general.context: A well-tuned ensemble of gradient-boosted trees and a neural network is already near its plateau. A large code addition introducing new neural architectures is likely to contain bugs or suboptimal defaults.
general.action: After the first integration causes a score drop, systematically fix data-flow issues (embedding dimensions, target handling, prediction key mismatches) and simplify/unify the wrapper code before re-tuning blend weights. Expect the first version to regress and budget a follow-up iteration for debugging and recovery.

instance.goal: Why did the large TabM/ODST addition hurt the score so much (0.69547 vs 0.69702), and where are the bugs?
instance.context: v29 added ~1.1k lines of new PyTorch modules, training loops, and blending logic all at once. The score dropped by 0.00155, suggesting integration errors rather than a fundamentally bad model.
instance.action: In v30, found and fixed issues: categorical embedding size variable was wrong (CAT_EMB_SIZE vs CAT_EMB_SIZE_C), prediction dictionary keys were inconsistent (e.g., 'TabM_Reg1' vs 'Reg1'), duplicate class predictions existed, and model wrapper naming was inconsistent. After these fixes the score recovered by 0.00121.

general.goal: When a large code addition causes an unexpected score regression, how should the debugging be prioritized?
general.context: A single commit introduced new model architectures, training loops, data pipelines, and ensemble integration simultaneously, making it hard to isolate the cause of the regression.
general.action: Focus first on data-flow correctness: verify that feature encodings (embedding dimensions, categorical mappings) match the new model's expectations, that prediction keys are consistent across training and inference, and that duplicate or misnamed outputs are eliminated. These mechanical bugs typically account for most of the regression and can be found by unifying naming conventions and tracing the prediction dictionary end-to-end.

episode.objective: Fix sign inversion bug in prediction pipeline to get correct leaderboard score.
episode.outcome: Bug fixed, score jumped to 0.69005 (v2). NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Why is the leaderboard score (~0.29) far below what the model should achieve for a concordance-index-based metric?
instance.context: The competition metric is a stratified concordance index (higher is better). A score near 0.29 suggests predictions are nearly anti-concordant, which is consistent with the sign of the risk score being inverted relative to what the metric expects.
instance.action: Negate the predicted risk scores (preds = -preds) before writing the submission CSV. The score jumped from ~0.29 to ~0.69, confirming the sign was inverted.

general.goal: Why is the ranking metric score far worse than expected, close to the complement of a good score?
general.context: When a concordance or ranking metric yields a score near (1 − expected), the most likely cause is that the predicted scores have the wrong sign convention (e.g., predicting survival time when the metric expects a hazard/risk score, or vice versa).
general.action: Negate the predictions and resubmit. If the score jumps to roughly (1 − old_score), the sign was inverted. Always verify whether the evaluation expects higher predictions to mean higher risk or longer survival, and align accordingly.

episode.objective: Improve reproducibility by adding explicit RNG seed control and deterministic flags.
episode.outcome: Seed infrastructure added; slight regression to 0.68967 (v3). v4 is noop.

instance.goal: Will enforcing full determinism (seeding numpy, random, torch, CUDA, cuDNN deterministic flags) improve or at least maintain the leaderboard score?
instance.context: The pipeline already scored 0.69005. It uses PyTorch with multiple training epochs and repeated prediction loops, so non-determinism from GPU operations and unseeded RNGs could cause variance across runs.
instance.action: Added a set_seed function seeding Python random, numpy, torch (CPU+CUDA) and setting cuDNN deterministic/benchmark flags. Called it with an incrementing global counter at the start of each epoch and each repeat loop. The LB dropped slightly from 0.69005 to 0.68967.

general.goal: Will forcing fully deterministic execution improve or preserve model quality on the public leaderboard?
general.context: A deep-learning pipeline with GPU training and multiple repeated inference passes has some run-to-run variance. The practitioner wants reproducibility before scaling up ensembling.
general.action: Seed all RNG sources (language-level, array library, framework CPU and GPU) and enable deterministic backend flags. Be aware this can slightly hurt performance: deterministic GPU kernels may be slower or change optimization trajectories, and locking seeds removes beneficial stochastic diversity in ensembles. Verify the score does not regress before building on top of it.

instance.goal: After adding seed control caused a small score drop, how can the lost performance be recovered while keeping reproducibility?
instance.context: Seeding reduced the score from 0.69005 to 0.68967. Hindsight shows the author next increased the number of ensemble repeats from 5 to 6, then further, recovering and exceeding the original score (0.69039, 0.69047).
instance.action: The author kept the deterministic seeding infrastructure but compensated by increasing the number of repeated runs (ensemble members), which restored and improved the score. The seed infrastructure made each repeat reproducible while more repeats reduced variance.

general.goal: How can a small accuracy loss from enforcing determinism be recovered?
general.context: Deterministic execution removed beneficial stochastic diversity that previously helped when averaging multiple runs, causing a slight score regression.
general.action: Increase the number of ensemble members or repeated runs. Deterministic seeds make each member reproducible, and adding more distinct-seed members restores the variance-reduction benefit that was partially lost by fixing randomness within each run.

episode.objective: Find optimal number of internal/external repeats and COLLAPSE hyperparameter for best ensemble score.
episode.outcome: Best at v7 (0.69078) with 10 repeats; v8-v9 regressed when adjusting COLLAPSE and repeats together.

instance.goal: How many repeated seeded runs (internal and external) give the best ensemble score before returns diminish or reverse?
instance.context: Starting from 5 repeats each (NREPEATS_INTERNAL, NREPEATS_EXTERNAL), the author incrementally tried 6, 7, 10, and 13. LB improved monotonically from 5→6→7→10 (0.69039→0.69047→0.69078) but dropped at 13 (0.69063) and further dropped when combined with a COLLAPSE change at 7 (0.69004).
instance.action: Sweep the number of multi-seed ensemble repeats upward one step at a time, submitting each. Stop increasing when the LB score drops compared to the previous best. The optimum here was 10 repeats; going to 13 hurt, likely due to overfitting noise or runtime-induced issues. Revert to the best-performing count.

general.goal: How many independent seeded reruns should be averaged to maximize ensemble quality on a noisy metric?
general.context: Averaging predictions from multiple random-seed reruns reduces variance and can improve leaderboard score, but beyond a point the gains plateau or reverse (possibly due to computational constraints, subtle overfitting, or metric noise).
general.action: Incrementally increase the number of seeded reruns, submitting after each increase. Track the metric at each step. Stop and revert to the previous count when the score drops for the first time, as the variance-reduction benefit has been exhausted.

instance.goal: Can changing the COLLAPSE hyperparameter (target-transform factor) together with reducing repeats recover or improve the score?
instance.context: After the repeat count of 13 already showed a slight drop (0.69063 vs 0.69078 at 10), the author changed COLLAPSE from 1.3 to 1.25 while also reducing repeats from 13 to 7. The result was a further drop to 0.69004, well below the best of 0.69078.
instance.action: Changing two hyperparameters simultaneously (COLLAPSE and repeat count) made it impossible to attribute the regression. The author later (v10) tuned COLLAPSE alone, recovering to 0.69054. Lesson: when sweeping, change only one variable at a time to isolate effects.

general.goal: When a hyperparameter sweep stalls, is it safe to change a second hyperparameter simultaneously to save time?
general.context: A sweep over one hyperparameter has found a tentative optimum. The practitioner wants to also adjust a second hyperparameter and considers changing both at once.
general.action: Avoid changing two hyperparameters in the same submission: if the score drops, the cause is ambiguous. Instead, fix the first hyperparameter at its best value and sweep the second independently. This costs more submissions but preserves attribution of gains and losses.

episode.objective: Tune COLLAPSE hyperparameter alone to recover from regression.
episode.outcome: COLLAPSE=1.35 improved to 0.69054 (v10), but still below v7 best.

instance.goal: After a regression caused by changing multiple settings at once (v8→v9), which single parameter change can recover performance?
instance.context: v9 scored 0.69004, a regression from v7's best of 0.69078. v9 had adjusted both the ensemble budget and the COLLAPSE target-transform factor simultaneously. The author needed to isolate which change hurt.
instance.action: Reverted to tuning only the COLLAPSE parameter (from 1.25 to 1.35), leaving other settings unchanged. This recovered to 0.69054, partially restoring the lost performance.

general.goal: After a score regression caused by changing multiple hyperparameters simultaneously, how can the harmful change be identified and reversed?
general.context: A previous edit modified two or more settings at once and the metric dropped, making it unclear which change was responsible for the regression.
general.action: Isolate each changed hyperparameter and adjust them one at a time. Start by reverting or re-tuning the parameter most likely to affect the target transform or loss landscape, keeping all other settings fixed, and submit to confirm which change caused the regression.

instance.goal: What is the right value for the COLLAPSE factor that controls the survival-target transformation?
instance.context: The COLLAPSE parameter had been changed from its earlier value to 1.25 in v9, which coincided with a score drop. The best prior score was 0.69078 (v7). The author suspected the COLLAPSE value was suboptimal.
instance.action: Increased COLLAPSE from 1.25 to 1.35 in a single-line change. The LB improved from 0.69004 to 0.69054, confirming the parameter matters but the optimal value was not yet found (still below v7's 0.69078).

general.goal: How sensitive is the score to a scalar factor applied during target transformation in a survival regression pipeline?
general.context: A scalar parameter controls how survival times or hazards are collapsed/scaled before being used as regression targets. Small changes to this factor have produced measurable leaderboard differences.
general.action: Probe the parameter in small increments (e.g., steps of ~0.1) with single-variable submissions. Track the leaderboard response to map the sensitivity curve and find the local optimum. If partial recovery is seen, continue probing in the improving direction.

episode.objective: Add TabM-mini MLP model with rtdl embeddings, warmup scheduler, and BCE loss to ensemble with existing ODST model.
episode.outcome: After bug fix in v12, score jumped to 0.69423. NEW BEST. v13 is noop verification.

instance.goal: The existing ODST model has plateaued around 0.690; where can further gain come from without just adding more repeat seeds?
instance.context: Increasing ensemble repeats from 5→8 yielded diminishing returns (0.69039→0.69078→0.69063), and tuning the COLLAPSE hyperparameter didn't help much (0.69054). A fundamentally different model architecture could add diversity.
instance.action: Added a TabM-mini MLP with rtdl piecewise-linear numeric embeddings, one-hot categorical handling, linear warmup + cosine LR schedule, and BCE loss. Ensembled its predictions with the existing ODST model. This jumped LB from 0.69054 to 0.69423.

general.goal: A single model type has plateaued and adding more seeds or tuning hyperparameters gives diminishing returns; how can the ensemble be strengthened?
general.context: Repeated runs of the same architecture converge to similar predictions, so averaging more of them adds little diversity. Hyperparameter tuning within the same model family also shows diminishing gains.
general.action: Introduce a structurally different model family (e.g., an MLP with learned feature embeddings alongside a tree-based or attention-based model). Ensure the new model uses compatible but distinct preprocessing (e.g., different categorical encoding, numeric embeddings). Blend its predictions with the existing model to gain diversity-driven improvement.

instance.goal: The new TabM model was added but the first submission attempt wasn't made; what could be wrong with the data pipeline for the new model?
instance.context: v11 added the TabM model but was not submitted (likely a runtime error). The numeric embedding bins were being computed from a variable (train_fold_1) that didn't exist or referred to the wrong data split.
instance.action: Fixed the variable name from train_fold_1 to train_1 in the rtdl_num_embeddings.compute_bins() call so bins are computed from the correct training split. This fix enabled a successful run and a large LB improvement to 0.69423.

general.goal: A newly added model component fails or produces poor results on the first attempt; how to diagnose the issue efficiently?
general.context: When integrating a new model that requires feature-specific preprocessing (e.g., computing discretization bins or normalization statistics), the preprocessing step must reference the correct data split variable. A variable name mismatch from copy-paste or refactoring can silently use wrong data or cause a runtime error.
general.action: After adding a new model component, verify that every data-dependent preprocessing step (bin computation, normalization, encoding) references the correct split variable. Check variable names at the boundary between the data pipeline and the new model before running the full training loop.

episode.objective: Increase repeat count from 5 to 7 to improve ensemble stability with new TabM model.
episode.outcome: Slight regression to 0.69390 (v14).

instance.goal: After adding a new TabM model that achieved a new best (0.69423), can increasing ensemble repeats from 5 to 7 further improve the score?
instance.context: Earlier history showed that increasing repeats from 5→6→7→8 on the ODST-only model gave diminishing and then negative returns (peaked at 7 repeats with 0.69078, dropped at 8). Now with a new TabM+ODST ensemble at 5 repeats scoring 0.69423.
instance.action: Increased NREPEATS_INTERNAL and NREPEATS_EXTERNAL from 5 to 7. Score dropped from 0.69423 to 0.69390, confirming that more repeats did not help after the model architecture change.

general.goal: After a significant model or architecture change yields a new best score, does the previously optimal ensemble repeat count still hold?
general.context: The optimal number of ensemble repeats was established for a prior model configuration. A new model component has been added, changing the variance-bias profile of predictions.
general.action: Re-probe the ensemble repeat count after major model changes, but expect that the optimal count may differ. If increasing repeats hurts on the leaderboard (as it did before at high counts), revert promptly rather than continuing to increase. The sweet spot depends on the model mix and may need to be re-discovered each time.

instance.goal: Is there a pattern to when adding more seeded repeats helps versus hurts on this competition's metric?
instance.context: Across the full history: 5→6 (+0.008), 6→7 (+0.031), 7→8 (−0.015), then after TabM addition 5→7 (−0.033). Gains from more repeats plateau and reverse, and the turning point shifted after adding a second model.
instance.action: The author tried increasing repeats multiple times. The pattern shows diminishing returns that eventually turn negative, and the inflection point is lower when the ensemble already contains diverse model types (which themselves reduce variance).

general.goal: How many repeated seeded runs should be averaged before the benefit of variance reduction is outweighed by other effects?
general.context: Averaging more seeds reduces prediction variance but can also wash out beneficial signal diversity. When the ensemble already combines heterogeneous model families, each individual family contributes less variance, so fewer repeats per family are needed.
general.action: Increase repeat count incrementally and monitor the leaderboard. Stop and revert as soon as the score drops. After adding a new diverse model to the ensemble, reset the repeat count to a lower baseline because the cross-model diversity already reduces variance, making additional same-model repeats less valuable.

episode.objective: Compute survival targets separately per race group to improve equity-aware metric.
episode.outcome: After fixing encoding bug in v16, achieved 0.69457. NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Can computing survival targets (Kaplan-Meier/Nelson-Aalen transforms) separately within each race group improve the equity-aware stratified concordance metric?
instance.context: The competition metric averages C-index per race group and penalizes variance across groups. Previously, targets were computed on the full dataset, meaning the survival baseline mixed all race groups together, potentially disadvantaging groups with different survival distributions.
instance.action: Created a make_target_by_race function that filters the training data by each race_group value, applies the survival target transform (make_target) within each subset, then concatenates results. This replaced the single global make_target call. Score improved from 0.69390 to 0.69457.

general.goal: Can stratifying the target construction by the grouping variable improve a fairness-aware metric that evaluates per-group performance?
general.context: When the evaluation metric averages a ranking metric across demographic groups and penalizes cross-group variance, a globally computed survival transform may bias groups whose baseline hazard differs from the population average.
general.action: Compute the target transformation (e.g., survival curve estimate or cumulative hazard) separately within each group defined by the fairness variable, then concatenate. This calibrates each group's targets to its own baseline, improving both per-group accuracy and cross-group equity.

instance.goal: Why did the initial per-race target construction not produce the expected improvement?
instance.context: After label-encoding categorical features, the race_group column contained integer codes (0–5) rather than original string values ('Asian', etc.). The first implementation filtered on string values, so no rows matched and the function silently failed or produced incorrect results.
instance.action: Replaced string-valued race group filters with the corresponding integer codes used after label encoding. This fixed the bug and the submission achieved a new best LB score of 0.69457.

general.goal: What can go wrong when filtering a dataframe by categorical values after the column has been encoded?
general.context: When categorical columns are label-encoded before a downstream step that filters by category, using the original string labels will silently match no rows (or wrong rows), producing incorrect results without raising an error.
general.action: After label encoding, always filter using the encoded integer codes rather than the original string labels. Verify the filter by checking that the number of matched rows per group equals the expected counts before proceeding.

episode.objective: Tune COLLAPSE hyperparameter to optimize score after race-stratified targets.
episode.outcome: Incremental gains: 0.69474 (v17), 0.69481 (v18). Both NEW BEST.

instance.goal: What is the optimal value of the COLLAPSE parameter for the race-stratified target transformation?
instance.context: After introducing race-stratified target creation (v15-v16) and achieving a new best LB of 0.69457, the COLLAPSE parameter was at 1.30. Earlier history showed COLLAPSE tuning (v9-v10) had meaningful impact on score.
instance.action: Incrementally increased COLLAPSE in small steps (1.30 → 1.325 → 1.35), submitting each to the leaderboard. Each step yielded a small improvement (+0.00016, then +0.00008), confirming the direction was beneficial. The diminishing gains suggest approaching the optimum.

general.goal: What is the best value of a continuous hyperparameter that controls target transformation after a major pipeline change?
general.context: A structural change to the pipeline (e.g., group-stratified target construction) has produced a new best score, but the existing hyperparameters were tuned for the old pipeline and may no longer be optimal.
general.action: Re-tune the hyperparameter by making small incremental changes in one direction, submitting each to the leaderboard. If consecutive steps both improve the score but with diminishing returns, continue until the gain becomes negligible or reverses, then stop near the last improving value.

episode.objective: Sharpen model sigmoid outputs by scaling logits to improve discrimination.
episode.lever: logit scaling factor in forward pass
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69540 (v19). NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Can the model's discrimination be improved by adjusting the sharpness of its sigmoid output without retraining?
instance.context: The model uses a sigmoid activation on its final logits to produce risk scores for a survival prediction task. The score had been incrementally improving through hyperparameter tuning (COLLAPSE) and ensembling, reaching LB 0.69481.
instance.action: Multiply the logits by a factor of 2 before applying sigmoid in the forward pass (i.e., sigmoid(2*x) instead of sigmoid(x)). This sharpens the output distribution, pushing predictions closer to 0 or 1. The change yielded +0.00059 improvement to LB 0.69540.

general.goal: Can prediction quality on a ranking metric be improved by rescaling the model's output without changing the learned weights?
general.context: A neural network produces scores through a bounded activation (e.g., sigmoid) and the evaluation metric is rank-based (concordance index). The sigmoid's default temperature may compress the score distribution, reducing separation between cases.
general.action: Apply a multiplicative temperature scaling factor (e.g., 2×) to the logits before the sigmoid activation at inference time. This stretches the score distribution and can improve rank discrimination. Treat the scaling factor as a tunable hyperparameter and validate on the leaderboard or a held-out set.

episode.objective: Increase repeat count to reduce variance after logit scaling improvement.
episode.outcome: Slight regression to 0.69534 (v20).

instance.goal: After achieving a new best score (0.69540) with logit scaling, can adding more ensemble repeats further stabilize and improve the result?
instance.context: Earlier in the notebook history (v5→v7), increasing repeats from 5→6→7 yielded steady improvements up to 0.69078, but going to 8 repeats (v7→v8) regressed. Now after a logit-scaling improvement, the author tries 5→6 repeats again.
instance.action: Incremented NREPEATS_INTERNAL and NREPEATS_EXTERNAL from 5 to 6. The LB score dropped slightly from 0.69540 to 0.69534, failing to improve.

general.goal: After a modeling change yields a new best score, will increasing the number of seed-averaged ensemble repeats consolidate or extend the gain?
general.context: The ensemble already uses enough repeats that variance reduction is near saturation. Historical evidence shows diminishing or negative returns from adding repeats beyond a moderate count.
general.action: Try a small increment in the repeat count. If the score does not improve (or slightly regresses), revert and invest effort in other levers such as architecture, optimizer, or loss changes instead of further repeat increases. Treat repeat-count tuning as a quick probe, not a reliable source of continued gains.

episode.objective: Experiment with optimizer choice (Lion vs QHAdam) and associated hyperparameters for classification head.
episode.outcome: Lion regressed to 0.69451 (v21); reverting to QHAdam with tuned HPs achieved 0.69568 (v22). NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Can switching from QHAdam to Lion optimizer improve the classification head's training and final ensemble score?
instance.context: The pipeline used QHAdam with cosine-warmup scheduling for the classification head, achieving LB 0.69534. The author wanted to explore whether a different optimizer (Lion) with MultiStepLR scheduling could do better.
instance.action: Switched to Lion optimizer with MultiStepLR scheduling, but LB dropped to 0.69451. Then reverted to QHAdam, adjusted classification hyperparameters (reduced epochs from 5→4, increased LR from 0.01→0.05, set batch size to 256), achieving LB 0.69568, a new best.

general.goal: Will a different optimizer improve training of a secondary model head in an ensemble pipeline?
general.context: The current optimizer and schedule produce a competitive score. A newer or trendier optimizer is available but untested on this task.
general.action: Try the alternative optimizer and note the leaderboard change. If it regresses, revert to the original optimizer but use the experiment as an opportunity to re-tune learning rate, epoch count, and batch size around the original optimizer. The act of experimenting often reveals that the original optimizer with refreshed hyperparameters outperforms both the old and new configurations.

instance.goal: After reverting an unsuccessful optimizer change, how should the restored optimizer's hyperparameters be adjusted to exceed the previous best?
instance.context: Lion with MultiStepLR hurt the score (0.69451 vs 0.69534). Reverting to QHAdam gave a chance to also revisit classification training settings (epochs, LR, batch size).
instance.action: Reduced classification epochs from 5 to 4, increased learning rate from 0.01 to 0.05 (5×), and explicitly set batch size to 256. This combination yielded 0.69568, surpassing the pre-experiment best of 0.69540.

general.goal: When reverting a failed change, how can the revert itself be turned into a net improvement?
general.context: A failed experiment (e.g., optimizer swap) forces a revert, but the surrounding hyperparameters were tuned for the old configuration and may not have been optimal.
general.action: When reverting, do not simply restore the old code verbatim. Instead, adjust two or three coupled hyperparameters (e.g., increase learning rate while reducing epoch count, or change batch size) so the reverted configuration is re-optimized. This often yields a score better than the pre-experiment baseline.

episode.objective: Remove training outliers to improve model robustness.
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69602 (v23). NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Can removing noisy or outlier training samples improve the concordance-index-based leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author had been iterating on ensemble size, hyperparameters, and model architecture, reaching LB 0.69568. A pre-computed outlier list (outliers_0.9.npy) was available, presumably identified via some threshold on predicted residuals or survival probabilities.
instance.action: Loaded a pre-computed list of outlier sample IDs and filtered them out of the training set (class 1 split) before model training. This yielded a small but consistent improvement to LB 0.69602.

general.goal: Can cleaning the training set of noisy or mislabeled examples improve a survival/ranking metric?
general.context: After extensive hyperparameter and architecture tuning has plateaued, the training data itself may contain samples that hurt generalization—especially in survival tasks where event labels or times can be noisy.
general.action: Pre-compute outlier scores (e.g., via out-of-fold residuals or prediction confidence thresholds) and remove the flagged samples from training. Use a held-out or public leaderboard score to verify the removal helps rather than hurts. Keep the threshold moderate to avoid discarding too much signal.

episode.objective: Tune number of repeats after outlier removal to find optimal ensemble size.
episode.outcome: 6 repeats regressed to 0.69581 (v24); reduced to 4 (v25, not submitted); v26 noop. No improvement over v23.

instance.goal: What is the optimal number of repeated seeded runs (ensemble size) after adding outlier removal, which changed the training data?
instance.context: After outlier removal (v23, LB 0.69602), the previous best repeat count was 5. Earlier history showed that increasing repeats from 5→6→7→8 had diminishing and sometimes negative returns (v5–v8), and after other changes 5 was again best (v19 vs v20). The author now re-sweeps repeats post-outlier-removal.
instance.action: Tried 6 repeats (v24, LB 0.69581, worse than 5's 0.69602), then tried 4 repeats (v25, not submitted but presumably checked locally). Concluded 5 repeats remained optimal and moved on to architectural changes in v27.

general.goal: How many repeated seeded runs should be averaged in the ensemble after a significant change to the training pipeline?
general.context: A pipeline change (e.g., data filtering) may shift the optimal ensemble size. Historical sweeps showed diminishing or negative returns beyond a moderate count, but the optimum could have moved.
general.action: Re-sweep the repeat count in both directions around the previous best (one step up, one step down). If neither direction improves the score, keep the previous value and move on to other levers rather than continuing to sweep further.

episode.objective: Replace/restructure model architecture to use TabM backbones and add ODST-based MLP to expand ensemble.
episode.lever: model architecture (TabM backbone swap, ODST-MLP addition)
episode.outcome: v27 regressed to 0.69385; v28 added ODST-MLP but not submitted. No improvement.

instance.goal: Can replacing the custom ODST+head architecture with TabM backbones for both regression and classification improve the ensemble score?
instance.context: The existing pipeline used a custom ODST tree-based neural network with a bespoke head. The best LB was 0.69602. The author had already successfully integrated TabM-mini MLP earlier (v11-v12) which boosted the score significantly.
instance.action: Replaced the custom ODST/head with two separate TabM Model backbone instances (TabM_R for regression, TabM_C for classification), adjusted optimizer parameter groups and prediction aggregation. This dropped LB from 0.69602 to 0.69385, a regression of ~0.002.

general.goal: Will swapping out a working model component for a different architecture improve the ensemble?
general.context: A multi-component ensemble has reached a strong score. One component uses a tree-based neural network with a custom head, and the author considers replacing it entirely with a different backbone architecture that worked well elsewhere in the pipeline.
general.action: When replacing a proven component wholesale with a new architecture, submit and check the leaderboard before building further on top.
