Expect the direct LB gain to be marginal; the main value is a cleaner, more reliable ensemble member that enables future gains when the ensemble selection is re-optimized.

instance.goal: What is the right way to integrate a neural network into a stacking ensemble alongside multiple GBDT pipelines for survival prediction?
instance.context: Multiple hist-gradient-boosting pipelines with different target transforms were already ensembled via AutoGluon with selected feature columns. The NN needed fold-aligned out-of-fold predictions to be a valid stacking input.
instance.action: Trained the NN with the same KFold splits, collected out-of-fold predictions per fold, saved fold models with joblib/torch, and added the NN prediction column to the ensemble's selected_features. The small LB improvement (+0.00003) suggests the NN's marginal contribution was limited but the infrastructure was now correct for future tuning.

general.goal: How should a heterogeneous model (e.g., a neural network) be added to a stacking ensemble of tree-based models so its predictions are valid for the meta-learner?
general.context: The stacking ensemble uses out-of-fold predictions from K-Fold CV as meta-features. A new model type must produce fold-aligned out-of-fold predictions to avoid leakage and be a valid ensemble member.
general.action: Use the identical K-Fold split indices for the new model as for existing members. Train one model per fold, generate out-of-fold predictions, and persist each fold's weights. Add the resulting prediction column to the meta-learner's input set. Verify the contribution is positive by checking whether ensemble selection retains the new column.

episode.objective: Speed up ranking post-processing with numba JIT and refine ensemble/component selection for race-aware concordance.
episode.lever: post-processing ranking logic and ensemble reorganization

instance.goal: Can a faster, JIT-compiled ranking/post-processing step improve the race-stratified concordance index beyond the current 0.69350?
instance.context: The ensemble pipeline already scored 0.69350 with multiple GBDTs and NNs. Post-processing of predicted risk scores (ranking, race-aware adjustments) was done in pure Python, which was slow and possibly suboptimal in how ties/ordering were handled.
instance.action: Replaced the pure-Python ranking logic with numba JIT-compiled binary-tree insert/rank routines, cleaned up unused imports (optuna, json, shutil) and removed old scoring blocks, and reorganized ensemble component selection. This yielded LB 0.69408 (+0.00058).

general.goal: Can optimizing the post-processing of predicted scores (ranking, calibration, or group-aware adjustments) yield metric gains beyond what model or ensemble changes provide?
general.context: When the evaluation metric depends on rank ordering within subgroups and the current post-processing is implemented naively, both correctness of tie-breaking and computational speed (enabling more iterations or finer adjustments) can be bottlenecks.
general.action: Rewrite the ranking/post-processing step with a JIT-compiled implementation (e.g., a binary-tree ranker) to make it exact and fast. This enables more thorough experimentation with rank transformations and group-aware adjustments, and can itself fix subtle ordering issues that hurt a rank-based metric.

instance.goal: Which ensemble components and code paths are actually contributing to the score, and which are dead weight?
instance.context: Over many versions, imports (optuna, json, shutil), old GBM model references, and a participant scoring block had accumulated but were no longer used. The ensemble selection had been toggled multiple times (v6-v8) showing sensitivity to which members are included.
instance.action: Removed unused imports and the old scoring block, reorganized the remaining model/post-processing code, and updated which components feed the ensemble. The cleanup coincided with a score improvement, suggesting either a subtle bug was fixed or the leaner pipeline allowed better component selection.

general.goal: How can accumulated dead code and unused pipeline components be identified and removed without risking regression?
general.context: After many iterative changes, notebooks accumulate unused imports, deprecated model references, and obsolete evaluation blocks that can mask bugs or interfere with resource usage.
general.action: Periodically audit and remove all unused imports, dead code blocks, and deprecated model paths in a single cleanup pass. Combine this with a submission to verify no regression. This often exposes subtle issues (e.g., stale variable references) whose fix yields a small but real gain.

episode.objective: Update ensemble members, data artifacts, and pretrained model paths to incorporate new model variants and improve blending.
episode.lever: ensemble member list and artifact paths
episode.outcome: v12 regressed to 0.69305; v11 and v13 not submitted. No improvement over v10's 0.69408.

instance.goal: Will expanding the ensemble member list with new model variants (ridge, elasticnet, exponential-rank, Nelson-Aalen targets) improve the stratified concordance index?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.69408. The author had new OOF predictions from additional model pipelines (different target transforms, regularization types, early stopping variants) available as artifacts.
instance.action: Expanded selected_features with many new prediction columns, switched OOF artifact folder from riza_04 to riza_05, and added exponential_rank non-FE variants for XGB/LGB/CB. The submitted version scored 0.69305, a regression of ~0.001 from the previous best.

general.goal: When many new candidate base-model predictions become available, how should they be incorporated into the stacking ensemble without hurting performance?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse base learners is already performing well. New base-model outputs trained with different target transformations and regularization methods are now available.
general.action: Add new members incrementally rather than in a single large batch. After each addition, check the validation metric. A large simultaneous expansion of ensemble inputs can introduce correlated or noisy members that degrade the meta-learner, as evidenced by a score drop when many columns are added at once.

instance.goal: How should artifact paths and model file references be managed when iterating on ensemble composition across multiple notebook versions?
instance.context: The author updated OOF paths (riza_04→riza_05), NN model paths (nn-models→cibmtr-pretrained-models), and removed stale path variables across three quick edits, but the submitted version regressed, suggesting possible misalignment between artifacts and code.
instance.action: Updated all artifact folder references and pretrained model paths in one pass, removed unused path variables to reduce confusion. The regression hints that path/artifact version mismatches or incompatible OOF predictions may have been introduced.

general.goal: How can one avoid silent errors when swapping in new pretrained model artifacts and out-of-fold prediction files during ensemble iteration?
general.context: Multiple external artifact directories supply OOF predictions and saved models. Changing one path without verifying consistency with the rest of the pipeline risks loading mismatched predictions.
general.action: When updating artifact paths, verify that column names, fold indices, and row counts of the new OOF files match what the ensembler expects. Remove or rename stale path variables immediately. Submit only after a local validation check confirms the new artifacts reproduce or improve the previous CV score.

episode.objective: Build initial ensemble infrastructure with KM survival transforms, external model imports, and feature engineering pipeline
episode.outcome: First submitted score 0.68865 at v3

instance.goal: How to build a competitive initial submission for a survival-prediction competition that requires both accuracy and fairness across subgroups?
instance.context: The competition uses a stratified concordance index (mean C-index per race group minus its std). Starting from scratch with ~28.8k patients and 57 features. External pretrained models and public notebooks are available on Kaggle.
instance.action: Built a full pipeline in one step: curated categorical/feature lists, added Kaplan-Meier survival-probability target transforms via lifelines, imported an external pretrained model (AbdBase) for blending, implemented a C-index scoring helper, and set up an ensemble infrastructure combining multiple model sources. This yielded LB 0.68865 on first submission.

general.goal: How to bootstrap a competitive first submission in a survival-prediction competition with a fairness-aware metric?
general.context: Starting from scratch in a competition where the metric rewards both predictive accuracy and equal performance across demographic subgroups, and where public pretrained models or shared solutions exist.
general.action: In the first version, assemble a complete pipeline that includes: (1) a non-parametric survival transform (e.g., Kaplan-Meier probabilities) as the regression target, (2) importing one or more external pretrained models for blending, (3) a local evaluation function matching the competition metric, and (4) an ensemble framework ready to accept additional models. This gives a strong baseline and infrastructure for iterative improvement.

instance.goal: What target transformation works well as a starting point for gradient-boosted tree regression in a survival analysis setting?
instance.context: The raw targets are event indicator (efs) and event time (efs_time). The metric is concordance index, which only requires correct ranking of risk scores. Lifelines library is available.
instance.action: Computed Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities as the transformed target for regression models. This converts the censored survival data into a continuous pseudo-target suitable for standard regression, preserving ranking information needed for the C-index.

general.goal: What target transformation converts censored survival data into a regression-friendly target that preserves risk ranking?
general.context: The evaluation metric is concordance-based (ranking metric), and the raw data includes censored event times and event indicators. Standard regression models (gradient-boosted trees) will be used.
general.action: Use a non-parametric survival estimator (e.g., Kaplan-Meier) to compute survival probabilities at each patient's event time, then use these probabilities as the regression target. This handles censoring naturally and produces a continuous target whose ranking aligns with the concordance metric.

episode.objective: Expand modeling options by adding survival-risk transforms, PyCox neural survival models, and deep tabular models into the ensemble
episode.outcome: Steady improvement to 0.69053 at v6, new best

instance.goal: Can adding neural survival models (CoxPH via pycox, deep tabular networks) to an existing GBDT-based ensemble improve the stratified concordance index?
instance.context: Starting ensemble of gradient-boosted models scored 0.68865. The competition metric rewards both accuracy and equity across race groups, suggesting diverse model families may help.
instance.action: Incrementally added: (1) survival-risk target transforms (KM, Nelson-Aalen, custom rank-based) as new label variants, gaining +0.00022; (2) a pycox CoxPH neural net with label encoding, median imputation, and scaling, gaining +0.00052; (3) deeper tabular models (categorical embeddings, AdamW, PyTorch Lightning infra) plus feature selection, gaining +0.00113. Each addition was submitted and confirmed to improve LB before proceeding.

general.goal: Can ensembling fundamentally different model families (tree-based and neural) improve a survival-prediction metric that rewards both accuracy and fairness?
general.context: An ensemble of tree-based models has plateaued on a survival prediction task with a composite metric (accuracy + equity across subgroups).
general.action: Add neural survival models (e.g., partial-likelihood-based deep networks with entity embeddings for categoricals) to the ensemble incrementally. For each addition, verify on the leaderboard or validation that the blended score improves before adding the next model family. Use standard preprocessing (label encoding, median imputation, scaling) tailored to neural inputs.

instance.goal: How can alternative survival-target transformations (beyond a single KM-based label) provide useful diversity for the ensemble?
instance.context: The initial pipeline used one Kaplan-Meier-based survival probability as the regression target. Multiple survival transforms (Nelson-Aalen, rank-based, neural-network-derived) could create complementary label variants.
instance.action: Implemented several survival-risk transforms (Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen, a custom rank-based transform) as separate label columns via get_tabm_features_02, trained models on each variant, and blended their predictions. This alone yielded a small but consistent LB gain (+0.00022).

general.goal: How much can target-encoding diversity (different transformations of the same survival outcome) contribute to ensemble performance?
general.context: A single target transformation is used for all base models in a survival-prediction ensemble. Different valid transformations of the censored outcome exist and could produce complementary predictions.
general.action: Create multiple regression targets from the same survival data using distinct statistical transforms of the censored outcome. Train separate base models on each target variant and blend their predictions. Even small per-model gains compound when the transforms are sufficiently decorrelated.

episode.objective: Tune ensemble composition by enabling/disabling members, adjusting weights, and updating dependencies
episode.outcome: Score dropped to 0.69043 at v11, slight regression from v6 best

instance.goal: Which subset of ensemble members and what blend weights maximize the stratified concordance index on the leaderboard?
instance.context: The author had reached LB 0.69053 with a large ensemble of XGBoost, CatBoost, LGBM, SVR, NN, TabNet, TabM, and TF-based models. They could toggle members on/off via commenting experiment paths and adjust model_weights entries.
instance.action: Over five versions, the author swept ensemble composition: first aggressively pruned most members (v7), then re-added one key member (v8), then re-enabled many members (v9), then submitted a version that excluded one NN experiment and included a TabM weight (v11). The final submitted blend scored 0.69043, slightly below the v6 baseline of 0.69053, indicating the particular exclusion/inclusion hurt slightly.

general.goal: How should ensemble members be selected and weighted to maximize a blended prediction's quality?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse model families has achieved a strong score, and the practitioner wants to know whether removing or re-weighting members can improve it further.
general.action: Toggle members on and off in small batches, submitting after each meaningful change, to isolate each member's marginal contribution. Start by disabling many members at once to find a strong core subset, then incrementally re-add members. If a configuration scores worse than the previous best, revert that change before trying the next. Keep changes small enough that regressions can be attributed to specific members.

instance.goal: Why did the ensemble composition sweep across v6–v11 fail to improve beyond the v6 best of 0.69053?
instance.context: The author made multiple toggling changes without submitting intermediate versions, so they could not isolate which inclusion/exclusion helped or hurt. The only submission (v11, LB 0.69043) was slightly worse. Hindsight shows v12–v13 found a bug in fold-level inference logic that, once fixed, recovered and exceeded the prior best.
instance.action: The episode demonstrates that when tuning ensemble composition, unsubmitted intermediate versions provide no feedback. The author should have submitted after each distinct configuration change (e.g., v7, v8, v9 separately) to get leaderboard signal on each. Additionally, a latent bug in the inference pipeline masked the true effect of composition changes, highlighting the need to verify the inference code is correct before sweeping blend weights.

general.goal: How can one efficiently get signal on which ensemble members help when each evaluation requires a submission?
general.context: Multiple configuration changes are made between submissions, making it impossible to attribute score changes to individual decisions. A bug in the prediction pipeline may also confound results.
general.action: Submit after each single, isolated change to the ensemble (one member added or removed, or one weight adjusted) so that the leaderboard delta can be attributed. Before sweeping composition, verify the end-to-end inference pipeline produces correct predictions (e.g., check shapes, fold alignment, and that all enabled members actually contribute to the output) to avoid confounding bugs.

episode.objective: Fix prediction-scope bug in fold-level inference (model.predict indentation) and retune blend weights
episode.outcome: Incremental improvements to 0.69067 at v14, new best

instance.goal: Why is the ensemble score not improving as expected when a TensorFlow-based model is included in the fold-level inference pipeline?
instance.context: The model.predict() call was either running unconditionally outside the fold==0 block (where features were computed) or was incorrectly scoped, causing predictions to be generated with wrong/stale data across folds. The author toggled the indentation back and forth across three versions (into fold==0, out of fold==0, back into fold==0), each time submitting to LB.
instance.action: Added a debug print statement to trace fold execution, then iteratively adjusted the indentation of model.predict() relative to the fold==0 conditional block, submitting each time to confirm which scoping was correct. The correct placement (inside fold==0) yielded the best score (0.69067), confirming the bug fix.

general.goal: Why does adding a model to an ensemble not yield the expected improvement during fold-level inference?
general.context: In a cross-fold inference loop, feature computation or data preparation may be gated by a conditional (e.g., only on the first fold), but the prediction call may accidentally sit outside that conditional, causing it to run on stale or undefined inputs for other folds.
general.action: Add logging inside the fold loop to verify which code paths execute per fold. Ensure the prediction call is scoped to the same block where its required inputs are prepared. Submit or validate after each scoping change to confirm the correct placement, since the error is silent (no crash, just wrong predictions).

instance.goal: After fixing the prediction-scope bug, can retuning ensemble blend weights extract additional gain?
instance.context: Between v12 and v13, the author both fixed the fold prediction scope and simultaneously reweighted many entries in the model_weights dictionary. The combined change improved LB from 0.69053 to 0.69066.
instance.action: After confirming the bug fix improved the score, the author retuned the numerical blend weights across all ensemble members in the same commit, achieving a +0.00013 improvement. The weight changes were applied to many members at once rather than one at a time.

general.goal: After correcting a bug in one ensemble member's inference, how much additional gain can come from re-optimizing the blend weights?
general.context: When a bug fix changes the quality or distribution of one member's predictions, the previously tuned blend weights are no longer optimal for the corrected ensemble.
general.action: After fixing an inference bug, retune all blend weights jointly rather than keeping old weights, since the corrected member's contribution has changed and the optimal allocation across all members shifts accordingly. Submit to verify the combined effect.

episode.objective: Test a pruned/simplified ensemble with fewer members and bypass blending loop
episode.outcome: Score dropped to 0.68867 at v16, abandoned

instance.goal: Is the full ensemble actually necessary, or could a smaller subset of models match or beat the current best score?
instance.context: The ensemble had grown to many members over successive versions, reaching LB 0.69067. The author wanted to test whether pruning to fewer members (leaving only one experiment with weight 0.02) could simplify without hurting.
instance.action: Commented out most model_weights entries, leaving only one active member. Submitted and observed LB dropped from 0.69067 to 0.69041, confirming the pruned ensemble was worse. Then further simplified by bypassing the blending loop entirely and using only the initial base predictions (ranked), which dropped to 0.68867. Both results confirmed the full ensemble was needed, so the author restored members in v17.

general.goal: Is the current multi-model ensemble over-engineered, or does each member contribute meaningfully to the final score?
general.context: An ensemble has been built incrementally over many iterations and the score has been climbing. It is unclear whether all members are necessary or some are redundant.
general.action: Ablate by disabling most ensemble members and submitting the reduced blend. If the score drops meaningfully, the removed members are contributing. Test progressively: first keep a small subset, then try a single base model alone. Use the magnitude of the drop to gauge each group's contribution. Restore the full ensemble once the probe confirms its value.

instance.goal: How much of the ensemble's performance comes from the blending/inference loop versus the initial base predictions?
instance.context: After pruning to one model (LB 0.69041), the author further tested bypassing the entire per-model inference loop and submitting only rankdata(initial_test_preds). This scored 0.68867, close to the v3 baseline before most ensemble work began.
instance.action: Commented out the blending loop and assigned submission predictions directly from the rank-transformed initial predictions. The large drop (0.69067 → 0.68867) confirmed that the blending loop and additional model predictions account for ~0.002 of the score, validating the ensemble infrastructure's importance.

general.goal: How much score improvement is attributable to the ensemble blending infrastructure versus the single strongest base prediction?
general.context: A complex inference pipeline blends multiple model outputs. It is unclear whether the pipeline's complexity is justified or the base prediction alone is nearly as good.
general.action: Submit the raw base prediction (rank-transformed) without any blending and compare to the full pipeline score. The gap quantifies the ensemble's marginal value. If the gap is large relative to recent incremental gains, the blending infrastructure is essential and should be kept and expanded rather than simplified.

episode.objective: Integrate additional pretrained NN experiment outputs with standardized imputation/scaling into the inference pipeline
episode.outcome: Score recovered to 0.69070 at v17, new best

instance.goal: How can the ensemble score be recovered and improved after a regression caused by pruning models from the blend?
instance.context: v14 achieved 0.69067 with a full ensemble. v15 pruned many models (0.69041) and v16 bypassed the blending loop entirely (0.68867), both regressing. The author needed to restore performance and go beyond the previous best.
instance.action: Restored the full inference/blending pipeline, re-enabled previously contributing models, and integrated a new pretrained neural network experiment (nn-exp-02) with proper imputation (KNNImputer) and scaling (StandardScaler) in the inference path. Added verbose logging to verify external model loading and predictions. This yielded 0.69070, a new best surpassing the pre-pruning score.

general.goal: How can ensemble performance be recovered and improved after a regression caused by removing ensemble members?
general.context: Ablation experiments that removed ensemble members caused a score drop, confirming those members contributed positively. Simply restoring the old configuration would only recover the old score, not improve it.
general.action: Restore all previously contributing members to recover the baseline, then simultaneously add a new diverse model (e.g., a pretrained neural network with different preprocessing) into the blend. This combines recovery with incremental improvement in a single step, and the net gain over the pre-pruning best confirms the new member's additive value.

instance.goal: What infrastructure is needed to reliably integrate an externally trained neural network's predictions into a multi-model ensemble at inference time?
instance.context: The nn-exp-02 model was trained externally and saved with joblib. The inference pipeline needed to apply the same imputation (KNNImputer) and scaling (StandardScaler) used during training, and the author had encountered bugs in prior versions where predictions were generated at the wrong scope.
instance.action: Added joblib import, instantiated matching KNNImputer and StandardScaler in the inference code, created a dedicated inference branch for nn-exp-02, and added extensive print/debug statements to verify the model loaded correctly and produced expected prediction shapes before blending.

general.goal: How should an externally trained model be integrated into an inference pipeline to ensure its predictions are correct and compatible with the ensemble?
general.context: An externally trained model requires the same preprocessing (imputation, scaling) it was trained with, and prior integration attempts had scope/logic bugs that silently produced wrong predictions.
general.action: Replicate the exact preprocessing pipeline (imputer, scaler) used during training, create a dedicated inference branch for the new model, and add verbose logging that prints input shapes, loaded model details, and output statistics. Verify these logs before trusting the blended result. This catches silent mismatches between training and inference preprocessing.

episode.objective: Add domain features (HCT-CI, HLA imputation, cat2num) and tune ensemble members/weights including tf-exp-01 toggling
episode.lever: feature engineering and tf-exp-01 ensemble toggling
episode.outcome: Score oscillated, ended at 0.68958 at v22, below v17 best

instance.goal: Will adding domain-specific engineered features (HCT-CI score, HLA imputation, categorical-to-numeric mappings) improve the ensemble's concordance index?
instance.context: The ensemble had reached LB 0.69070 using pretrained model outputs and basic features. The author added rich clinical domain features and new external model predictions (CatBoost/XGBoost experiments).
instance.action: Added HCT-CI comorbidity scoring, HLA imputation, and categorical-to-numeric mappings as new features, plus new external experiment predictions. The resulting score dropped to 0.68978, a significant regression from 0.69070. The new features were kept but did not help the ensemble.

general.goal: Will adding domain-engineered features to an already-strong ensemble of pretrained models improve the metric?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse pretrained models has reached a competitive score. New hand-crafted domain features are introduced alongside the existing blend.
general.action: Test the new features in isolation or with minimal ensemble changes first. If the score drops, the new features may be adding noise or conflicting with existing model outputs. Do not simultaneously change features and ensemble composition, as it confounds diagnosis of what helped or hurt.

instance.goal: Does toggling a specific ensemble member (tf-exp-01 with weight 0.03) in or out improve the blended score?
instance.context: After the feature engineering regression, the author toggled tf-exp-01 on (v20, LB 0.68959), off (v21, LB 0.68978), and on again (v22, LB 0.68958). The scores oscillated by ~0.0002 each time, consistently showing tf-exp-01 slightly hurts.
instance.action: Toggled tf-exp-01 on/off across three consecutive submissions. Each toggle produced a ~0.0002 change in the same direction, confirming the effect was real and reproducible. The author concluded tf-exp-01 should remain off (v21 was best at 0.68978 within this sub-episode).

general.goal: How can one reliably determine whether a single ensemble member with a small weight helps or hurts the blend?
general.context: A weighted ensemble is being tuned by toggling individual members on and off. Score differences are very small (on the order of noise).
general.action: Toggle the member on and off at least twice while keeping everything else fixed. If the score change is consistent in sign across toggles, the effect is likely real. If the magnitude is tiny and inconsistent, the member is near-neutral and can be dropped for simplicity. Avoid changing multiple members simultaneously.

instance.goal: Why did the new nn-exp-04 model's predictions degrade the ensemble score?
instance.context: After adding nn-exp-04 predictions, the score dropped. In v21 the author discovered that nn-exp-04 predictions needed sign negation (higher values meant lower risk, opposite to other models). Adding a special-case negation for nn-exp-04 recovered 0.0002 on LB.
instance.action: Added a conditional check: if the experiment is 'nn-exp-04', negate the test predictions before blending. This fixed the sign convention mismatch and improved the score from 0.68959 to 0.68978.

general.goal: What can go wrong when blending predictions from heterogeneous survival models that may use different output conventions?
general.context: Different survival models may output risk scores vs. survival probabilities, meaning higher values have opposite meanings. Blending them without alignment corrupts the ensemble.
general.action: Before blending, verify that all model outputs share the same monotonic direction with respect to the target. Compute rank correlations between each model's predictions and the others; if one is negatively correlated, negate its outputs. Add an explicit sign-correction step in the blending pipeline for any model whose convention differs.

episode.objective: Restructure blending pipeline: switch primary experiment, adjust weights, fix rank-transform post-processing
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69023 at v26 after fixing rankdata usage

instance.goal: Should the ensemble blend raw model predictions or rank-transformed predictions before combining, and when should the rank transform be applied?
instance.context: In v23, per-model predictions were rank-transformed before blending, scoring 0.68851. In v24, blending was changed to combine raw predictions and apply rank only at final submission, scoring 0.68964. In v25, rank was removed entirely (raw submission), scoring 0.68964. In v26, rank was restored at submission time, scoring 0.69023.
instance.action: Blend ensemble members using their raw (unranked) predictions, then apply rank transformation once at the very end when writing the submission. Do not rank individual model outputs before averaging, and do not submit raw scores without a final rank transform.

general.goal: At what stage in an ensemble pipeline should ordinal/rank normalization be applied when the evaluation metric depends only on prediction ordering?
general.context: When the evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., concordance index), both the combination method and the post-processing of the final predictions matter. Ranking each model's output before averaging can distort relative magnitudes that carry useful signal across models.
general.action: Combine ensemble members on their raw (or probability-scale) outputs to preserve relative magnitude information, then apply a single rank transformation to the final blended prediction before submission. Compare this against per-model ranking and no ranking to confirm the best approach.

instance.goal: Why did switching the primary experiment and reweighting the ensemble cause a large score drop?
instance.context: v22 scored 0.68958. In v23, the primary experiment path (first_best_index) was swapped and blend weights were changed, causing a drop to 0.68851. Subsequent steps (v24–v26) recovered by fixing the blending pipeline (raw blending + final rank) and correcting an accumulation bug, reaching 0.69023.
instance.action: When making multiple changes at once (switching base model, changing weights, changing post-processing), isolate each change. After the drop, the author systematically fixed the rank-transform pipeline and a variable accumulation bug across three submissions to recover and exceed the prior score.

general.goal: How to diagnose and recover from a score regression caused by simultaneous changes to an ensemble pipeline?
general.context: A score drop occurred after changing multiple aspects of the blending pipeline at once (base predictions, member weights, post-processing), making it unclear which change caused the regression.
general.action: Revert to a known-good configuration or, if that is impractical, fix one component per submission: first correct any accumulation or variable-naming bugs, then settle the post-processing (e.g., rank vs. raw), and finally tune weights. This isolates the source of regression and avoids compounding errors.

episode.objective: Switch base model to nn-exp-04 with rank-based blending and add lgbm-exp-05 to improve ensemble
episode.lever: base model swap and new LGBM member
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69133 at v28, new best

instance.goal: How can the ensemble score be improved when the current base/seed model (xgboost-exp-05) and raw-score blending have plateaued?
instance.context: The ensemble was using an XGBoost model as the seed/base and blending raw prediction scores. LB was 0.69023. The metric is concordance-based, meaning only the rank ordering of predictions matters, not their absolute values.
instance.action: Switched the base model from xgboost-exp-05 to nn-exp-04 (a neural network experiment) and changed the blending to rank-transform each model's predictions via rankdata before weighted aggregation. This yielded LB 0.69111 (+0.00088).

general.goal: How can ensemble blending be improved when the metric depends only on prediction ordering, not absolute values?
general.context: The evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., concordance index). Different ensemble members may produce predictions on different scales, so raw-score averaging can give disproportionate influence to members with larger variance.
general.action: Rank-transform each member's predictions before weighted averaging. This normalizes all members to the same scale and ensures the blend respects only ordinal information, which is what the metric evaluates. Also experiment with which model serves as the seed/base, since a stronger base can anchor the blend better.

instance.goal: Can adding another diverse model type (LGBM) and rebalancing weights further improve the rank-blended ensemble?
instance.context: After switching to rank-based blending with nn-exp-04 as base, LB was 0.69111. The ensemble already included XGBoost, CatBoost, and neural network models but no LightGBM member.
instance.action: Added lgbm-exp-05 to the inference pipeline with appropriate loading logic, rebalanced all member weights in the blend dictionary, and cleaned up dead code. This yielded LB 0.69133 (+0.00022), a new best.

general.goal: After establishing a strong blending strategy, where can incremental gains come from?
general.context: The ensemble already contains several model families and uses a well-calibrated blending method. Each additional member from the same family offers diminishing returns.
general.action: Add a member from a model family not yet represented in the ensemble (increasing diversity), then rebalance all member weights. Even a small-weight contribution from a diverse learner can improve a rank-based ensemble because it introduces uncorrelated ranking errors.

episode.objective: Add survival-derived targets, new feature pipelines, and tf-exp-01 member while fixing fold inference bug
episode.lever: feature pipelines and ensemble expansion with bug fix
episode.outcome: Incremental gains to 0.69146 at v31, new best

instance.goal: How much can adding survival-derived target transforms (Nelson-Aalen, Kaplan-Meier labels), richer feature pipelines, and new experiment-specific feature functions improve the ensemble?
instance.context: The ensemble was at LB 0.69133 after iterative weight tuning and model additions. The author had already used KM-based targets but hadn't systematically added Nelson-Aalen labels or experiment-specific feature engineering functions.
instance.action: Added get_tn_exp_02_features, get_vr_exp_01_features and similar per-experiment feature functions, categorical cleaning helpers (cyto_score, dri_score), a transform() computing naf_label and km_label from survival data, and standardized numeric features. This yielded LB 0.69139 (+0.00006).

general.goal: How much can enriching the feature set and adding survival-statistic-derived targets improve an ensemble for a concordance-based survival prediction task?
general.context: An ensemble of gradient-boosted and neural models has plateaued after weight tuning. Different member models may benefit from different feature representations and target transforms.
general.action: Create experiment-specific feature pipelines so each member model gets tailored features. Compute multiple survival-derived labels (e.g., cumulative hazard and survival probability transforms) as alternative regression targets. Standardize numeric features per-experiment. Expect small but consistent gains from better-aligned inputs.

instance.goal: Can re-enabling a previously disabled ensemble member (tf-exp-01 at weight 0.01) improve the blend after the feature pipeline changes?
instance.context: tf-exp-01 had been toggled on/off multiple times in earlier versions with mixed results (sometimes hurting LB). After v29's feature and target improvements, the ensemble context changed, potentially making tf-exp-01 complementary again.
instance.action: Uncommented tf-exp-01 with a very small weight (0.01) in the blend dictionary. LB improved from 0.69139 to 0.69145, confirming it now helped.

general.goal: When should a previously unhelpful ensemble member be re-tested for inclusion?
general.context: A model was removed from the blend because it hurt the score, but the ensemble composition and feature pipelines have since changed, altering the correlation structure among members.
general.action: After any substantial change to other ensemble members or their features, re-test previously excluded members at a small blend weight. A member that was harmful before may become complementary in the new context. Use a minimal weight to limit downside risk.

instance.goal: Why are fold-level predictions not being generated correctly for all folds during inference?
instance.context: The model.predict call was indented inside an 'if fold == 0' block, so predictions were only generated for the first fold. This same bug pattern had appeared and been fixed before (v13→v14), suggesting it recurred during code refactoring in v28→v29.
instance.action: Removed the extra indentation so model.predict runs for every fold. LB improved marginally from 0.69145 to 0.69146, confirming predictions were now correct across all folds.

general.goal: How can recurring bugs in fold-level inference loops be caught before they silently degrade predictions?
general.context: In a cross-validation inference pipeline, code refactoring can accidentally place the prediction call inside a conditional that restricts it to one fold. The resulting predictions may still produce a valid submission but with degraded quality, making the bug hard to detect.
general.action: After any refactor of the inference loop, verify that the prediction call executes for every fold by adding an assertion or log statement that counts predictions per fold. If the same bug pattern has appeared before, add a permanent guard (e.g., assert that the number of prediction batches equals the number of folds).

episode.objective: Add sklearn pipeline-based ensemble members (en-exp-02, dict-wrapped models) and custom PyTorch tabular NN with pairwise focal loss
episode.lever: new model types (sklearn pipeline, custom NN with focal loss)
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69296 at v33, new best; v34 fix was no-op

instance.goal: How much can the ensemble score improve by adding a structurally different model type (sklearn pipeline-wrapped dict models) alongside existing GBDT and NN members?
instance.context: The ensemble had reached LB 0.69146 with GBDT and neural survival models. Adding a new member type (en-exp-02, dict-wrapped models requiring sklearn pipeline with imputer) diversifies the blend.
instance.action: Added inference support for dict-wrapped models by constructing an sklearn pipeline (imputer + model) at inference time, included the new member in the blend with tuned weights, and also changed the seed/base model index. This yielded +0.00139 improvement to LB 0.69285.

general.goal: How much can an ensemble benefit from adding a structurally different model family to the blend?
general.context: An ensemble of similar model types (e.g., gradient-boosted trees plus one neural net) has plateaued, and the metric rewards both accuracy and fairness across subgroups.
general.action: Wrap the new model type in a compatible inference pipeline (e.g., adding imputation or scaling steps it needs) so it can produce predictions on the same test data, then include it in the rank-based blend with a small initial weight. Retune all blend weights after adding the new member.

instance.goal: Can a custom pairwise ranking loss (focal pairwise loss) for a tabular neural network improve concordance-based survival prediction beyond standard regression losses?
instance.context: The metric is a concordance index (ranking metric). Existing NN members used standard survival losses (CoxPH). A pairwise focal loss directly optimizes pair ordering, which aligns better with C-index.
instance.action: Implemented a PyTorch tabular NN with categorical embeddings, a FocalPairwiseLoss (pairwise ranking with focal weighting), and LR scheduling. Integrated it into the ensemble. Gained a small +0.00010 to LB 0.69296, confirming marginal but positive contribution.

general.goal: When the evaluation metric is a ranking metric, does training a neural network with a pairwise ranking loss yield better ensemble contributions than standard pointwise losses?
general.context: Existing ensemble members use pointwise or partial-likelihood losses. The evaluation metric is concordance-based, which measures pairwise ordering quality.
general.action: Implement a pairwise ranking loss (optionally with focal weighting to emphasize hard pairs) for a tabular neural network with categorical embeddings. Add it as a new ensemble member. Expect a small but positive marginal gain from the loss-metric alignment, mainly through diversity in the blend.

instance.goal: Why does the fold-level inference produce incorrect or missing predictions for some models?
instance.context: The model.predict call was outside the 'if fold == 0' block where FEATURES were computed, causing it to run with stale or undefined features. This same bug pattern had appeared and been fixed before (v13→v14, v30→v31).
instance.action: Indented the model.predict line by four spaces to place it inside the conditional block, ensuring features are generated before prediction. Score stayed at 0.69296 (no regression), confirming the fix was necessary for correctness.

general.goal: Why do recurring bugs keep appearing in the inference loop after adding new model types?
general.context: A notebook-based pipeline has a conditional block that generates features and then calls prediction. Each time new model handling code is added, the prediction call can accidentally end up outside the conditional scope.
general.action: After every code addition that modifies the inference loop, explicitly verify that the prediction call is inside the block where features are prepared. Consider extracting the feature-generation-then-predict pattern into a function to prevent scope/indentation errors from recurring.

episode.objective: Make imputation model-aware (fill -1 for RF experiments) to fix RF preprocessing
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69312 at v35, new best

instance.goal: Why might a random-forest-based experiment underperform or produce errors when the feature pipeline fills missing values with a strategy designed for gradient-boosted or neural models?
instance.context: The ensemble includes multiple model types (LGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, neural nets, and random forests). The shared feature-generation function used a single imputation strategy (e.g., NaN passthrough or median), but RF models in scikit-learn cannot handle NaN natively and need explicit fill values like -1.
instance.action: Pass the model_path into the feature-generation function and add a conditional branch: when the path indicates an RF experiment, fill NAs with -1 instead of the default strategy. This gave a +0.00016 LB improvement.

general.goal: How should missing-value imputation be handled when an ensemble contains model families with different native support for missing data?
general.context: Some model families (e.g., gradient-boosted trees) handle missing values natively, while others (e.g., random forests, linear models, neural nets) require explicit imputation. A shared feature pipeline that uses one strategy may silently degrade models that need a different treatment.
general.action: Make the feature-generation function model-aware by accepting a model identifier and branching on it: apply the imputation strategy each model family expects (e.g., sentinel value for tree models that lack native NaN support, median/mean for others). This ensures every ensemble member receives correctly preprocessed inputs.

episode.objective: Integrate nn-exp-06 and xgboost-exp-07 into the ensemble, fix sign-inversion and classifier+regressor post-processing bugs
episode.outcome: After severe regression (0.57664 at v37) and recovery, reached 0.69277 at v46; below v35 best

instance.goal: Why did the LB score drop catastrophically (0.69312 → 0.57664) after integrating nn-exp-06 into the ensemble?
instance.context: The nn-exp-06 neural net model was added to the inference pipeline. The score dropped by ~0.12, suggesting predictions had the wrong sign (higher risk scored as lower risk or vice versa).
instance.action: In v38, negated test_predictions (test_predictions = -test_predictions) for the nn-exp-06 branch, recovering the score to 0.69283. The author diagnosed the sign convention mismatch by adding debug prints and checking prediction distributions.

general.goal: Why does adding a new model to an ensemble cause a catastrophic score drop instead of a modest change?
general.context: When integrating a pretrained model whose output convention (sign, scale, or direction) is unknown, a sign or monotonic-direction mismatch can anti-correlate with the target, dragging the entire blend down dramatically.
general.action: Before blending, verify the new model's prediction direction by checking its standalone concordance or correlation with the target. If the metric is sign-sensitive (e.g., concordance index), negate or rank-transform the predictions and compare. Add debug prints of prediction statistics to catch the issue immediately.

instance.goal: How should the nn-exp-06 model's classifier and regressor outputs be combined for best ensemble contribution?
instance.context: nn-exp-06 produced both a binary classifier output and a continuous regression prediction. In v41, using only the negated regression output scored 0.69056. In v45, combining classifier+regressor (adding +0.2 where classifier==1) scored 0.69275, which was better than the raw combined approach in v38 (0.69283 → 0.68844 after adding more models) but the author iterated through multiple post-processing variants.
instance.action: Tested three post-processing variants: (1) combined classifier+regressor with stacking (v38), (2) raw negated regression only (v41), (3) classifier-boosted regression with a fixed offset (+0.2) for positive class (v45). Compared LB scores across variants and selected the classifier-boosted version. Also ensured that models not needing fold-averaging (like xgboost-exp-07) were excluded from the divide-by-folds step (v46).

general.goal: When a model produces both a classification head and a regression head, how should they be combined for a ranking metric?
general.context: A survival/ranking model outputs both a binary event classifier and a continuous risk score. Naively stacking both can hurt if the classifier is noisy, but ignoring it loses information about high-confidence event cases.
general.action: Test at least three strategies: (1) use only the continuous score, (2) stack both outputs as separate features, (3) add a fixed bonus to the continuous score for samples the classifier labels as positive. Compare on the leaderboard or validation. The fixed-bonus approach is simple and avoids overfitting a stacking layer.

instance.goal: Why did re-enabling all ensemble members after a successful single-model test (v41: 0.69056) cause the score to drop (v43: 0.68864)?
instance.context: In v41 a break statement limited inference to one model (nn-exp-06), scoring 0.69056. Removing the break in v42 and re-running in v43 scored 0.68864. The issue was that other models (xgboost-exp-09, lgbm-exp-08) had incorrect preprocessing or post-processing (e.g., wrong fold-averaging, missing feature prep).
instance.action: Fixed each model's preprocessing individually: added get_lgbm_exp_08() with proper NaN/category handling (v44, recovering to 0.69265), fixed xgboost-exp-07 fold-averaging bug (v46). Each model-specific fix was validated by checking the LB score incrementally.

general.goal: Why does an ensemble score worse than a single member even though each member is individually reasonable?
general.context: After enabling all ensemble members, the blended score drops below a single-model baseline. This typically indicates that one or more members have preprocessing or post-processing bugs (wrong averaging, missing imputation, incorrect feature encoding) that inject noise into the blend.
general.action: Isolate each member by running it solo or adding members one at a time. When a member degrades the blend, inspect its preprocessing pipeline (missing value handling, categorical encoding, fold-averaging logic) for mismatches with what the model expects. Fix each member's pipeline before re-enabling it in the ensemble.

episode.objective: Sweep ensemble blend weights and swap model checkpoints to find optimal combination
episode.outcome: Best was 0.69315 at v50; ended at 0.69235 at v53

instance.goal: Which combination of pretrained model checkpoints and blend weights yields the best stratified concordance index?
instance.context: The author had reached LB 0.69277 with a multi-model ensemble (CatBoost, XGBoost, LGBM, neural nets, TabM, etc.) and was sweeping blend weights and swapping checkpoint paths across 7 submissions. The best result in this sweep was 0.69315 (v50), but most perturbations degraded the score.
instance.action: Performed a manual grid/sweep: each submission changed the model_weights dictionary (adding/removing members, adjusting weights, swapping checkpoint versions) and sometimes changed the primary seed model. After finding a new best at v50, subsequent attempts to further improve by swapping nn-exp-04→nn-exp-06 or changing the base model to xgboost-exp-09 all scored lower, indicating the v50 configuration was a local optimum.

general.goal: How to efficiently find the best blend weights and member selection for a large ensemble of diverse pretrained models?
general.context: An ensemble of many heterogeneous models (tree-based, neural, etc.) is already performing well, and the practitioner wants to squeeze out marginal gains by adjusting which members are included and their relative weights.
general.action: Sweep one or two changes at a time (member inclusion, weight magnitude, or checkpoint version) and submit to evaluate. Record the best configuration. When multiple consecutive perturbations all degrade the score relative to the current best, stop the sweep and revert to the best-found configuration rather than continuing to explore. Avoid changing too many weights simultaneously, as it makes it hard to attribute gains or losses.

instance.goal: Does switching the primary/seed model used for initial inference (e.g., from CatBoost to XGBoost) improve the ensemble's leaderboard score?
instance.context: At v52 (LB 0.69271), the author changed first_best_index from a CatBoost checkpoint to an XGBoost checkpoint (v53), hoping the different base predictions would improve the blend. The score dropped to 0.69235.
instance.action: Swapped the base model that provides the initial fold-level predictions and simultaneously rebalanced blend weights. The result was worse, suggesting the original base model was better suited. The author did not pursue this direction further.

general.goal: When blending many models, does the choice of which model provides the base/seed predictions matter significantly?
general.context: The ensemble pipeline uses one model's fold-level predictions as a starting point, then blends in other models' predictions. Changing this seed model changes the correlation structure of the blend.
general.action: Test swapping the seed model independently from weight changes. If the swap degrades performance, revert it. The seed model's predictions anchor the blend, so a model with consistently strong per-subgroup performance is preferable as the seed, even if another model has a marginally higher overall score.

episode.objective: Integrate prlnn-exp-01 pretrained model as primary and re-enable tf-exp-01 in the blend
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69310 at v55

instance.goal: Can a newly trained pretrained neural network (prlnn-exp-01) improve the ensemble when used as the primary model instead of the current base?
instance.context: The ensemble had plateaued around 0.6924–0.6932 after many weight-tuning attempts. A new pretrained neural survival model (prlnn-exp-01) was available as a Kaggle dataset input, trained separately.
instance.action: Integrated prlnn-exp-01 as the primary/base model in the inference pipeline (loading checkpoints, feature preprocessing, forward pass), replacing the previous base. This yielded LB 0.69304, a +0.00069 improvement over v53.

general.goal: When ensemble weight tuning has plateaued, where can the next meaningful gain come from?
general.context: Reweighting existing ensemble members yields diminishing returns; the blend composition has been extensively searched.
general.action: Introduce a new, independently trained model (different architecture or training procedure) as an ensemble member or primary base. A genuinely diverse model adds orthogonal signal that weight tuning alone cannot recover.

instance.goal: Does re-enabling the small-weight TensorFlow model (tf-exp-01 at 0.03) help after changing the primary base model?
instance.context: tf-exp-01 had been toggled on/off many times in earlier versions with mixed results. After switching the primary model to prlnn-exp-01 (v54, LB 0.69304), the ensemble composition changed enough that previously marginal members might now contribute.
instance.action: Uncommented tf-exp-01 with weight 0.03 in the blend dictionary. LB improved slightly to 0.69310 (+0.00006), confirming a small positive contribution in the new ensemble context.

general.goal: After changing a major component of an ensemble, should previously unhelpful members be re-evaluated?
general.context: A model that was neutral or slightly harmful in a prior blend may become beneficial when the base or dominant member changes, because the correlation structure among members shifts.
general.action: After any significant change to the ensemble (new primary model, architecture swap), re-test previously excluded or marginal members one at a time with small weights. Accept them if the metric improves, even marginally.

episode.objective: Tune ensemble weights and include prlnn-exp-01 classifier in binary post-processing
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69317 at v57, new best

instance.goal: Can including a neural network classifier's binary predictions in the post-processing step (alongside existing classifiers) improve the ensemble's concordance index?
instance.context: The ensemble already used binary classifier outputs from some models to boost continuous survival predictions (e.g., +0.2 where classifier==1). A new pretrained model (prlnn-exp-01) had been integrated for regression but its classifier output was not yet used in the binary aggregation step. A prior weight-only rebalance (v55→v56) caused a tiny regression (-0.00004).
instance.action: Added 'prlnn-exp-01' to the condition that accumulates binary classification predictions into the ensemble post-processing, so its classifier output contributes to the binary boost rule. This recovered and exceeded the previous best, gaining +0.00010 to a new best of 0.69317.

general.goal: When a newly added model contributes only its regression output to the ensemble, can its auxiliary classification output also be leveraged to improve the blended prediction?
general.context: The ensemble post-processing applies a discrete bonus to the continuous risk score based on aggregated binary classifier predictions from multiple models. A new model has both regression and classification heads but only the regression head is currently used.
general.action: Include the new model's binary classification output in the aggregation that drives the discrete post-processing rule. This adds diversity to the binary vote without changing blend weights, and can recover small score losses from weight-only tuning.

instance.goal: After many rounds of weight tuning, is further rebalancing of ensemble blend weights still productive or has it plateaued?
instance.context: Scores had been oscillating in a narrow band (0.69235–0.69315) across many weight-tuning edits. The v55→v56 change only adjusted blend weights and produced a tiny regression of -0.00004, suggesting diminishing returns from weight changes alone.
instance.action: Rather than continuing to tweak weights, the author shifted to incorporating an unused signal (the classifier head of an existing model) in v56→v57, which yielded a new best (+0.00010). This indicates that when weight tuning stalls, adding a qualitatively different signal source is more productive.

general.goal: When repeated adjustments to ensemble member weights yield diminishing or negative returns, where should effort be redirected?
general.context: The ensemble score has been oscillating in a narrow band across several weight-tuning iterations, with the latest pure weight change producing a slight regression.
general.action: Stop pure weight tuning and instead look for unused outputs or auxiliary predictions from already-integrated models (e.g., a classification head, an intermediate representation) that can be incorporated as a new signal. This adds orthogonal information without requiring new model training and can break through the plateau.

episode.objective: Add ri-exp-06 and xgboost-exp-10 models with feature pipelines and retune ensemble weights
episode.outcome: Incremental gains to 0.69325 at v60, new best

instance.goal: Can adding another pretrained model (ri-exp-06) with its own feature pipeline improve the ensemble's stratified concordance index beyond 0.69317?
instance.context: The ensemble already contains many diverse models (LGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, neural nets, TF models) and the score has been incrementally improving. A new pretrained model artifact (ri-exp-06) is available as a Kaggle input dataset.
instance.action: Added ri-exp-06 to the input paths, created an inference conditional branch for it, added it to model_weights with a small weight, rebalanced existing weights, and added debug prints to inspect fold predictions. After verifying correctness (v58→v59 cleanup), submitted and gained +0.00007.

general.goal: Can incorporating one more diverse pretrained model into a large ensemble still yield measurable gains when the score has nearly plateaued?
general.context: An ensemble of many heterogeneous models is already near its plateau on a ranking metric, but a new pretrained model trained on the same data with a different algorithm or configuration is available.
general.action: Integrate the new model with a small blend weight, add any model-specific preprocessing as a dedicated feature pipeline branch, and use debug prints to verify predictions look reasonable before submitting. Even at plateau, a single new diverse member can yield small but consistent gains.

instance.goal: Does adding xgboost-exp-10 with a custom feature pipeline (sex_match_bool, factorize categoricals) and rebalancing weights push the score above 0.69324?
instance.context: After integrating ri-exp-06 the score reached 0.69324. Another xgboost experiment (exp-10) is available but requires its own preprocessing (specific NaN filling, boolean feature, factorized categoricals).
instance.action: Created add_features_xgboost_exp_10 and get_xgboost_exp_10_features functions with model-specific preprocessing, added an inference branch for xgboost-exp-10, inserted it into model_weights, and slightly adjusted other weights. Gained +0.00001 to 0.69325.

general.goal: When each model in the ensemble was trained with its own feature engineering, how should a new model's preprocessing be handled at inference time?
general.context: Different models in the ensemble expect different feature sets and encodings (e.g., one needs NaN filled with a sentinel, another needs factorized categoricals). Sharing a single preprocessing path causes errors or suboptimal predictions.
general.action: Create a dedicated feature-preparation function for each model that replicates the exact preprocessing used during that model's training (specific imputation, encoding, derived features). Route inference through the correct function based on model identity. This avoids cross-contamination of preprocessing assumptions across ensemble members.

episode.objective: Include SVR variant (svr-exp-06) in inference/ensemble with special feature prep and binary post-processing
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69354 at v62, new best

instance.goal: Can adding a different model type (SVR) to an already large ensemble of GBDTs and neural nets further improve the stratified concordance index?
instance.context: The ensemble already contained XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, neural nets, and random forest models at LB 0.69325. Adding model diversity through a support vector regressor variant with its own feature pipeline and binary post-processing was untested.
instance.action: Integrated svr-exp-06 into the inference pipeline with a dedicated feature-preparation function (get_exp_05_features), used predict_proba for its classifier output, included it in the binary thresholding post-processing list, and assigned it a blend weight. This yielded LB 0.69354, a new best.

general.goal: Can a fundamentally different model family still add value to an already diverse ensemble of tree-based and neural models?
general.context: An ensemble of multiple gradient-boosted tree variants and neural networks has plateaued, and all members share similar inductive biases despite different hyperparameters.
general.action: Add a model from a structurally different family (e.g., kernel-based) with its own feature preprocessing pipeline. Even if the standalone model is weaker, its uncorrelated errors can improve the blend. Assign it a small weight initially and verify the ensemble score improves before committing.

instance.goal: How should ensemble blend weights be adjusted when adding new members to avoid degrading the existing score?
instance.context: The author had ~15+ ensemble members with carefully tuned weights at LB 0.69325. Before adding svr-exp-06, they first rebalanced all existing weights in v61 (not submitted), then added the new model in v62 and submitted.
instance.action: Split the change into two steps: first rebalance/retune existing member weights without adding the new model (v61, not submitted), then add the new model with its pipeline and a small weight (v62, submitted). This two-step approach isolated the effect of the new model and achieved a new best of 0.69354.

general.goal: How can one safely integrate a new ensemble member without accidentally degrading the blend?
general.context: A large ensemble with many tuned weights is at risk of destabilization when a new member is added, because weight rebalancing and the new member's contribution are confounded.
general.action: Separate the change into two commits: first rebalance existing weights to a clean baseline, then add the new member with a small initial weight. Submit only after the second step so the incremental effect of the new model is observable. This isolates the contribution and reduces risk of regression.

episode.objective: Add lir-exp-01 pipeline model, retune ensemble weights, and clean up SVR binary post-processing
episode.outcome: Score regressed to 0.69329 at v63, recovered to 0.69348 at v66 on re-run

instance.goal: Will adding a new model type (lir-exp-01, a linear pipeline model) and retuning ensemble weights improve the blended concordance score beyond 0.69354?
instance.context: The ensemble already contained many diverse models (LGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, neural nets, SVR) at LB 0.69354. A new linear model was available as a saved sklearn pipeline artifact.
instance.action: Added lir-exp-01 with its own inference branch and retuned blend weights. Score dropped to 0.69329. Then cleaned up SVR binary post-processing and re-ran without code changes, recovering to 0.69348 — still below the prior best of 0.69354.

general.goal: When does adding another model family to a large ensemble stop helping?
general.context: An ensemble of many diverse model families already achieves a strong score. A simpler model type (e.g., a linear model) is available but may not add complementary signal when the ensemble is already rich.
general.action: Add the new model with a small blend weight and compare the leaderboard score. If the score drops or stays flat, the new member adds noise rather than diversity; remove it or keep its weight near zero. Diminishing returns from additional members are a sign to stop expanding the ensemble and focus on other levers.

instance.goal: Can cleaning up post-processing logic (including SVR in binary prediction aggregation, removing dead code) recover score lost from a bad weight change?
instance.context: After adding lir-exp-01 the score dropped from 0.69354 to 0.69329. The SVR model's binary predictions were not being included in the ensemble's binary post-processing step, and there was stale commented-out code.
instance.action: Fixed SVR inclusion in binary post-processing, removed obsolete special-case code, and re-ran. The score recovered to 0.69348, partially closing the gap — suggesting the post-processing fix helped but the weight retuning still hurt slightly.

general.goal: How much score can be recovered by fixing post-processing bugs versus reverting weight changes?
general.context: A score regression occurred after simultaneously adding a new ensemble member and changing weights. A known bug exists where one model's auxiliary predictions are excluded from a post-processing aggregation step.
general.action: Fix the post-processing bug first and re-evaluate before reverting the weight changes. If the fix partially recovers the score, the remaining gap is attributable to the weight change, which can then be reverted independently. Isolate changes to diagnose which modification caused the regression.

episode.objective: Introduce a PyTorch CNN-based survival model with channelized dataset adapter for ensemble inclusion
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.69358 at v67, new best

instance.goal: Can a CNN architecture applied to tabular survival data (with features arranged into channels) improve the ensemble beyond the current tree-based and MLP models?
instance.context: The ensemble already includes GBDTs (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), SVR, and various neural nets (TabM-style, custom MLP with pairwise ranking loss). LB score plateaued around 0.6935. The author hypothesized that a CNN treating feature groups as channels could capture local feature interactions differently.
instance.action: Built a PyTorch SurvivalRegressionCNN with channel-based input construction (grouping related features into channels with padding), NaN-safe preprocessing, careful weight initialization, and a DataLoader-compatible ChannelDataset. Integrated it into the existing ensemble pipeline. Achieved a small improvement to 0.69358.

general.goal: Can a fundamentally different model architecture extract complementary signal from the same tabular features to improve an already-strong ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of gradient-boosted trees and fully-connected neural networks has plateaued on a tabular prediction task. All current models treat features as flat vectors.
general.action: Introduce a convolutional model that reshapes flat tabular features into a multi-channel 1-D representation (grouping semantically related features into channels, with padding for unequal group sizes). Add NaN-safe preprocessing, stable weight initialization, and a dataset adapter compatible with the training loop. Blend its predictions into the existing ensemble with a small weight. Even a tiny concordance gain confirms the architecture captures complementary patterns.

instance.goal: How can numerical instability (NaN/Inf) in a new PyTorch survival model be prevented during training on clinical data with many missing values?
instance.context: The clinical dataset has extensive missingness and mixed feature types. Prior neural net experiments likely encountered NaN issues. The author added explicit NaN checks, warnings, and stable initialization to the CNN pipeline.
instance.action: Added NaN detection utilities that check inputs and outputs at each stage, replaced NaN values with safe defaults before channel construction, used careful weight initialization (e.g., Xavier/Kaiming), and inserted print/warning statements for numerical stability monitoring throughout the forward pass and training loop.

general.goal: How can training stability be ensured when adding a new neural network to a pipeline that processes data with heavy missingness?
general.context: A tabular dataset has many missing values and mixed types. A new neural network architecture is being integrated into an existing pipeline where simpler models handle missingness natively.
general.action: Add explicit NaN/Inf checks on both inputs and intermediate outputs at each pipeline stage. Replace missing values with a safe sentinel before feeding data to the network. Use stable weight initialization schemes. Insert runtime warnings that fire when any tensor contains non-finite values, so problems are caught immediately rather than silently corrupting predictions.

episode.objective: Establish initial baseline submission.
episode.outcome: Baseline score of 0.69332 at v2.

instance.goal: What is a reasonable baseline score for predicting post-HCT survival risk using the stratified concordance index metric?
instance.context: Starting from scratch on a survival prediction task with ~28.8k patients, 57 features, and a metric that rewards both accuracy and equity across race groups. No prior code or submissions exist.
instance.action: Built an initial pipeline (likely involving survival target transformation and GBDT/ensemble modeling) and submitted to establish a baseline LB score of 0.69332.

general.goal: What score range is achievable with a straightforward first approach on a new prediction task?
general.context: Starting a competition with no prior submissions; the metric and data characteristics are known but no empirical signal exists yet.
general.action: Build and submit a complete end-to-end pipeline as quickly as possible to establish a numeric baseline. This anchors all future experiments and reveals whether the task is easy or hard relative to the leaderboard distribution.

episode.objective: Optimize ensemble blend weights across three ranked models to maximize leaderboard score.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.69348 at v5; later weight changes did not beat it. Many versions not submitted. Final submitted score at v10 was 0.69319.

instance.goal: What blend weights across three ranked model submissions maximize the stratified concordance index on the leaderboard?
instance.context: Three ranked prediction files are available. The initial weights (0.25, 0.45, 0.30) scored 0.69332. The author has limited daily submissions, so a manual sweep is used rather than an automated grid search.
instance.action: Manually sweep blend weights across 10 versions, submitting 5 to the leaderboard. The best result (0.69348) came from weights (0.35, 0.50, 0.15), giving rank2 the dominant share. Moves that shifted weight away from rank1 toward rank3 hurt (0.69275). The author converged toward giving rank2 roughly half the weight and rank1 about a third.

general.goal: What combination weights for an ensemble of a small number of models maximize the evaluation metric?
general.context: A small number of base predictions are available and the metric is non-differentiable or only observable via leaderboard submissions, so analytical optimization is impractical.
general.action: Manually sweep weights in increments of roughly 0.05–0.15, submitting after each change. Start by swapping the weights of two models to gauge their relative strength, then shift weight toward the strongest contributor. Track which direction improves the score and make progressively smaller adjustments. Stop when further changes of ~0.05 no longer improve the score.

instance.goal: How sensitive is the leaderboard score to small changes in ensemble weights?
instance.context: Moving rank1 from 0.35→0.15 (and rank3 from 0.15→0.35) caused a drop of 0.00073, while moving rank1 from 0.30→0.35 (rank3 from 0.20→0.15) gained only 0.00005. The total range across all tried weights was about 0.00073.
instance.action: The author observed that large weight swings (±0.20) produced noticeable score changes, while small tweaks (±0.05) produced near-noise-level changes. This suggests the score surface is relatively flat near the optimum and further fine-tuning of weights alone offers diminishing returns.

general.goal: When does further tuning of ensemble blend weights stop being productive?
general.context: After several weight adjustments, the score differences between nearby weight configurations become comparable to leaderboard noise (order of a few ten-thousandths).
general.action: Compare the magnitude of score changes from recent small weight adjustments to the magnitude from earlier large adjustments. When small adjustments produce changes an order of magnitude smaller than the initial large swaps, treat the weights as approximately optimal and invest effort elsewhere.

episode.objective: Set up infrastructure (GPU/CPU toggling, dependencies, extra data) and get the notebook running correctly
episode.outcome: Notebook stabilized on CPU with no submission; v5 is a no-op checkpoint

instance.goal: How to get a multi-model notebook (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, neural net) running correctly in the Kaggle environment when GPU availability is uncertain?
instance.context: The notebook used GPU device flags for tree models and .cuda() calls for a neural network. Initial runs likely failed or were incompatible with the available Kaggle kernel (no GPU accelerator). The author toggled GPU on in v2, then back to CPU in v3–v4.
instance.action: First attempted enabling GPU across all models (v2). When that didn't work, switched all models back to CPU: commented out GPU/device parameters for gradient-boosted trees, removed .cuda() calls for the neural net, and disabled the Trainer's CUDA accelerator (v3–v4). Verified with a clean re-run (v5).

general.goal: How to resolve device-compatibility failures when a notebook trains multiple model types (tree-based and neural) on a shared compute environment?
general.context: A notebook references GPU acceleration for both gradient-boosted tree models and a neural network, but the execution environment may not have a GPU or the correct drivers.
general.action: Systematically disable GPU flags for every model family: comment out or remove device/task-type GPU parameters in tree models, remove explicit tensor .cuda() calls, and switch the deep-learning trainer's accelerator to CPU. Re-run the full notebook to confirm no remaining GPU references cause errors before proceeding to modeling work.

instance.goal: Which ensemble combination method — rank-averaging or weighted raw-score averaging — is more appropriate for combining survival risk predictions from multiple models?
instance.context: The initial code used rank-based averaging (scipy rankdata) to combine predictions. In v3 the author replaced this with a pd.merge-based weighted average of raw predictions, suggesting they wanted finer control over model contributions and possibly better calibration for the concordance-index metric.
instance.action: Replaced rank-averaging with a merge of raw prediction DataFrames and a weighted average using explicit per-model weights. This preserves the scale of individual model outputs, which matters when the evaluation metric (concordance index) only cares about ordering but downstream post-processing (mask adjustments seen in later versions) operates on raw scores.

general.goal: How should predictions from several models be combined when the metric is rank-based but post-processing adjustments will be applied to the raw scores?
general.context: Rank-averaging destroys magnitude information. If subsequent steps (e.g., group-specific additive corrections) modify the combined score arithmetically, they need meaningful raw values, not uniform ranks.
general.action: Use a weighted average of raw predictions instead of rank-averaging when any downstream post-processing step adds or scales the combined score. Assign explicit weights to each model and merge predictions on the sample identifier before averaging, so the resulting scores retain interpretable magnitudes for further tuning.

episode.objective: Tune the classifier-mask additive boost and switch ensemble from weighted average to rank average to improve score
episode.lever: classifier mask boost value and ensemble blending method
episode.outcome: First submission at v10 with LB 0.69330; mask boost settled at 0.25, rank-average ensemble adopted

instance.goal: What is the optimal additive boost to apply to pairwise-ranking predictions where a binary classifier mask indicates positive?
