instance.action: The author submitted the same unchanged notebook many times (v98–v106) and observed the score distribution. The variance (~0.024 range) was comparable to or larger than the effect of switching model checkpoints, meaning single-submission comparisons between configurations are unreliable.

general.goal: How reliable is a single leaderboard submission for comparing two configurations when the inference pipeline has stochastic elements?
general.context: When the pipeline includes non-deterministic operations (e.g., GPU floating-point non-determinism, data-loading order, or test-time augmentation), repeated identical submissions can produce meaningfully different scores.
general.action: Submit the same unchanged code multiple times (5–10 runs) to estimate the run-to-run variance. Only trust a configuration change as an improvement if its score difference exceeds this measured noise floor. Otherwise, average multiple submissions or enforce full determinism before drawing conclusions.

instance.goal: After achieving a strong multi-model ensemble score (0.313), is it worth reverting to a single model to understand individual checkpoint quality?
instance.context: The best score so far (v94, 0.313) used a 6-model ensemble (indices 0,4,8,12,16,20). The author then tested single models: model 0 scored ~0.323–0.347 across runs, model 4 scored ~0.328. Neither single model matched the ensemble. The author never recovered the 0.313 score in this episode.
instance.action: The author disabled the multi-model ensemble (v95) and toggled between model indices 0 and 4 (v95–v97). Both single-model scores were substantially worse than the ensemble. The episode confirmed the ensemble's value but consumed many submissions without improving the best score.

general.goal: After finding a strong ensemble configuration, is it productive to decompose it into single members to understand their individual contributions?
general.context: A multi-member ensemble has achieved the best score so far. The practitioner considers testing individual members to understand which are strongest, but each test costs a submission and the single-member scores are expected to be worse.
general.action: Avoid spending many submissions testing individual ensemble members after the ensemble is already validated. Instead, use held-out validation to assess member quality offline. If leaderboard submissions are limited or noisy, keep the best ensemble as the baseline and only test modifications that add to it rather than subtract from it.

episode.objective: Capitalize on improved upstream models via re-runs and add softmax post-processing and two-model ensemble to push score lower.
episode.lever: softmax postprocessing and ensemble composition (0 vs 0+4)
episode.outcome: Best score 0.28870 at v122 with model 0 and softmax applied.

instance.goal: Why does the leaderboard score keep improving across re-runs with zero code changes (e.g., v108→v109 dropped 0.013, v109→v110 dropped 0.014)?
instance.context: The inference notebook references upstream model checkpoints stored as Kaggle datasets. Repeated no-code re-runs produced large, consistent score improvements (0.32→0.30→0.29), suggesting the upstream training pipeline was still producing better checkpoints between re-runs.
instance.action: The author repeatedly re-ran the unchanged inference notebook to pick up improved upstream model artifacts, submitting each time to track whether the upstream training had produced better checkpoints. This continued until scores stabilized, confirming the upstream improvement had been captured.

general.goal: How can an inference-only notebook benefit from improvements happening in a separate training pipeline without code changes?
general.context: When the inference notebook loads model checkpoints from a mutable external source (e.g., a versioned dataset that the training pipeline updates), re-running inference with no code changes can yield different predictions if the upstream artifacts have been refreshed.
general.action: After updating the training pipeline, re-run the inference notebook multiple times and submit each time. Compare scores to confirm the new upstream checkpoints are being picked up. Continue re-running until scores stabilize, indicating no further upstream improvement is available.

instance.goal: Should model outputs be converted to probabilities before averaging across ensemble members, or should raw logits be averaged and then converted?
instance.context: In v112 the author added softmax (gezi.torch_softmax) as a final post-processing step after ensemble averaging. In v113 they moved softmax to right after each model's prediction, before adding to the ensembler, so that averaging happens in probability space. Scores were similar (~0.300-0.301) but the probability-space approach was kept.
instance.action: Applied softmax to each model's raw logits immediately after prediction, then averaged the resulting probabilities across models. Removed the duplicate softmax that had been applied after averaging. This became the default pipeline going forward.

general.goal: At what point in an ensemble pipeline should raw model outputs be converted to probabilities when the evaluation metric operates on probability distributions?
general.context: When the loss/metric is a divergence between predicted and target probability distributions (e.g., KL divergence), the order of softmax and averaging matters: averaging logits then applying softmax gives a different result than averaging probabilities.
general.action: Apply the softmax (or other normalization) to each individual model's output before averaging across ensemble members, so that the ensemble operates in probability space. Verify by comparing leaderboard or validation scores against the alternative order, and keep whichever is better.

general.action: Submit the same unchanged code several times and record the score range. Use that range as a noise floor: only treat configuration changes that produce improvements larger than this range as genuine. For changes within the noise floor, gather multiple submissions before concluding.

Use the mean or median across runs, not the best single run, to decide which configuration is truly superior. A more robust approach (visible from the broader history) would be to use the multi-fold ensemble that had a better expected score and submit it multiple times, selecting the best.

general.goal: When selecting a final submission from many re-runs, how can one avoid overfitting to public evaluation noise?
general.context: A configuration with lower expected error (e.g., a larger ensemble) may appear worse than a lucky single run of a simpler configuration. Selecting the minimum score across many re-runs of a noisier setup biases the estimate downward.
general.action: Prefer the configuration with the best average score across multiple runs rather than the one that produced the single best run. If forced to pick one submission, choose from the more robust (lower-variance) configuration even if its single best run is slightly worse, because it is more likely to generalize to the private evaluation set.

general.goal: Can replacing one ensemble member with a weaker but more diverse one improve the overall blend?
general.context: An ensemble of fold checkpoints is already performing well. Some available checkpoints score worse individually but may contribute different error patterns.
general.action: Swap individual members one at a time, replacing each with an alternative checkpoint, and submit to evaluate. A member that is individually weaker can still improve the ensemble if it is sufficiently diverse. Keep the swap only if the overall metric improves; otherwise revert.

episode.objective: Sweep individual model indices (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20) to find the best single checkpoint.
episode.outcome: Best single-model score 0.24449 at v199 with model 0; none beat ensemble.

instance.goal: Which individual fold checkpoint (0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20) performs best on its own, to inform future ensemble composition?
instance.context: The best score so far (0.23903) used a 4-model ensemble (indices 16,4,8,12). The author needed to know each checkpoint's standalone quality to decide which to include or exclude in future blends.
instance.action: Swept each checkpoint index one at a time (0→16→8→12→4→20→0) submitting each to the leaderboard. Scores ranged from 0.244 to 0.249. Model 0 was consistently among the best single models (~0.245–0.249), while no single model beat the earlier 4-model ensemble (0.239).

general.goal: How strong is each fold checkpoint individually, and which ones should be included in or excluded from an ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of several fold checkpoints has achieved the current best score, but it is unclear whether all members contribute positively or whether some hurt the blend.
general.action: Run a systematic single-checkpoint sweep: submit each fold checkpoint alone, record its standalone score, then rank them. Use these rankings to select the top-performing members for the final ensemble and drop weak ones. Expect that no single checkpoint will beat a well-chosen ensemble, but the sweep reveals which members are strongest.

instance.goal: Why do repeated submissions of the same single checkpoint (e.g., model 0) yield different leaderboard scores (0.244–0.249)?
instance.context: Model 0 was submitted at v193 (0.24498) and again at v199 (0.24449), with earlier history showing even larger variance for the same index across runs (e.g., 0.254–0.269 in earlier versions). This makes it hard to reliably rank checkpoints.
instance.action: The author implicitly acknowledged the noise by testing model 0 multiple times across the episode and broader history. The sweep still provided a rough ranking, but the variance (~0.005) meant fine distinctions between checkpoints were unreliable from single submissions.

general.goal: How reliable are leaderboard scores for comparing individual model variants when the test set is noisy or small?
general.context: Repeated identical submissions produce different scores, indicating non-trivial evaluation noise (from hidden test sampling, non-deterministic inference, or metric variance). Score differences between variants are on the same order as the noise.
general.action: When leaderboard noise is comparable to the gap between variants, submit the same configuration more than once to estimate variance before drawing conclusions. Treat score differences smaller than the observed noise as inconclusive, and prefer ensembles (which are more stable) over picking a single 'best' checkpoint based on one submission.

episode.objective: Re-run model 0 inference many times and disable fcwt-py install to verify score stability.
episode.outcome: Scores ranged 0.24559–0.25219; no improvement over ensemble best.

instance.goal: How much score variance comes from non-deterministic inference runs (e.g., GPU non-determinism, data loading order) rather than from actual model/config changes?
instance.context: Across v199–v210, the same code with model index 0 was re-run ~8 times with no code changes, yielding LB scores ranging from 0.24449 to 0.25075 — a spread of ~0.006. The best-ever score at episode start was 0.23903. The author also toggled between model indices 0 and 4.
instance.action: Re-ran the identical notebook many times (v199–v205, v207–v210) to observe the range of scores from pure run-to-run variance. This revealed ~0.006 spread, meaning small apparent improvements from checkpoint swaps could be noise. The author used this to gauge whether a single-run score difference is meaningful before committing to a configuration.

general.goal: How much of the observed leaderboard score fluctuation is due to non-deterministic inference rather than genuine configuration improvements?
general.context: When inference involves GPU floating-point non-determinism, random data-loading order, or test-time augmentation randomness, identical code can produce different scores across runs.
general.action: Re-run the exact same code and configuration multiple times (at least 5–8 runs) and record the score range. Use this measured variance as a noise floor: only treat a configuration change as a real improvement if its score gain exceeds the observed run-to-run spread. This prevents chasing noise when toggling hyperparameters or ensemble members.

instance.goal: Does removing the fcwt-py package install step affect inference results or just speed up the notebook?
instance.context: The notebook had shell commands copying and pip-installing a local fcwt-py package. The author commented these out at v203 to clean up. Subsequent runs (v203–v210) showed scores in the same noisy range as before, confirming the install was unnecessary for the active inference path.
instance.action: Commented out the dependency install commands and verified over multiple re-runs that scores remained in the same range, confirming the package was not used by the active inference code path and could be safely removed.

general.goal: How can unused dependency installations in an inference pipeline be safely identified and removed without risking score regression?
general.context: An inference notebook installs a package that may or may not be used by the active code path. Removing it would speed up execution but risks breaking inference if it is actually needed.
general.action: Comment out the install step and re-run inference multiple times. Compare the resulting score distribution against the known run-to-run variance from before the change. If scores stay within the established noise band, the dependency is confirmed unused and can be permanently removed.

episode.objective: Disable mixed-precision (AMP/FP16) during inference to improve numerical stability.
episode.outcome: Score worsened to 0.25970 at v211; idea abandoned.

instance.goal: Does disabling mixed-precision (AMP/FP16) during inference improve prediction quality for this EEG classification task?
instance.context: The author had been achieving scores around 0.24–0.25 with AMP/FP16 enabled during inference. They hypothesized that FP16 numerical precision might be degrading softmax probability outputs for the KL-divergence metric.
instance.action: Switched amp=True/fp16=True to amp=False/fp16=False in the inference call. The score worsened from ~0.25194 to 0.25970, so the author reverted in subsequent versions and went back to testing checkpoint combinations.

general.goal: Does reducing floating-point precision during inference hurt prediction quality when the evaluation metric is sensitive to probability calibration?
general.context: When the evaluation metric directly compares predicted probability distributions (e.g., KL divergence), small numerical errors from half-precision arithmetic could theoretically degrade scores. The model was already performing well with mixed precision enabled.
general.action: Test inference with mixed precision disabled (full FP32). If the score worsens or stays the same, keep mixed precision for its speed benefit. In this case the score got worse, indicating that the precision difference was not the bottleneck and the run-to-run variance or other factors dominated.

episode.objective: Sweep model indices (0 vs 4 vs 5) and fold count (4 vs 5 vs 6) to find optimal inference configuration.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.24408 at v218 with folds=6 and model 0.

instance.goal: Which combination of model checkpoint index (0, 4, 5) and fold count (4, 5, 6) yields the best leaderboard score for this inference ensemble?
instance.context: Prior best was 0.23903 with a multi-model ensemble. After disabling mixed-precision hurt the score (0.25970), the author reverted and began sweeping single-model indices and fold counts. Scores varied substantially across reruns even without code changes (e.g., 0.24487 vs 0.25074 for the same config), indicating high submission noise.
instance.action: Swept model indices [0, 4, 5] and fold counts [4, 5, 6] one at a time across 7 submissions. Best result in this episode was model 0 with 6 folds (0.24408), but no configuration clearly beat the pre-episode best. The high run-to-run variance (~0.005) made it hard to draw firm conclusions from single submissions.

general.goal: How can one reliably identify the best checkpoint/fold configuration when the evaluation metric has high submission-to-submission variance?
general.context: When identical code produces scores differing by ~0.005 across reruns (due to non-determinism in data loading, hardware numerics, or private/public split noise), single-submission comparisons between configurations are unreliable.
general.action: Submit each configuration multiple times and compare the mean or median score rather than a single observation. If submission budget is limited, prefer configurations that show consistently good scores across reruns over one-off bests. Recognize that differences smaller than the observed run-to-run variance are not meaningful.

instance.goal: Does increasing the number of cross-validation folds averaged at test time improve the KL-divergence score?
instance.context: The author had trained models across multiple folds. Going from 4 folds (model 0, LB 0.25121) to 5 folds (model 0, LB 0.24721) improved the score, and going from 5 folds to 6 folds (model 0, LB 0.24408) improved it further, though run-to-run noise complicates interpretation.
instance.action: Increased FLAGS.folds from 4→5 (v213→v214) and later from 5→6 (v217→v218). Each increase appeared to yield a modest improvement (~0.003–0.004), suggesting that averaging more fold predictions helps even when individual fold quality varies.

general.goal: Does averaging predictions from more cross-validation folds at test time improve a probabilistic classification metric?
general.context: Multiple fold checkpoints are available from training. The evaluation metric (a divergence between predicted and target distributions) rewards well-calibrated probability estimates, which benefit from reduced variance through averaging.
general.action: Incrementally increase the number of fold predictions averaged at inference and monitor the evaluation metric. Averaging more folds typically reduces prediction variance and improves calibration. Continue adding folds as long as the metric improves and inference time/memory permits.

episode.objective: Refactor inference loop to dynamically read num_models.txt, recreate dataset per model, and expand ensemble to models [0,1,2,3,4] with path fix.
episode.lever: inference loop refactor and ensemble expansion
episode.outcome: Best score 0.23868 at v222 with 5 models and path fix.

instance.goal: How can more checkpoint members be added to the ensemble without running out of GPU memory during inference?
instance.context: Expanding from models [0] to [0,1,2,3,4] would increase memory usage. Previous inference used batch size 64. The author needed to fit 5 model checkpoints into the inference pipeline.
instance.action: Halved the inference batch size from 64 to 32 when expanding the ensemble from 1 to 5 members, preventing OOM while allowing more checkpoints to contribute to the averaged predictions. This yielded a new best LB of 0.23868.

general.goal: How can more models be added to an inference-time ensemble without exceeding available memory?
general.context: Each additional model checkpoint loaded during inference increases peak memory. The inference batch size is a direct lever on memory consumption.
general.action: When expanding the number of ensemble members, proportionally reduce the inference batch size to keep peak memory within budget. Process one model at a time, accumulate predictions, and average at the end.

instance.goal: How can the inference loop be made flexible enough to automatically handle varying numbers of fold checkpoints without manual edits each time?
instance.context: The author had been manually toggling model indices and fold counts across dozens of versions (v145–v218), each time editing hardcoded lists. This was error-prone and slow.
instance.action: Refactored the inference loop to read num_models.txt from the checkpoint directory to dynamically determine how many folds to iterate over, iterate over root/{fold} paths, and recreate the test dataset inside each model loop. Then expanded models to [0,1,2,3,4] and fixed path.txt lookups to use root instead of model_dir. The resulting flexible loop achieved a new best score of 0.23868 and enabled easy further expansion (v222→v224 added models 6–10).

general.goal: How should an inference pipeline be structured so that adding or removing ensemble members does not require repeated manual code edits?
general.context: Manually editing hardcoded model indices and fold counts for each submission attempt is slow and error-prone, especially when searching over many ensemble compositions.
general.action: Store the number of checkpoints in a metadata file alongside the saved weights. Have the inference loop read that file to determine iteration bounds, construct paths programmatically per fold/model, and recreate any data pipeline inside the loop if each model requires different preprocessing. This makes expanding the ensemble a one-line config change rather than a code refactor.

episode.objective: Progressively add more model checkpoints (6-9, 10, 11-23) to the ensemble to improve blended predictions.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.23565 at v228 with 24 models.

instance.goal: How many model checkpoints should be averaged in the ensemble to minimize KL divergence on the leaderboard?
instance.context: Starting from 5 checkpoints (models 0-4) at LB 0.23868, the author had access to ~24 trained fold/checkpoint variants. Adding members monotonically improved score: 5→0.23868, 9→0.23650, 10→0.23642, 20→0.23622, 24→0.23565. Intermediate tests with single models (index 11 or 12 alone) scored much worse (~0.24469–0.24618).
instance.action: Progressively added checkpoint indices to the ensemble list (first 6-9, then 10, then 11-19, then 20-23), submitting after each addition. Each time the score improved, the new members were kept. When a single-model ablation scored worse, the author reverted to the full ensemble and continued expanding. Stopped at 24 members when all available checkpoints were included.

general.goal: How many independently trained checkpoints should be averaged at inference to maximize ensemble benefit?
general.context: Multiple fold or seed checkpoints of the same architecture are available. The evaluation metric rewards well-calibrated probability distributions (e.g., KL divergence). Individual checkpoints vary in quality but their errors are partially uncorrelated.
general.action: Add checkpoints to the ensemble incrementally, submitting after each addition. Keep adding as long as the metric improves. Verify with single-model ablations that the ensemble is indeed better than any individual member. Continue until all available checkpoints are included or gains plateau.

instance.goal: Are individual new checkpoints (models 11, 12) strong enough to contribute to the ensemble, or do they hurt?
instance.context: After reaching LB 0.23642 with 10 models, the author tested model 12 alone (LB 0.24469) and model 11 alone (LB 0.24618). Both were substantially worse than the 10-model ensemble, confirming that individual members are weaker but may still contribute when blended.
instance.action: Tested single-model inference for candidate ensemble members (v225, v226). Both scored worse than the full ensemble, so the author included them in the larger blend (v227) rather than using them standalone. The resulting 20-model ensemble (0.23622) beat the previous 10-model best (0.23642), confirming the new members added value through averaging even though they were individually weaker.

general.goal: When a candidate checkpoint scores poorly on its own, can it still improve an ensemble?
general.context: A checkpoint tested in isolation scores noticeably worse than the current best ensemble. The question is whether to discard it or include it in the blend.
general.action: Do not reject a checkpoint solely because its standalone score is worse than the ensemble. Include it in the blend and evaluate the combined score. Weak individual members often reduce ensemble variance and improve the averaged prediction, especially for metrics sensitive to calibration.

episode.objective: Test single model 0 inference (revert to 1 model) and deal with unstable re-runs including a catastrophic 1.948 score.
episode.outcome: Scores ranged 0.24029–1.94830; single model much worse than ensemble.

instance.goal: How much score does a single model (model 0) lose compared to the full ensemble of ~11 checkpoints that achieved 0.23565?
instance.context: The best ensemble (v228) scored 0.23565 using many model indices. The author switched to models=[0] only to test single-model performance.
instance.action: Replaced the multi-model list with a single model index [0]. The single model scored 0.31671, confirming the ensemble of ~11 checkpoints was far superior (~0.08 better). The author later reverted to the full ensemble.

general.goal: How much does each component contribute to an ensemble's advantage over a single member?
general.context: A multi-checkpoint ensemble has reached a new best score and the practitioner wants to verify the ensemble gain is real before adding complexity.
general.action: Temporarily replace the ensemble with a single member and submit. Compare the single-member score to the ensemble score. If the gap is large (here ~0.08 on a 0.23 baseline), the ensemble is clearly beneficial and should be kept or expanded.

instance.goal: Why do identical re-runs of the same inference notebook produce wildly different leaderboard scores (0.30–1.95)?
instance.context: Versions 229–235 had zero code changes yet scores varied from 0.24029 to 1.94830. The pipeline likely includes randomized on-the-fly EEG preprocessing or non-deterministic GPU operations, and one run (v233) catastrophically failed with 1.948.
instance.action: The author re-ran the same code multiple times (v229–v235), observed the catastrophic 1.948 outlier, and continued re-running until obtaining a reasonable score (0.24029 at v235). This confirmed the pipeline had significant run-to-run variance and that outlier submissions should be discarded rather than debugged as code errors.

general.goal: How should one interpret large score fluctuations across identical re-runs of an inference pipeline?
general.context: The inference pipeline includes randomized data augmentation or non-deterministic operations (e.g., on-the-fly signal processing, GPU non-determinism), and repeated identical submissions yield very different scores, including occasional catastrophic outliers.
general.action: Re-run the identical pipeline several times and collect the distribution of scores. Treat extreme outliers (scores orders of magnitude worse) as runtime failures rather than model issues. Use the median or best of multiple identical runs as the true estimate, and consider fixing random seeds or disabling test-time augmentation randomness to stabilize results.

episode.objective: Try model indices 1 and then [0,1] to find the best small ensemble composition.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.23496 at v237 with models [0,1].

general.goal: Which single checkpoint among several trained folds or variants gives the best standalone prediction quality?
general.context: Multiple checkpoints are available from different folds or training runs, and their individual quality on the public leaderboard is unknown.
general.action: Evaluate each checkpoint individually by submitting its solo predictions. Identify the strongest single checkpoint before building ensembles, so the ensemble is anchored on the best member.

instance.goal: Does adding the previously-used model 0 to the already-strong model 1 improve the ensemble beyond model 1 alone?
instance.context: Model 1 alone scored 0.23560 (new best). Model 0 alone had scored 0.24029. Combining them could reduce variance if they are complementary.
instance.action: Changed models list from [1] to [0,1], averaging both checkpoints' predictions. The ensemble scored 0.23496, a further improvement over model 1 alone, confirming the pair is complementary.

general.goal: Does averaging a weaker checkpoint into the current best single checkpoint improve or hurt the ensemble?
general.context: The best single checkpoint has been identified. A second checkpoint scores worse alone but may contribute complementary information.
general.action: Add the weaker checkpoint to the ensemble and submit. If the combined score improves, keep it; if not, drop it. Even a checkpoint that is individually weaker can reduce ensemble error when its mistakes are uncorrelated with the stronger member's.

episode.objective: Verify single model 0 vs ensemble via many re-runs, then expand to 6 models [0-5] with hack_count tuning.
episode.outcome: Score 0.22970 at v252 pending; re-runs showed 0.23546–0.24155.

instance.goal: How much run-to-run variance exists in the inference pipeline's public leaderboard score when no code is changed?
instance.context: The author had achieved a best score of 0.23496 with models [0,1]. They then ran the identical notebook (model 0 only) approximately 10 times without code changes, observing LB scores ranging from 0.23546 to 0.24155 — a spread of ~0.006.
instance.action: Re-ran the identical inference notebook many times (v238–v250) and collected the resulting LB scores to estimate the noise floor. This revealed ~0.006 variance, meaning small score differences between configurations are unreliable and only larger improvements (well above 0.006) should be trusted.

general.goal: How much score variation comes from non-deterministic inference (random augmentation, data loading order, floating-point non-determinism) rather than from actual model/ensemble changes?
general.context: When the inference pipeline includes stochastic elements (e.g., on-the-fly data augmentation, non-deterministic GPU operations), the public leaderboard score can fluctuate between identical runs.
general.action: Before drawing conclusions from small score changes, re-run the exact same code multiple times and measure the spread of scores. Use this spread as a noise floor: only trust configuration changes whose improvement exceeds the observed run-to-run variance by a clear margin.

instance.goal: After confirming single-model variance, what ensemble size and configuration should be used for the final submission?
instance.context: Earlier history showed that expanding from 1 model to many (e.g., models 0–10) steadily improved scores from ~0.245 to ~0.235. The author confirmed via repeated runs that a single model (index 0) averages around 0.237. In v251 they expanded to models [0,1,2,3,4,5] and reduced hack_count from 2700 to 270, and the subsequent version (v252) with full inference achieved 0.22970, confirming the larger ensemble helps.
instance.action: After establishing the noise floor with repeated single-model runs, expanded the ensemble from 1 to 6 models and adjusted the batch/processing count to fit within runtime constraints. The post-episode result (0.22970 → 0.22659 with 20 models) confirmed that more ensemble members continued to help.

general.goal: How many independently trained checkpoints should be averaged at inference time to maximize score improvement within compute constraints?
general.context: Historical submissions show a monotonic trend: adding more diverse fold/seed checkpoints to the ensemble improves the metric, but each additional model costs inference time and memory. A noise floor has been established so real gains can be distinguished from variance.
general.action: Incrementally add checkpoints to the ensemble, submitting after each addition. When the improvement from adding one more member falls within the noise floor, stop. If runtime is the binding constraint, reduce per-sample processing cost (e.g., smaller batch counts or fewer augmentation passes) to fit more models within the time budget.

episode.objective: Expand ensemble from 6 to 20-22 models with tuned per-model weights to maximize final submission score.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.22608 at v255 with 20 models and tuned weights; v256 added 2 more models (0.22622).

instance.goal: How many model checkpoints should be included in the ensemble to minimize KL divergence on the leaderboard?
instance.context: Starting from 6 models (v251), the author progressively expanded to 20 then 22 models. Each addition yielded diminishing but consistent improvements: 6→20 models gave -0.00311, 20→22 gave -0.00019.
instance.action: Incrementally added model checkpoints to the ensemble (6→20→22), submitting after each expansion. Gains diminished but remained positive up to 22 models, confirming more members helped. The author stopped expanding at 22.

general.goal: How many independently trained checkpoints should be averaged in an ensemble to maximize prediction quality?
general.context: When each additional checkpoint still improves the public metric, even by a small margin, and inference time/memory permits more members.
general.action: Add checkpoints incrementally, submitting after each addition. Track the marginal improvement per added member. Continue adding until the marginal gain becomes negligible or turns negative, then stop at the best count.

instance.goal: Can non-uniform per-model weights improve the ensemble beyond simple averaging?
instance.context: A 22-model uniform-weight ensemble scored 0.22640. The author tried replacing uniform weights with tuned per-model weights (likely optimized offline on validation data).
instance.action: Reduced to 20 models with explicit per-model weights, achieving 0.22608 (new best). Then tried 22 models with a different weight vector, which scored 0.22622 (slightly worse). The 20-model weighted version was best, suggesting weight tuning helps but adding weaker members with suboptimal weights can hurt.

general.goal: After building a large uniform-weight ensemble, can assigning different weights to each member improve the combined prediction?
general.context: A uniform-average ensemble of many checkpoints has plateaued. Some members may be stronger or more diverse than others.
general.action: Optimize per-member weights on a held-out validation set (e.g., via constrained optimization of the target metric). Compare the weighted blend against uniform averaging. If adding extra members with tuned weights does not beat a smaller weighted subset, prefer the smaller set—extra members with poorly calibrated weights can degrade performance.

episode.objective: Establish baseline inference with EfficientNet spectrogram model
episode.outcome: New best 0.46256 at v2

instance.goal: Which pretrained EfficientNet spectrogram checkpoint yields the best baseline KL-divergence score on the leaderboard?
instance.context: The author has an inference notebook and multiple saved model checkpoint directories from different training runs (e.g., 'baseline_experiment' vs 'efficientnetv2_spectrogram'). No prior submission score exists yet.
instance.action: Swapped the model checkpoint directory from 'baseline_experiment' to 'efficientnetv2_spectrogram' and submitted, achieving LB 0.46256. This establishes a first baseline by probing which available checkpoint performs best.

general.goal: Which of several available pretrained checkpoints gives the strongest starting point for a submission?
general.context: Multiple model checkpoints from different training configurations exist, and no leaderboard score has been established yet. The inference pipeline is already written and only needs the checkpoint path changed.
general.action: Swap the checkpoint path to each candidate and submit to the leaderboard to identify the best-performing one before investing in further improvements. Start with the checkpoint expected to be strongest based on training setup (e.g., a more specialized architecture or longer training).

episode.objective: Try smaller EfficientNetV2-Tiny backbone with bug fixes and TTA toggling
episode.outcome: Score regressed to 0.51388 at v6; abandoned

instance.goal: Will switching from a larger EfficientNet backbone to a smaller EfficientNetV2-Tiny backbone improve or hurt the leaderboard score?
instance.context: The previous EfficientNet spectrogram model scored 0.46256. The author swapped to an EfficientNetV2-Tiny checkpoint directory (v1.1), expecting a potentially better or comparable result.
instance.action: Pointed inference to the new smaller-backbone checkpoint. The score degraded substantially to 0.51664. Subsequent versions (v1.2, v1.3 checkpoints, visible in hindsight) were needed to recover, suggesting the v1.1 checkpoints were undertrained or misconfigured. The author continued iterating on the same backbone rather than reverting immediately.

general.goal: When replacing a proven backbone with a smaller variant, how much regression in score should be expected before the new variant's training is fully tuned?
general.context: A well-tuned larger model already has a strong baseline score. Switching to a smaller model with early-stage checkpoints may initially regress.
general.action: After swapping to the smaller backbone, if the score regresses significantly, do not immediately abandon the variant. Instead, iterate on checkpoint quality (retrain or use later training snapshots) and inference settings before concluding the variant is inferior. Track whether successive checkpoint versions close the gap.

instance.goal: How should test-time augmentation (flip-based TTA) be configured when using a new, not-yet-validated backbone to avoid hurting the score?
instance.context: After switching to EfficientNetV2-Tiny, the author found a file-path bug (spectrogram_id cast to int) and disabled two of the flip-based TTA variants. Enabling TTA later (v5→v6) gave only a marginal 0.00276 improvement, and hindsight shows the best score (0.45957) came with TTA enabled but on better checkpoints (v1.3).
instance.action: First fix data-loading bugs (e.g., filename type casting) and disable TTA to get a clean baseline with the new model. Then toggle TTA on and measure the delta. If the gain is small or negative, the issue is likely checkpoint quality rather than TTA configuration. Only combine TTA with well-trained checkpoints.

general.goal: When debugging a new model variant that underperforms, how should test-time augmentation be handled relative to other fixes?
general.context: Multiple potential issues exist simultaneously: data-loading bugs, undertrained checkpoints, and TTA configuration. Changing everything at once makes it impossible to attribute score changes.
general.action: First fix any data-loading or preprocessing bugs and disable test-time augmentation to establish a clean single-pass baseline. Only after confirming the baseline is reasonable, toggle augmentation on and measure its isolated effect. If the gain is negligible, focus effort on improving the model weights rather than augmentation strategy.

episode.objective: Sweep EfficientNetV2-Tiny checkpoint versions (v1.2–v1.7) and TTA on/off to find best combination
episode.outcome: Best 0.45957 at v8 (v1.3+TTA); later versions regressed

instance.goal: Which of several trained checkpoint versions (v1.2–v1.7) yields the best leaderboard score for the EfficientNetV2-Tiny spectrogram model?
instance.context: The author had regressed from LB 0.46256 (v1.1 checkpoints) to 0.51+ after switching to a different checkpoint. They systematically swept checkpoint versions v1.2 through v1.7, submitting each to the leaderboard.
instance.action: Tested each checkpoint version sequentially on the leaderboard. v1.3 with TTA gave the best score (0.45957). Later versions (v1.4–v1.7) all scored worse (0.466–0.487), confirming v1.3 as the best checkpoint. The sweep was exhaustive across available versions.

general.goal: Which version of retrained/fine-tuned model weights performs best when multiple training runs or training stages have produced different checkpoints?
general.context: When multiple checkpoint versions exist from iterative training experiments and there is no reliable offline validation to distinguish them, each must be evaluated on the held-out test metric.
general.action: Sweep all available checkpoint versions by submitting each to the leaderboard (or evaluating on a trusted validation set). Record every score. Do not assume newer checkpoints are better—performance can be non-monotonic across training iterations. Select the version with the best metric.

instance.goal: Does flip-based test-time augmentation help or hurt the EfficientNetV2-Tiny spectrogram predictions on this EEG classification task?
instance.context: TTA was toggled on/off across multiple checkpoint versions. With v1.3: TTA on gave 0.45957 (best), TTA off was not tested alone. With v1.7: TTA off gave 0.48671, TTA on gave 0.47129 (better). The effect of TTA was consistently positive but interacted with checkpoint quality.
instance.action: For each promising checkpoint, tested both TTA on and TTA off, comparing leaderboard scores. TTA improved scores in both cases where the comparison was possible (v1.2 no-TTA 0.498 vs v1.3 with-TTA 0.460; v1.7 no-TTA 0.487 vs v1.7 with-TTA 0.471). Kept TTA enabled for the best configuration.

general.goal: Does test-time augmentation improve predictions for a spectrogram-based image classification model, and does its benefit depend on which checkpoint is used?
general.context: Test-time augmentation (e.g., flipping inputs) can reduce variance but may also introduce noise if the augmentations are not semantically valid. Its benefit can vary across model checkpoints.
general.action: For each candidate checkpoint, evaluate with and without test-time augmentation. Do not assume the TTA effect is constant across checkpoints—always test the combination. When the metric consistently improves with TTA across checkpoints, keep it enabled in the final submission.

episode.objective: Add channel transform and per-class probability multipliers to post-processing
episode.outcome: Score 0.46329 at v14, slight regression from v8 best

instance.goal: Can post-hoc per-class probability rescaling improve the KL-divergence score of the spectrogram model ensemble?
instance.context: The best LB so far was 0.45957 (v8). The current submission (v13) scores 0.47129. The author suspects the predicted class distribution is miscalibrated relative to the expert vote distribution.
instance.action: Added per-class multipliers to scale individual class prediction columns of the spectrogram model output, then renormalized rows to sum to 1. Also refactored the channel dimension handling into a proper transform. The result (0.46329) improved over v13 but did not beat the best v8 score.

general.goal: Can the gap between predicted and target class distributions be closed by adjusting predictions after the model has produced them?
general.context: A classification model's output probabilities are evaluated with a divergence metric that penalizes distributional mismatch. The model may systematically over- or under-predict certain classes.
general.action: Apply per-class multiplicative scaling factors to the predicted probabilities, then renormalize each sample's predictions to sum to 1. Choose the factors by estimating the ratio of true class frequencies (or vote shares) to predicted class frequencies on a validation set. Submit and compare against the uncalibrated baseline.

episode.objective: Sweep checkpoint versions v1.8–v1.10 with TTA and per-class multiplier tuning
episode.outcome: No improvement over v8 best; v21 at 0.48815

instance.goal: Which combination of checkpoint version, TTA on/off, and per-class multipliers yields the best KL-divergence score?
instance.context: The best LB so far was 0.45957 (v1.3 checkpoints + TTA). The author has been iterating through checkpoint versions (v1.7–v1.10), toggling TTA, and adjusting per-class multipliers, but none of v1.8–v1.10 beat the earlier best. All submitted versions in this episode (0.47356–0.48815) regressed.
instance.action: Systematically swept checkpoint versions v1.8→v1.10, toggling TTA on/off for each, and adjusting/removing per-class multipliers (GPD 1.25→1.5, LRDA 1.5→1.75, commenting out seizure/other). Each combination was submitted to the leaderboard. None improved, so the author later reverted to a newer checkpoint (v1.11) without multipliers (v22, LB 0.46118).

general.goal: How to efficiently search over multiple interacting inference-time knobs (model checkpoint, test-time augmentation, post-hoc class reweighting) when each submission is costly?
general.context: Several discrete choices interact: which trained checkpoint to use, whether to apply test-time augmentation, and how to reweight per-class probabilities. The search space is small but combinatorial, and each evaluation requires a leaderboard submission.
general.action: Change only one knob at a time (checkpoint version, TTA toggle, or class multipliers) so each submission isolates one effect. When a new checkpoint is introduced, first test it without post-hoc adjustments to get a clean baseline, then layer on TTA and multipliers. If several consecutive changes all regress, revert to the last-known-best configuration before continuing.

instance.goal: Do per-class multiplicative adjustments to predicted probabilities improve KL-divergence on this EEG classification task?
instance.context: In v14 the author introduced per-class multipliers (e.g., GPD ×1.25, LRDA ×1.5) followed by row normalization. Across this episode, commenting them out (v17: 0.47356) was slightly better than having them (v21: 0.48815), and the post-episode v22 that disabled multipliers scored 0.46118 vs v23 with multipliers at 0.46547.
instance.action: Tried multipliers at several magnitudes (GPD 1.25→1.5, LRDA 1.5→1.75) and also fully disabled them. Every time multipliers were active the score was worse than the corresponding no-multiplier variant. The author eventually dropped them in v22, confirming they hurt.

general.goal: Does manually rescaling per-class predicted probabilities before normalization help when the evaluation metric is a divergence between predicted and target distributions?
general.context: The metric penalizes miscalibrated probability distributions (e.g., KL divergence). A well-trained model's class probabilities may already be near-optimal, so post-hoc reweighting can introduce systematic bias that worsens the score.
general.action: Test per-class multipliers by enabling and disabling them as a single controlled change. If the metric worsens or is inconsistent across checkpoint versions, the multipliers are likely adding noise rather than correcting a real bias—remove them and rely on the model's calibrated outputs.

episode.objective: Sweep checkpoint versions v1.11–v1.13 while toggling class multipliers on/off
episode.outcome: New best 0.45926 at v25 (v1.13)

instance.goal: When iterating over new model checkpoint versions, do manual per-class probability multipliers help or hurt the score?
instance.context: Earlier versions (v14, v20, v21) applied per-class multipliers to reweight predictions before normalization, with mixed results. The author now has checkpoint v1.11 available and wants to isolate whether the multipliers or the checkpoint quality drives score changes.
instance.action: For each new checkpoint version, first submit without per-class multipliers (v22: 0.46118, v24: 0.46551, v25: 0.45926), then try re-enabling them (v23: 0.46547). The multipliers consistently hurt or didn't help compared to the raw checkpoint output, so the author kept them disabled for the best-scoring submission.

general.goal: When sweeping model checkpoints, how can one tell whether a post-processing calibration step is still beneficial or has become harmful?
general.context: Post-processing adjustments (e.g., per-class scaling of predicted probabilities) were tuned for an earlier checkpoint and may not transfer well to newer checkpoints whose output distribution has shifted.
general.action: For each new checkpoint, submit once with and once without the post-processing adjustment. If the adjustment consistently fails to improve or worsens the score across multiple checkpoint versions, disable it permanently and let the model's own calibration stand.

instance.goal: Across a sequence of retrained checkpoint versions (v1.10 through v1.13), which one yields the best leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author has been iterating on training and producing new checkpoint versions. Not every newer version is better (v1.10: 0.483, v1.11: 0.461, v1.12: 0.465, v1.13: 0.459). The only reliable signal is the public leaderboard score.
instance.action: Systematically submit each checkpoint version with a consistent inference setup (no multipliers, same preprocessing). Keep the version that achieves the best LB score (v1.13 at 0.45926). The sweep is cheap—only the directory path changes—so every version is tested.

general.goal: How should one efficiently identify the best-performing checkpoint when multiple retrained versions are available?
general.context: Retraining produces a sequence of checkpoint versions, but newer does not always mean better due to differences in training randomness, hyperparameters, or overfitting.
general.action: Hold all other inference settings constant (no post-processing tweaks, same augmentation) and submit each checkpoint version in turn. This isolates the checkpoint effect. Keep the best-scoring version and use it as the baseline for further experiments.

episode.objective: Try EfficientNet-B0 backbone variant instead of V2-Tiny
episode.outcome: Regressed to 0.47345 at v26; abandoned

instance.goal: Would switching from EfficientNetV2-Tiny to EfficientNet-B0 as the backbone improve the spectrogram classification score?
instance.context: The best LB score so far (0.45926) was achieved with EfficientNetV2-Tiny v1.13 checkpoints. A fresh set of EfficientNet-B0 v1.0 checkpoints was available to try.
instance.action: Swapped the checkpoint directory from efficientnetv2tiny_spectrogram_v1.13 to efficientnetb0_spectrogram_v1.0. The score worsened from 0.45926 to 0.47345, so the author reverted to the V2-Tiny family in the next version.

general.goal: When the current backbone variant has plateaued after many checkpoint iterations, could a different backbone variant from the same model family yield a better score?
general.context: One backbone variant has been iteratively refined through many checkpoint versions and reached a strong score. An alternative variant (different size or architecture generation within the same family) is available but only at an early checkpoint iteration.
general.action: Test the alternative backbone variant on the leaderboard. Compare its first-iteration score against the mature variant's best score. If the early-iteration alternative already underperforms the mature variant significantly, return to the mature variant and continue refining it rather than investing in the new one. Do not abandon a well-tuned variant for an untested one without evidence.

episode.objective: Try EfficientNetV2-Tiny with channel-wise instance normalization preprocessing
episode.outcome: New best 0.45265 at v27

instance.goal: How can spectrogram preprocessing be improved to better match what the model expects and reduce prediction error?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.45926 with EfficientNetV2-Tiny checkpoints (v1.13). Switching to EfficientNet-B0 hurt (0.47345). The author had tried various preprocessing (log1p, clip+log, center-crop+resize) with mixed results, suggesting preprocessing-model alignment matters.
instance.action: Switched back to EfficientNetV2-Tiny checkpoints and replaced the spectrogram transform pipeline with channel-wise instance normalization (normalizing each channel independently with an epsilon parameter), achieving a new best LB of 0.45265.

general.goal: How can input normalization be adjusted to improve predictions from a pretrained image backbone on spectrogram-like inputs?
general.context: Global normalization or simple log transforms have been tried but scores plateau or regress. Spectrograms have channels with very different intensity distributions.
general.action: Apply channel-wise instance normalization (zero-mean, unit-variance per channel per sample) instead of global transforms. This aligns each channel's distribution independently, which better suits multi-channel spectrograms where channels have heterogeneous scales.

instance.goal: Which backbone variant and checkpoint version should be used when multiple options have been tried with varying results?
instance.context: The author tested many checkpoint versions (v1.1–v1.13) and two backbone variants (EfficientNetV2-Tiny vs EfficientNet-B0). EfficientNet-B0 scored 0.47345 while the best EfficientNetV2-Tiny scored 0.45926. Reverting to the better backbone family and pairing it with improved preprocessing yielded 0.45265.
instance.action: Returned to the backbone variant that had historically performed best (EfficientNetV2-Tiny) rather than persisting with the worse-performing alternative, and combined it with a new preprocessing change to achieve a compound improvement.

general.goal: When a backbone switch degrades performance, how should the search continue?
general.context: A new backbone variant was tried and scored worse than the incumbent. Meanwhile, a preprocessing improvement idea is available to test.
general.action: Revert to the better-performing backbone and apply the new preprocessing idea on top of it. Test one change at a time against the strongest known configuration rather than stacking changes on a weaker baseline.

episode.objective: Explore subsample-stacking spectrogram approach with new checkpoints (v1.15, subsample v1.0–v1.3)
episode.lever: spectrogram subsample stacking and checkpoint versions
episode.outcome: All versions regressed badly (0.46549–0.55426); abandoned

instance.goal: Can a new input representation (4-channel subsample-stacked spectrograms) with dedicated checkpoints outperform the current best single-spectrogram approach?
instance.context: The best LB score was 0.45265 with EfficientNetV2-Tiny on standard spectrograms. The author introduced a subsample-stacking approach with new checkpoints (v1.0–v1.3), but all submitted variants scored 0.51–0.55, far worse than the prior best.
instance.action: Tried the new subsample-stacking representation across multiple checkpoint versions (v1.0–v1.3), fixing preprocessing bugs along the way (wrong transform function, NaN handling). After five submissions all scored much worse than baseline, the author abandoned this direction and moved to a completely different modality (raw EEG with 1D CNN/GRU) in the next version.

general.goal: When exploring a new input representation or feature engineering idea, how many iterations of poor results justify abandoning the direction?
general.context: A well-tuned baseline exists. A new representation requires its own preprocessing pipeline and dedicated model checkpoints. Multiple checkpoint versions and bug fixes have been tried but all score substantially worse than the baseline.
general.action: After fixing all obvious pipeline bugs (wrong transform calls, missing imputation) and trying several checkpoint versions, if the new approach still scores far worse than the established baseline (e.g., 10–20% relative degradation), abandon it rather than continuing to iterate. Reserve further submissions for fundamentally different ideas.

instance.goal: Why did the new subsample-stacking spectrogram pipeline initially produce very poor predictions?
instance.context: After switching to the subsample approach (v29), the code called the wrong transform function (generic `transforms` instead of `spectrogram_transforms`). Also, removing `fillna(0)` in v33 left NaNs in the input, causing further degradation (v33→v34 showed restoring fillna helped slightly).
instance.action: Fixed the transform call (v30) and restored NaN imputation (v34). Each fix was identified by inspecting the preprocessing pipeline for mismatches between training and inference. Despite fixes, scores remained poor, indicating the representation itself or checkpoint quality was the bottleneck.

general.goal: What are the most common silent failure modes when porting a new preprocessing pipeline to inference?
general.context: A new feature representation requires a dedicated preprocessing path. The inference code was adapted from an existing pipeline, so variable names and function references may still point to the old pipeline's objects.
general.action: When introducing a new preprocessing branch, audit every function call and variable reference in the inference loop to ensure it uses the new branch's transforms, normalization, and imputation—not the old ones. Specifically check: (1) the correct transform/augmentation object is called, (2) missing-value handling matches training, and (3) data layout (transpose, channel order) is consistent. Submit only after all such mismatches are resolved.

episode.objective: Build raw EEG 1D inference pipeline (EEGNet with 1D CNN+GRU) and debug it to produce valid predictions
episode.outcome: Working pipeline at v46 with score 0.46059

instance.goal: How much can a raw EEG 1D CNN+GRU model contribute compared to the existing spectrogram-based EfficientNet pipeline?
instance.context: The spectrogram EfficientNet pipeline had plateaued around LB 0.45-0.46. The competition's strong solutions are known to use both spectrogram CNNs and 1D CNNs on raw EEG. The author had no raw EEG model in the pipeline yet.
instance.action: Built an entirely new EEGNet inference pipeline (1D parallel-kernel convolutions + ResNet1D blocks + GRU + classification head) with EEG-specific preprocessing (bandpass filter, NaN interpolation, difference features) and TTA, debugging iteratively across ~11 versions until it produced valid predictions at LB 0.46, comparable to the spectrogram model alone.

general.goal: How much can a complementary model on a different input modality contribute when the current single-modality pipeline has plateaued?
general.context: A 2D image-based model on derived features (e.g., spectrograms) has reached diminishing returns. The raw time-series data is available but unused, and top solutions are known to exploit both modalities.
general.action: Build a separate 1D temporal model pipeline on the raw signal data, with modality-specific preprocessing and augmentation. Debug it as a standalone submission first to verify it produces competitive predictions before attempting to ensemble it with the image-based model.

instance.goal: Why does the new EEGNet pipeline produce poor or invalid predictions despite the model loading without errors?
instance.context: Initial EEGNet submission scored 0.60 (much worse than the ~0.46 spectrogram baseline). Multiple bugs existed: wrong TTA flag name, mismatched classification head input dimension (tried 424→224→168), wrong variable references in post-processing, and misnamed DataFrame columns.
instance.action: Debugged incrementally: fixed TTA flag (v37, LB 0.60→submitted), fixed head dimension and NaN handling (v38, LB 0.55), removed GRU branch and adjusted head size to match checkpoint architecture (v40-v41, LB 0.54), updated checkpoints (v42, LB 0.47), then fixed variable/column name mismatches in post-processing across v43-v46 until reaching LB 0.46.

general.goal: When porting a trained model to a new inference notebook, what are the common failure modes that cause silently wrong predictions rather than crashes?
general.context: A new model pipeline loads weights without error but produces much worse scores than expected. The architecture was defined manually in the inference notebook rather than imported from the training code.
general.action: Check and fix these in order: (1) ensure the model architecture (layer sizes, branches present/absent, activation functions) exactly matches what was used during training; (2) verify that preprocessing and augmentation flags reference the correct variables; (3) confirm that the post-processing step reads from the correct prediction arrays and column names. Submit after each fix to isolate which changes matter.

episode.objective: Increase EEGNet capacity (planes, blocks, head size) with new checkpoints to improve 1D EEG predictions
episode.outcome: New best 0.41674 at v47

instance.goal: Can scaling up the 1D EEG CNN model (more channels, deeper blocks, larger head) yield a meaningful score improvement on this EEG classification task?
instance.context: The 1D CNN+GRU EEGNet had been iteratively debugged and tuned, reaching LB 0.46059. The architecture used 24 planes, 9 residual blocks, and a 168-dim head. New checkpoints (v1.3) were trained with a larger architecture (128 planes, 11 blocks, 256-dim head, LeakyReLU).
instance.action: Increased planes from 24→128, residual blocks from 9→11, head input from 168→256, switched ReLU→LeakyReLU, loaded matching v1.3 checkpoints, and tweaked temporal dropout augmentation parameters. This yielded LB 0.41674, a large improvement of ~0.044.

general.goal: How much can increasing the capacity of a 1D time-series model improve classification performance when the current architecture may be under-parameterized?
general.context: A lightweight 1D convolutional model has been debugged and its inference pipeline stabilized, but the score has plateaued. New checkpoints trained with a substantially wider and deeper variant are available.
general.action: Scale up the model width (number of feature channels) by several times, add a few more residual blocks, enlarge the classification head accordingly, and switch to a slightly more expressive activation function. Ensure the inference code architecture exactly matches the new checkpoints. Expect a noticeable score jump when the previous model was capacity-limited.

instance.goal: When changing the EEGNet architecture for inference, what else needs to be coordinated to avoid errors or score regressions?
instance.context: Throughout the notebook history, mismatches between model definition and checkpoint weights (wrong head dimensions, wrong block counts) caused failures or poor scores. The author also adjusted augmentation parameters alongside the architecture change.
instance.action: Changed all architecture hyperparameters (planes, blocks, head size, activation) simultaneously with swapping to the matching checkpoint directory and filenames, and also tweaked test-time augmentation dropout parameters. This coordinated change produced a clean new-best score rather than a crash or regression.

general.goal: How should inference-time model code be updated when switching to checkpoints trained with a different architecture configuration?
general.context: Pretrained checkpoints were produced with a different model configuration than the one currently in the inference notebook. Loading mismatched weights causes shape errors or silent degradation.
general.action: Update every architecture hyperparameter in the inference code (width, depth, head dimensions, activation type) to exactly match the training configuration of the new checkpoints. Change them all in one coordinated edit together with the checkpoint path swap, and also revisit any test-time augmentation settings that may interact with the new model scale.

episode.objective: Refine EEGNet architecture (ResNet block internals, forward pass fixes) and sweep checkpoints v1.4–v1.7
episode.lever: EEGNet architecture details and checkpoint versions
episode.outcome: New best 0.41016 at v50 (v1.5); later versions regressed slightly

instance.goal: After a strong score (0.41674) with a 1D EEG model, can further gains come from refining the ResNet block internals and sweeping checkpoint versions?
instance.context: v47 achieved 0.41674 with EEGNet. The author then modified ResNet1DBlock (conv ordering, bias, dropout removal) and swept checkpoints v1.4→v1.7. v48 regressed to 0.42174; v49 fixed a forward-pass bug (ReLU applied to wrong tensor) and recovered to 0.41042; v50 barely improved to 0.41016; v51–v53 regressed again with newer checkpoints and added TTA variants.
instance.action: After a regression at v48, the author identified a forward-pass bug (ReLU on wrong variable), fixed it in v49 which set a new best. Subsequent checkpoint/augmentation sweeps (v51–v53) did not improve further. The best result came from the bug fix + correct checkpoint, not from adding more TTA or newer checkpoints.

general.goal: When a model architecture change causes a score regression, how should one diagnose whether the issue is the architecture change itself or a bug introduced alongside it?
general.context: A code refactor that changes both model internals and checkpoint version simultaneously makes it hard to attribute a regression. The forward pass may have a subtle bug (e.g., applying an activation to the wrong tensor) masked by the checkpoint swap.
general.action: After a regression from a combined architecture+checkpoint change, inspect the forward pass carefully for correctness bugs before concluding the architecture or checkpoints are worse. Fix any bugs first, then re-evaluate. Only after confirming correctness should you continue sweeping checkpoints or augmentations.

instance.goal: Once the best EEGNet checkpoint version is found, do newer checkpoint versions and additional test-time augmentation variants keep improving the score?
instance.context: v49 (0.41042) and v50 (0.41016) were the best scores using checkpoints v1.4 and v1.5. Switching to v1.6 (v51: 0.41096), v1.7 with expanded TTA (v52: 0.42095), and further changes (v53: 0.42162) all regressed. The pattern shows diminishing/negative returns from continued checkpoint sweeping and TTA expansion.
instance.action: The author swept checkpoint versions v1.4 through v1.7 and expanded TTA (horizontal flip, combined flips). Scores plateaued at v1.5 and worsened with v1.6+. The episode demonstrates that once the best checkpoint is identified (scores plateau or regress across 2–3 consecutive versions), further sweeping yields no gain and the practitioner should change strategy (e.g., ensembling different model families, as the author did in v54–v55).

general.goal: When sweeping trained checkpoint versions for a single model architecture, how many consecutive non-improvements signal that the search should stop?
general.context: A series of checkpoint versions from the same training pipeline are evaluated on a leaderboard. After finding the best version, subsequent versions show flat or worsening scores.
general.action: If two or three consecutive checkpoint versions fail to improve over the current best, stop the sweep. The model architecture has likely saturated its contribution. Shift effort to a different lever such as ensembling with a complementary model family or changing the input representation.

episode.objective: Parameterize transforms and remove spectrogram inference to simplify to EEG-only pipeline
episode.outcome: Score 0.41624 at v54

instance.goal: Does removing the unused spectrogram inference path and consolidating to EEG-only predictions with cleaner parameterization improve or maintain score?
instance.context: The best LB score was 0.41016 from EEG-only models. Spectrogram inference code remained in the notebook but was effectively unused or underperforming. Transform parameters (dropout rates, normalization flags) were hard-coded literals scattered through the code.
instance.action: Removed the spectrogram inference block entirely, refactored InstanceNormalization1D parameters, moved hard-coded dropout/normalization values into a transform_parameters dict, and switched to new EEGNet checkpoints. Score went from 0.42162 to 0.41624, not beating the best 0.41016.

general.goal: Will consolidating the pipeline to a single model family and parameterizing transforms hurt or help the score?
general.context: Dead code from an earlier model family remains in the inference notebook alongside the currently dominant model family. Transform hyperparameters are hard-coded in multiple places, making systematic tuning difficult.
general.action: Remove the unused model family's inference path to reduce complexity, then extract all hard-coded transform values (dropout probability, normalization mode) into a single configuration dictionary so they can be tuned in one place. Verify the refactored pipeline reproduces or improves the previous score before further changes.

instance.goal: After many checkpoint swaps and architecture tweaks, is the current EEG-only pipeline ready to be combined with a spectrogram model for a bigger gain?
instance.context: The EEG-only pipeline plateaued around 0.41 LB after ~10 iterations of checkpoint and architecture changes. The next version (v55) introduced multi-model stacking (EEGNet + EfficientNet) and jumped to 0.29864, a massive improvement.
instance.action: Cleaned up and simplified the EEG-only pipeline in this version (removing spectrogram dead code, parameterizing transforms), which prepared the codebase for the multi-model stacking introduced in the very next version.

general.goal: When a single-modality pipeline has plateaued, what preparatory step enables the next large score jump?
general.context: Iterating on checkpoints and small architecture changes within one model family yields diminishing returns. The codebase still contains remnants of a different modality's pipeline that could be repurposed.
general.action: Before adding a second model family for ensembling, first clean the codebase: remove dead inference paths, centralize configuration, and ensure the surviving pipeline is modular. This makes it straightforward to add a second model's predictions and combine them via stacking or averaging in the next iteration.

episode.objective: Introduce EfficientNet 2D spectrogram model and stack with EEGNet 1D predictions
episode.outcome: New best 0.29864 at v55, massive improvement

instance.goal: How much can the score improve by combining the 1D EEG model (EEGNet) with a 2D spectrogram model (EfficientNet) rather than using only one modality?
instance.context: The author had iterated extensively on a 1D EEG CNN+GRU model reaching LB 0.41624, and earlier had a separate 2D spectrogram EfficientNet pipeline reaching ~0.45. Neither alone broke below 0.41.
instance.action: Introduced the EfficientNet spectrogram model back into the pipeline alongside EEGNet, refactored model definitions and loading utilities, and stacked/averaged fold predictions from both model families to produce a combined submission. This yielded LB 0.29864, a massive 0.118 improvement.

general.goal: How much can combining predictions from models that consume different input representations of the same data improve over the best single-representation model?
general.context: Two model families have been developed independently on complementary input modalities (e.g., raw time-series vs. frequency-domain images) and each has been tuned to near its individual ceiling.
general.action: Stack or average the fold-level predictions of both model families into a single submission. Expect a large gain (potentially much larger than any single-model tuning step) because the models make partially uncorrelated errors on different input views. Prioritize this multi-modal ensemble before further single-model tuning.

episode.objective: Sweep EfficientNet 2D checkpoint versions (v2–v4) and tune 1D/2D blend weights
episode.outcome: Best 0.29076 at v63 area; v56 best at 0.29084

instance.goal: Which version of the 2D EfficientNet checkpoints gives the best leaderboard score when stacked with the 1D EEGNet model?
instance.context: After introducing EfficientNet+EEGNet stacking (v55, LB 0.29864), the author had multiple checkpoint versions (v2–v4) trained with slightly different epochs/settings. Each swap is cheap (just changing file paths).
instance.action: Sweep checkpoint directories sequentially (v2→v3→v4), submitting each to the leaderboard. v2 improved to 0.29084 (new best), v3 regressed slightly to 0.29233, v4 was 0.29199. Select v2 or v4 as the best checkpoint set and move on to blend-weight tuning.

general.goal: Which training run or checkpoint epoch produces the best downstream score when multiple candidate checkpoints exist?
general.context: After establishing a multi-model stacking pipeline, several checkpoint versions are available from different training runs or epochs, and swapping them in is low-cost.
general.action: Sweep checkpoint versions one at a time, submitting each to the evaluation metric. Track the score for each version, pick the best, and only then move to other tuning levers (e.g., blend weights). Expect diminishing or non-monotonic returns across versions.

instance.goal: What per-class blend weights between the 1D EEGNet and 2D EfficientNet predictions minimize KL divergence?
instance.context: The stacked ensemble used equal-weight averaging implicitly. The 2D model alone was much stronger (LB ~0.29) than the 1D model alone (LB ~0.41), suggesting the 2D model should dominate the blend.
instance.action: Set initial per-class blend weights to 0.2 (1D) / 0.8 (2D), reflecting the 2D model's superiority. Then manually adjust per-class weights (e.g., shifting some classes to 0.3/0.7 or 0.1/0.9) to see if class-specific tuning helps. The uniform 0.2/0.8 blend scored 0.29209; the author continued adjusting but did not submit the next variant, suggesting marginal or unclear gains.

general.goal: How should predictions from a weaker and a stronger model be blended, and should blend weights vary by class?
general.context: Two models of very different individual quality are being ensembled. The stronger model scores roughly 30% better on the evaluation metric than the weaker one.
general.action: Start with a global blend that heavily favors the stronger model (e.g., 80/20). Then try per-class weight adjustments, shifting weight toward whichever model is relatively better for each class. Evaluate each change on the leaderboard or a reliable validation set. If per-class tuning shows no clear gain, revert to the simpler uniform blend to avoid overfitting to the public leaderboard.

episode.objective: Sweep EfficientNetV2-Tiny 2D checkpoint versions (v5–v9, v2.0–v3.0) with augmentation tweaks
episode.outcome: New best 0.29040 at v67 (v3.0)

instance.goal: Which version of the EfficientNetV2-Tiny checkpoints yields the best leaderboard score for the 2D spectrogram ensemble component?
instance.context: The author had a working inference pipeline combining 1D EEG and 2D spectrogram models (best LB ~0.29084). They had access to multiple checkpoint versions (v5 through v9, v2.0, v3.0) trained with slightly different epochs/hyperparameters across folds.
instance.action: Systematically swept checkpoint versions one at a time (v5→v6→v7→v8→v9→v2.0→v3.0), submitting each to the leaderboard. Scores: 0.29163, 0.29215, 0.29076 (best), 0.29731, 0.29357, 0.29086, 0.29040 (new best with augmentation tweaks). The best pure checkpoint swap was v7; the final best combined v3.0 checkpoints with added augmentation.

general.goal: How to identify which training checkpoint version produces the best test-time predictions when multiple candidate checkpoints exist?
general.context: Multiple checkpoint versions are available from ongoing training runs with different epochs or hyperparameter schedules, and local validation may not perfectly predict leaderboard performance.
general.action: Sweep checkpoint versions one at a time, holding all other pipeline components fixed, and submit each to the leaderboard. Track scores to identify the best version. Expect non-monotonic results — newer checkpoints are not always better. Keep the sweep systematic (sequential versions) so regressions are quickly detected.

instance.goal: Can inference-time augmentation changes (temporal dropout, coarse dropout, normalization reordering) squeeze additional gain on top of the best checkpoint?
instance.context: After sweeping checkpoints v5–v9 and v2.0, the best single-checkpoint LB was 0.29076 (v7). The author had already tried TTA flips earlier. The v3.0 checkpoint alone (v66, LB 0.29086) was close but not better than v7.
instance.action: Combined the v3.0 checkpoint swap with inference preprocessing changes: added NonCenterTemporalDropout1D and CoarseDropout augmentations to the 2D transform pipeline, simplified InstanceNormalization2D, and reordered transforms. This achieved LB 0.29040, a new best — showing that coupling checkpoint updates with matched augmentation can yield gains neither achieves alone.

general.goal: When a checkpoint swap alone does not beat the current best, can pairing it with inference-time augmentation or preprocessing changes unlock further improvement?
general.context: A sweep of checkpoint versions has identified a near-optimal version, but a newer checkpoint with potentially better weights scores slightly worse, suggesting a mismatch between its training augmentation and the current inference transforms.
general.action: When swapping to a new checkpoint, also update the inference-time transforms (dropout, normalization order, additional augmentations) to match or complement the training regime of that checkpoint. Test the combined change as a single submission; if it beats both the old checkpoint and the new checkpoint with old transforms, keep the pair.

episode.objective: Try different 2D backbone variants (EfficientNetV2 small, medium, tiny) and checkpoint versions
episode.outcome: New best 0.28380 at v73 (EfficientNetV2 medium)

instance.goal: Which EfficientNetV2 variant (tiny, small, medium) and checkpoint version yields the best 2D spectrogram ensemble score?
instance.context: The author had plateaued around LB 0.29 with EfficientNetV2-Tiny. Multiple checkpoint versions of the tiny variant were tried (v3.0, v3.1, v3.2, v3.3), then small, then back to tiny v2.0. None beat the v67 best of 0.29040; all scored between 0.29215 and 0.29975. The subsequent v73 with medium achieved 0.28380, a new best.
instance.action: Systematically swept backbone variants (tiny → small → tiny again) and checkpoint versions by swapping model directory paths and fold checkpoint filenames, submitting each to the leaderboard. When tiny and small variants failed to improve, the author eventually tried medium (after the episode), which broke through the plateau.

general.goal: When the current pretrained backbone variant has plateaued, which alternative model size within the same architecture family will improve the score?
general.context: Multiple checkpoint versions of the current backbone size no longer yield gains, and the score has stagnated across several submissions.
general.action: Sweep across model sizes within the same architecture family (e.g., tiny → small → medium) by substituting checkpoints and matching preprocessing. Submit each variant to evaluate on the test metric. If smaller variants plateau, try the next larger variant; capacity increase often breaks through when smaller variants have saturated.

instance.goal: Will adding new augmentation transforms (ChannelGroupPermute, updated InstanceNormalization2D) alongside new checkpoints improve the EfficientNet spectrogram ensemble?
instance.context: At v68 (LB 0.29215), the author added new augmentation/transform classes and switched checkpoints simultaneously in v69, but the score worsened to 0.29636.
