In v70, the added transforms were removed (unused imports cleaned) while only checkpoints changed, scoring 0.29975—also worse.
instance.action: The author bundled preprocessing changes with checkpoint swaps, making it hard to attribute degradation. The lesson observed: when both changes hurt, the author reverted the augmentation additions and continued sweeping only the backbone/checkpoints in subsequent steps.

general.goal: How can the effect of new preprocessing or augmentation changes be isolated from the effect of switching model weights?
general.context: Changing both the model checkpoint and the data transforms in a single submission makes it impossible to attribute score changes to either factor.
general.action: Change only one factor per submission—either the model weights or the preprocessing/augmentation pipeline—so that score movements can be attributed. If both are changed at once and the score worsens, revert the augmentation first (it is cheaper to re-test) and re-evaluate the checkpoint alone before deciding.

episode.objective: Add CoaT-Lite model to ensemble and blend multiple 2D models (EfficientNet + CoaT)
episode.outcome: New best 0.27414 at v76 with 50/50 blend

instance.goal: Can scaling up the backbone variant (EfficientNetV2 tiny → medium) improve the ensemble's leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author had been cycling through EfficientNetV2 tiny checkpoints for many versions, with the best LB around 0.29. Switching to a medium variant with its own trained checkpoints was a natural next step.
instance.action: Replaced the EfficientNetV2-tiny checkpoint directory and filenames with EfficientNetV2-medium ones (different folds/epochs). This alone improved LB from 0.29425 to 0.28380.

general.goal: Can a larger variant of the same backbone family improve predictions when the smaller variant's score has plateaued?
general.context: Multiple checkpoint swaps of the same small backbone variant have yielded diminishing returns, and larger variants of the same family are available with trained weights.
general.action: Swap in the larger backbone variant's checkpoints while keeping the rest of the pipeline identical. If the score improves, keep it; the cost is mainly inference time.

instance.goal: How much can adding a structurally different 2D model (CoaT-Lite transformer) to the existing EfficientNet CNN ensemble improve the score?
instance.context: The pipeline already had a strong EfficientNetV2-medium CNN. Adding a vision-transformer-style model (CoaT-Lite via timm) provides architectural diversity. The author built infrastructure to accumulate and average predictions from multiple 2D model families.
instance.action: Added a CoaT-Lite model class wrapping a timm backbone, loaded its fold checkpoints, ran inference alongside EfficientNetV2, then blended the two 2D models' predictions with equal (50/50) weights. LB improved from 0.28380 to 0.27414 across the steps.

general.goal: How much does adding an architecturally diverse model (e.g., a transformer alongside a convolutional network) to an inference ensemble improve the metric?
general.context: The ensemble currently contains only one backbone family. A second backbone with a fundamentally different inductive bias (e.g., attention vs. convolution) is available with trained fold checkpoints.
general.action: Integrate the new backbone into the inference loop so it produces per-sample predictions in the same format. Average the two model families' outputs with equal weights as a starting point. If the combined score improves, keep both; then optionally tune the blend ratio.

episode.objective: Add more 2D backbones (CoAtNet, NextViT, MaxViT, Swin) and find best multi-model blend
episode.outcome: New best 0.26879 at v84 with 5-model blend

instance.goal: Which combination of diverse 2D backbone architectures (EfficientNetV2, CoAtLite, MaxViT, NextViT, Swin) yields the best ensemble blend for EEG spectrogram classification?
instance.context: Blending two 2D models (EfficientNetV2 + CoAtLite) already achieved 0.27414. The author had trained checkpoints for several additional architectures (MaxViT-tiny, NextViT-large, Swin-small) and could test each individually and in combination.
instance.action: First tested each new backbone individually by swapping it into the ensemble slot (v77–v80, v82–v83), observing that none alone beat the existing best. Then in v84, loaded all five backbone families simultaneously, ran inference for each, and blended their normalized predictions with equal weights (0.2 each), achieving a new best of 0.26879.

general.goal: How many and which diverse model architectures should be included in a prediction ensemble to maximize performance?
general.context: A blend of two architectures already performs well, and checkpoints from several additional architecture families are available. Individual substitution of one backbone for another does not consistently improve the score.
general.action: First evaluate each candidate backbone individually to confirm it produces reasonable predictions. Then include all viable backbones simultaneously with equal blend weights. Adding more diverse architectures tends to reduce variance and improve the ensemble even when no single new backbone beats the current best alone.

instance.goal: When testing new backbone candidates, is it better to swap them in one-at-a-time or add them all at once?
instance.context: Swapping NextViT for MaxViT (v78: 0.28559) or Swin for NextViT (v79: 0.28050) each scored worse than the two-model blend baseline (0.27414). Replacing one model with another only tests relative quality, not complementarity.
instance.action: After individual A/B swaps showed no single backbone was clearly superior, the author loaded all five model families and blended equally (v84), achieving 0.26879—substantially better than any two-model combination. The individual swap phase served as a sanity check that each backbone produced valid predictions before committing to the full blend.

general.goal: When exploring candidate models for an ensemble, how should one transition from evaluating individuals to combining them?
general.context: Swapping one ensemble member for another tests relative single-model quality but not the diversity benefit of adding members. Each candidate individually may score worse than the current blend.
general.action: Use individual swaps only as a sanity check that each candidate produces reasonable predictions. Then combine all candidates with equal weights in a single blend. Diversity across architectures often yields gains that pairwise comparisons cannot reveal, so do not discard a candidate solely because it underperforms when substituted one-for-one.

episode.objective: Add EKG-augmented checkpoints, ConvNeXt backbone, and tune ensemble blend weights
episode.outcome: New best 0.26809 at v90

instance.goal: How much does each individual model in a multi-model ensemble contribute to the final score, and which combination yields the best blend?
instance.context: The author had 6+ diverse 2D models (EfficientNetV2, CoaTLite, MaxViT, NextViT, Swin, ConvNeXt) plus 1D EEGNet, all producing fold-averaged predictions. The previous best (v84, 0.26879) used an equal blend of all models.
instance.action: Systematically tested single-model submissions (CoaTLite→MaxViT→Swin) in v85-v87 to gauge individual model quality, then switched back to the full blend in v88 (0.26916), added ConvNeXt in v89, and enabled all models with tuned weights in v90 to achieve 0.26809. This isolate-then-blend workflow identified which models help and which hurt.

general.goal: How should individual model quality be assessed before committing to a multi-model ensemble blend?
general.context: When an ensemble of many diverse models is available and the blend score is already strong, it is unclear whether every member helps or whether some degrade the result.
general.action: Submit each model's predictions individually to the leaderboard to rank their standalone quality. Use these rankings to decide inclusion and to set blend weights proportional to individual performance, then verify the full blend still beats the best single model before finalizing.

instance.goal: Can adding a new backbone architecture (ConvNeXt) and re-enabling the full ensemble improve the blended score beyond the current best of 0.26879?
instance.context: After switching to EKG-augmented checkpoints (v85, 0.27935) the score regressed, but individual model probing (v86-v87) and returning to the blend (v88, 0.26916) showed the blend was close to the previous best. A ConvNeXt wrapper was added in v89 but only that single model was submitted (0.27823).
instance.action: In v90, uncommented the loop guard so all models (including the new ConvNeXt) were processed, assigned a small blend weight (~0.17) to ConvNeXt, and submitted the full blended predictions. This achieved a new best of 0.26809, confirming the additional diverse backbone improved the ensemble.

general.goal: When is it worthwhile to add yet another backbone family to an already large ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of several architectures is near its best score. A candidate new architecture has been integrated but its standalone score is worse than the blend.
general.action: Give the new architecture a small blend weight proportional to its relative standalone quality, re-run the full ensemble, and check whether the combined score improves. Even a model that is individually weaker can help if it is architecturally diverse, but verify with a submission rather than assuming diversity always helps.

episode.objective: Add 600-second spectrogram models (EfficientNet, Swin, CoaT-Lite) to ensemble
episode.outcome: Initial regression to 1.60 then recovered to 0.35192 at v95; still worse than raw EEG ensemble

instance.goal: How much can adding a new modality (600-second spectrogram models) improve the existing raw-EEG ensemble that scores 0.268?
instance.context: The author had a strong raw-EEG 1D+2D ensemble at LB 0.268. Spectrogram data (precomputed by Kaggle) was available but unused. Multiple pretrained spectrogram model checkpoints (EfficientNetV2, Swin, CoaT-Lite) were ready.
instance.action: Introduced spectrogram models incrementally: first added EfficientNetV2 and Swin with new transforms (v91), fixed preprocessing bugs (v92), tested individual models (v93), added CoaT-Lite and rebalanced weights (v94), then submitted the blended spectrogram ensemble (v95) reaching 0.352. Later (v96) blending 85% raw-EEG + 15% spectrogram yielded a new best of 0.267.

general.goal: How much can adding a complementary input modality improve an already-strong single-modality ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models on one modality has plateaued. A second modality covering the same samples is available with pretrained checkpoints but has not been integrated.
general.action: Build and debug the new-modality pipeline in isolation first, verify each model individually by submitting its standalone predictions, then blend the new modality into the existing ensemble at a small weight (e.g., 10–20%). Even if the new modality is much weaker alone, a small blend weight can still yield a modest improvement on the combined submission.

instance.goal: When introducing new spectrogram models with many new transforms, how can a catastrophic score regression (LB 1.60 vs prior 0.268) be diagnosed and fixed quickly?
instance.context: v91 added spectrogram models plus many new augmentation/normalization transforms in one large commit and scored 1.60 (terrible). The author suspected preprocessing bugs rather than model quality.
instance.action: In v92, fixed transform signatures (renamed 'image' to 'inputs', corrected shape indexing) and added log1p scaling to spectrogram data. This single fix recovered the score to 0.363, confirming the regression was a preprocessing bug. The author then iterated model-by-model (v93–v95) to refine the ensemble.

general.goal: When a large code change causes a dramatic score regression, how can the root cause be isolated efficiently?
general.context: A single commit introduced both new models and new data transforms, and the score degraded catastrophically, suggesting a bug rather than a modeling issue.
general.action: Focus first on the data preprocessing and augmentation code rather than the model definitions. Check that transform function signatures, tensor shapes, and scaling conventions match what the pretrained models expect. Fix those issues in a minimal follow-up commit and verify recovery before iterating on model selection or blending.

instance.goal: When multiple new spectrogram models are available, how should they be evaluated and combined before blending with the main ensemble?
instance.context: Three spectrogram model families (EfficientNetV2, Swin, CoaT-Lite) were loaded. The author needed to know which to use and whether blending them helps before mixing with the raw-EEG ensemble.
instance.action: Submitted individual model predictions first (EfficientNetV2 at 0.363, Swin at 0.363, CoaT-Lite at 0.358), then submitted the blend of all three at 0.352. Each addition improved the score incrementally, confirming diversity. Only after validating the spectrogram blend was it combined with the raw-EEG ensemble.

general.goal: When integrating several new models into an existing ensemble, how should they be evaluated to confirm they add value?
general.context: Multiple candidate models for a new modality or architecture family are available, and the practitioner wants to know which ones contribute before adding them to the main blend.
general.action: Submit each candidate model's predictions individually to get standalone scores, then submit their equal-weight blend. If the blend outperforms every individual model, the candidates are diverse enough to warrant inclusion. Only then blend the sub-ensemble into the main pipeline at a conservative weight.

episode.objective: Blend raw EEG and spectrogram predictions with weighted combination
episode.outcome: New best 0.26734 at v96

instance.goal: How much can combining raw EEG model predictions with spectrogram model predictions improve the overall ensemble score?
instance.context: The raw EEG 2D ensemble alone scored 0.26809 (best), and the spectrogram ensemble alone scored around 0.35192. The two modalities capture different signal representations and their errors may be partially uncorrelated.
instance.action: Blended raw EEG and spectrogram predictions with weights 0.85 and 0.15 respectively, heavily favoring the stronger modality. Also fixed a stray 'continue' statement that was preventing the raw EEG model loop from running. This achieved 0.26734, a new best.

general.goal: How much can combining predictions from two different input modalities improve ensemble performance?
general.context: One modality's ensemble is substantially stronger than the other's (e.g., one scores ~25% better), but both capture complementary aspects of the same underlying signal.
general.action: Blend the two modality predictions with a heavily skewed weight favoring the stronger modality (e.g., 85/15 split). Even a weak secondary modality can contribute a small but meaningful gain when its errors are partially uncorrelated with the primary modality's errors.

instance.goal: Why is the raw EEG model not producing predictions even though its code and checkpoints are present?
instance.context: A stray 'continue' statement in the raw_eeg_2d model inference loop was silently skipping all model processing, so no raw EEG predictions were being generated. The submission was using only spectrogram predictions.
instance.action: Removed the errant 'continue' statement so the loop body executes and raw EEG predictions are computed and available for blending.

general.goal: Why does a model component in a multi-model inference pipeline produce no predictions despite being configured?
general.context: A complex inference notebook with multiple model loops and conditional logic can contain leftover control-flow statements (e.g., a skip/continue used during debugging) that silently prevent a model from running.
general.action: Before blending, verify that each model component actually produces non-trivial predictions (e.g., check array shapes or print summary statistics). Inspect loop bodies for stray early-exit or skip statements that may have been left from debugging.

episode.objective: Replace 600s spectrogram models with 50s variants and adjust blend
episode.outcome: New best 0.26658 at v98

instance.goal: Can switching from 600-second spectrogram models to 50-second spectrogram models improve the ensemble's KL divergence score?
instance.context: The best score (0.26734) used a blend of 0.85 raw EEG + 0.15 spectrogram (600s). The competition labels correspond to 50-second EEG windows, so 600s spectrograms may include irrelevant temporal context. New 50s spectrogram checkpoints were available.
instance.action: Replaced all 600s spectrogram model checkpoints and transforms with 50s variants, adjusted the blend weights to 0.6 raw EEG + 0.4 spectrogram (giving more weight to the now better-matched spectrogram), achieving a new best of 0.26658.

general.goal: When blending models that use different temporal windows of the input, which window duration should the auxiliary model use?
general.context: The target labels correspond to a specific short time window, but auxiliary models were trained on a much longer context window that may dilute the relevant signal with irrelevant data.
general.action: Retrain or swap in auxiliary models whose input window matches the label's temporal scope. When the auxiliary model's input better aligns with the labeled segment, increase its blend weight (here roughly doubling the spectrogram weight) since its predictions become more informative.

instance.goal: After changing the spectrogram duration variant, what blend ratio between raw EEG and spectrogram models works best?
instance.context: Previously the blend was 0.85/0.15 favoring raw EEG when using 600s spectrograms. With 50s spectrograms better aligned to the 50s label window, the spectrogram signal quality likely improved.
instance.action: Increased the spectrogram blend weight from 0.15 to 0.4 (and decreased raw EEG from 0.85 to 0.6). This yielded a small but consistent improvement (0.26734 → 0.26658), suggesting the better-aligned spectrogram deserved more weight.

general.goal: How should ensemble blend weights be adjusted when one component model is replaced by a qualitatively better variant?
general.context: An ensemble member was replaced with a version expected to produce higher-quality predictions due to better input alignment with the target.
general.action: Re-increase the weight of the improved component rather than keeping the old ratio. Start by roughly doubling or tripling its share, then verify on the leaderboard or validation set that the new ratio outperforms the old one.

episode.objective: Add ConvNeXt and MaxViT spectrogram models, fix submission bugs, and tune 3-model spectrogram blend
episode.outcome: New best 0.24782 at v105 with 3-model spectrogram blend

instance.goal: How much can the score improve by adding new backbone architectures (ConvNeXt, MaxViT) to the spectrogram model ensemble and tuning their blend weights?
instance.context: The author had a working ensemble of raw EEG models and one spectrogram model (EfficientNetV2) scoring 0.26658. New pretrained checkpoints for ConvNeXt and MaxViT spectrogram models were available.
instance.action: Added ConvNeXt (v100, LB 0.25311) then MaxViT (v104) spectrogram models one at a time, first testing each alone to gauge standalone quality, then blending all three with weights 0.25/0.5/0.25 (EfficientNetV2/ConvNeXt/MaxViT) to reach 0.24782. The strongest standalone model (ConvNeXt) received the highest blend weight.

general.goal: How should new model architectures be integrated into an existing prediction ensemble to maximize score improvement?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models is already producing competitive predictions, and additional pretrained models with different backbones are available.
general.action: Add each new model one at a time: first evaluate it in isolation to gauge its standalone quality, then include it in the blend. Assign higher blend weight to the model with the best standalone performance. Verify each addition improves the combined score before keeping it.

instance.goal: Why are new models not contributing to the submission despite being loaded and configured?
instance.context: Across multiple versions (v98→v99, v100→v101, v101→v102, v102→v103), stray 'continue' statements left from debugging caused model loops to skip inference, and the submission CSV was assigned from the wrong prediction columns, masking the effect of newly added models.
instance.action: Systematically removed stray 'continue' statements in model loops and corrected the submission column assignment to point to the intended blended predictions. Each fix yielded a score improvement (e.g., v98→v99: −0.010, v102→v103: −0.004), confirming the models were being silently skipped.

general.goal: Why does adding a new component to the inference pipeline not change the output or score?
general.context: During iterative development, temporary control-flow statements (early returns, skips) are inserted to test individual components, and the final output assignment may still point to an older variable.
general.action: Before submitting, audit the full inference loop for leftover skip/continue/break statements that bypass newly added components, and verify that the submission output references the intended blended prediction variable rather than a single-model or stale variable. Each such fix can yield a meaningful score gain.

episode.objective: Add spectrogram visualization, fix 50/10s spectrogram features, and tune cross-modality blend
episode.lever: spectrogram feature pipeline and blend weights
episode.outcome: New best 0.24265 at v111

instance.goal: Why did the score regress sharply (0.24782 → 0.32415) after adding a new ConvNeXt spectrogram model and modifying post-processing?
instance.context: In v106, the author added a new spectrogram model, changed model output normalization (commented out sigmoid/normalization), and added visualization utilities. The score jumped from 0.24782 to 0.32415.
instance.action: In v107, the author fixed the spectrogram feature input (using differenced EEG signals instead of raw), recovering to 0.25048. Then across v108–v111, they incrementally fixed bugs (removed accidental 'continue' statements skipping models, fixed submission column assignments) and tuned blend weights, ultimately reaching 0.24265—a new best.

general.goal: How can a large score regression after a complex multi-change commit be diagnosed and recovered?
general.context: A single commit bundles several changes (new model, altered post-processing, new feature transforms) and the metric worsens substantially, making it unclear which change caused the regression.
general.action: Revert or fix one change at a time in subsequent micro-commits, submitting after each, to isolate the harmful change. Prioritize fixing feature-pipeline mismatches (e.g., wrong input signal fed to a transform) first, then fix integration bugs (skipped models, wrong output columns), then tune blend weights.

instance.goal: How should the submission column assignment be managed when multiple model groups (raw EEG, 50s spectrogram, 50/10s spectrogram) each produce separate prediction columns?
instance.context: Across v108–v111, the author repeatedly had bugs where the submission CSV used single-model or intermediate blend columns instead of the final combined blend columns. In v109, removing a 'continue' that skipped a model and switching to the correct blend columns gave a new best (0.24490). In v111, switching from a sub-blend to the full blend columns gave another new best (0.24265).
instance.action: After adding any new model group to the ensemble, always verify that (1) no model loop is accidentally skipped (check for stray 'continue'/'break'), (2) the new model's predictions are included in the final blend computation, and (3) the submission assignment references the final combined blend columns, not an intermediate or single-model set.

general.goal: What are common integration pitfalls when adding a new model to a multi-model ensemble inference pipeline?
general.context: An ensemble pipeline processes multiple model groups sequentially, each writing predictions to separate columns, then blends them. Debugging statements or leftover control-flow from testing can silently skip models or write the wrong columns to the submission.
general.action: After each addition, check three things before submitting: (1) no loop-skipping logic (debug continues/breaks) remains, (2) the new model's normalized predictions are included in the blend formula, and (3) the final output references the fully-blended columns. Submit a micro-change fixing only the output assignment to confirm the blend is active.

instance.goal: What is the best weighting across raw EEG models, 50s spectrogram models, and 50/10s spectrogram models for the final blend?
instance.context: The author had raw EEG 2D models, 50s spectrogram models, and newly added 50/10s spectrogram models. Previous best used 0.4 raw_eeg + 0.6 spectrogram_50s. Adding the third modality required rebalancing.
instance.action: Set weights to 0.3 raw_eeg, 0.3 spectrogram_50s, 0.4 spectrogram_50_10s (giving more weight to the newest, presumably strongest modality). This three-way blend at v111 achieved 0.24265, a new best over the two-way blend's 0.24490.

general.goal: How should blend weights be redistributed when a new complementary modality is added to an existing weighted ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of two modalities with tuned weights is extended by a third modality that captures different signal characteristics. Simply appending equal weight may dilute strong contributors.
general.action: Allocate the largest share to the newest modality if it is expected to be the strongest standalone, while reducing existing shares proportionally. Submit and compare against the previous best; if improved, the new modality adds complementary information. Iterate weights in small increments if the first attempt does not improve.

episode.objective: Add raw EEG ConvNeXt/MaxViT 50s and 10s models, tune which model groups contribute to ensemble
episode.lever: raw EEG model variants and ensemble composition
episode.outcome: Score around 0.25–0.27; v120 at 0.24466 after fix

instance.goal: When adding new model families (ConvNeXt, MaxViT for raw EEG) to an already-strong ensemble, how can their individual contribution be assessed before committing to the full blend?
instance.context: The author had a best LB of 0.24265 from a multi-model ensemble. They added new raw EEG ConvNeXt and MaxViT models but initially tested them individually (using `continue` statements to skip other models) before enabling all models together.
instance.action: First submit each new model family alone (v114 convnext-only → 0.27136, v115 maxvit-only → 0.26568), then enable all models and submit the blend (v116 → 0.25928). Compare individual vs blended scores to confirm the new models add value. Only after confirming, integrate into the full ensemble (v120 → 0.24466).

general.goal: When introducing new model variants into an existing ensemble, how can their marginal contribution be evaluated efficiently?
general.context: A multi-model ensemble already achieves a strong score. New model families have been trained but their standalone quality and complementarity to the existing blend are unknown.
general.action: Use conditional skip flags to first evaluate each new model in isolation on the leaderboard, then enable all models together and submit the blend. Compare standalone scores against the blended score to confirm diversity benefit before permanently including them. Remove models whose standalone performance is too weak or that degrade the blend.

instance.goal: Why does the score degrade sharply when replacing a well-tuned ensemble with a newly restructured one, and how should recovery proceed?
instance.context: v111 scored 0.24265. After a major restructuring (v112: new ConvNeXt raw EEG models, Butterworth filter, removed many previous models), the score jumped to 0.26665. Over the next 8 versions the author incrementally re-enabled models, fixed skipped loops, swapped checkpoints, and corrected the submission column assignment, eventually reaching 0.24466 at v120.
instance.action: After a large refactor that worsens the score, systematically re-enable each model group one at a time (fix stray `continue` statements in v118, swap checkpoint versions in v119, correct the submission output column in v120). Each fix is a small, testable change. Do not abandon the new models; instead iteratively restore the full ensemble while keeping the new additions.

general.goal: How should one recover when a major pipeline refactor causes a large score regression despite adding potentially valuable new components?
general.context: A complex inference pipeline with many model groups was restructured to add new components, but the refactor inadvertently disabled or misconfigured existing components, causing a significant score drop.
general.action: Make one small fix per submission: re-enable skipped model loops, correct output column assignments, and swap checkpoint versions individually. Verify each fix's effect on the leaderboard before proceeding. This isolates which changes caused the regression and confirms each restoration step helps, eventually recovering and surpassing the pre-refactor score.

instance.goal: Which prediction columns should the final submission CSV use when multiple blend levels exist (per-model, per-modality, overall)?
instance.context: The notebook maintained separate prediction column sets: raw_eeg_blend_prediction_columns, spectrogram_blend_prediction_columns, and blend_prediction_columns (the overall blend). In v116 the submission used raw_eeg_blend only; in v120 switching to blend_prediction_columns (the full blend) improved from ~0.259 to 0.24466.
instance.action: Always verify the submission assignment points to the final combined blend columns, not an intermediate per-modality blend. A single-line fix (v120) switching from the raw-EEG-only blend to the overall blend recovered ~0.015 in KL divergence.

general.goal: How can one avoid accidentally submitting partial ensemble predictions when the pipeline maintains multiple intermediate and final blend variables?
general.context: A multi-stage ensemble pipeline stores predictions at several aggregation levels (per-model, per-modality, overall). During iterative development, the submission output assignment can inadvertently point to an intermediate rather than the final blend.
general.action: After any refactor, explicitly check that the submission output references the final combined blend variable. Name intermediate and final prediction columns with a clear hierarchy. Treat the submission assignment line as a critical checkpoint and verify it matches the intended aggregation level before each submission.

episode.objective: Add mel-spectrogram feature extraction and MaxViT/ConvNeXt mel-spectrogram models to ensemble
episode.outcome: Scores 0.25992–0.26600; worse than best, partially abandoned

instance.goal: Can mel-spectrograms computed from raw EEG via librosa improve the ensemble beyond the existing spectrogram and raw-EEG 2D models?
instance.context: The best LB was 0.24265 using an ensemble of raw-EEG 2D models and pre-computed spectrogram models. Mel-spectrograms offer a different frequency representation that might capture complementary information.
instance.action: Added librosa-based mel-spectrogram extraction from EEG difference signals, loaded MaxViT and ConvNeXt checkpoints trained on mel-spectrograms, ran inference with TTA, and blended predictions. The new mel-spectrogram models alone scored ~0.26, worse than the existing best blend (0.24265), and were not successfully integrated to beat the prior best during this episode.

general.goal: Will adding a new feature representation (alternative spectral transform) to an already-strong ensemble improve the overall score?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models on existing feature representations has reached a strong score. A new spectral feature extraction method is available that could provide complementary signal.
general.action: First test the new feature representation with a single model to gauge standalone quality. If standalone performance is substantially worse than the current best ensemble, the new representation may not add enough diversity to help. Verify by checking whether blending it in improves or hurts the combined score before committing to it.

instance.goal: When a newly added model family hurts the ensemble score, how can the author efficiently diagnose whether the problem is the model, the feature extraction, or the blending?
instance.context: After adding mel-spectrogram MaxViT and ConvNeXt models, the LB worsened from 0.24466 to ~0.26. The author iterated through toggling which models run, swapping checkpoint epochs, switching which model's predictions go into the submission, and fixing variable name bugs across v122–v126.
instance.action: Isolate each new model by submitting its predictions alone (or swapping it in/out of the blend) to see individual contribution. Toggle loop skip conditions to include/exclude specific model indices. Fix variable name mismatches that silently produce wrong outputs. This systematic toggling across 4 micro-edits helped identify that the mel-spectrogram models were not improving the blend.

general.goal: When adding a new component worsens ensemble performance, how can the root cause be isolated efficiently?
general.context: A multi-model ensemble pipeline has many moving parts: feature extraction, model weights, output normalization, and blending weights. A new component was added and the score degraded.
general.action: Submit predictions from each new model in isolation to measure standalone quality. Then toggle inclusion/exclusion of each model in the blend via loop skip conditions. Check for variable name or column assignment bugs that silently use wrong predictions. Only after confirming a model helps individually and the plumbing is correct, include it in the final blend.

episode.objective: Tune which model groups and checkpoints contribute to ensemble, remove mel-spectrogram models
episode.lever: ensemble member selection and checkpoint tuning
episode.outcome: New best 0.24021 at v134 after removing mel-spectrogram

instance.goal: Are the mel-spectrogram models (MaxViT, ConvNeXt on mel features) actually helping the ensemble, or are they hurting the blended score?
instance.context: Mel-spectrogram models were added in v120-v122 and never clearly improved the best score. Over v126-v133 the author toggled various model groups on/off, swapped checkpoints, and tested individual model outputs, but scores stayed worse than the prior best (0.24265). The mel-spectrogram models were still included in the blend.
instance.action: In v134, removed all mel-spectrogram feature extraction and prediction code (commented out concatenation, normalization, assignment), removed stray 'continue' statements blocking other model loops, and re-enabled the intended raw-EEG and spectrogram models. This yielded a new best of 0.24021, confirming mel-spectrogram models were hurting.

general.goal: Is a recently added model family actually contributing positively to the ensemble, or is it degrading the blended score?
general.context: A new feature representation and associated models were added to an ensemble but the combined score has not improved beyond the previous best, despite several rounds of checkpoint and weight tuning.
general.action: Completely disable the suspect model family (remove its predictions from the blend) while ensuring all other intended models run correctly. Compare the resulting score to the best achieved with the family included. If the score improves, permanently remove that family and clean up its code.

instance.goal: How can the correct ensemble composition be identified when many model groups, checkpoint variants, and skip/continue flags interact in the inference notebook?
instance.context: Across v126-v133, the author repeatedly swapped checkpoint filenames, toggled 'continue' statements to skip/enable model groups, and changed which prediction columns fed the submission. Many versions were not submitted or scored worse, often due to bugs (wrong column variable, stray continues blocking models). The best result came only after a systematic fix in v134.
instance.action: Iterate by: (1) changing one model group or checkpoint set at a time, (2) submitting single-model predictions to gauge individual quality (v129, v131, v132), (3) fixing column references and stray skips before blending (v129 fix, v130 fix), and (4) once individual quality is known, enabling all intended models and submitting the blend (v130, v134). Always verify the submission actually uses the intended prediction columns.

general.goal: How can one efficiently search over which model groups and checkpoints to include in a multi-model ensemble when the inference pipeline has many toggles?
general.context: An inference notebook has multiple model families, each with selectable checkpoints and skip flags. Bugs from wrong column names or leftover skip statements frequently produce misleading scores.
general.action: First, test each model group in isolation by skipping all others and submitting its solo predictions to establish per-group quality. Fix any column-reference or control-flow bugs before blending. Then enable all groups that individually score well, blend them, and submit. After each change, verify the submission file actually contains the intended columns. Remove groups whose solo score is much worse than the blend target.

episode.objective: Clean up mel-spectrogram code and fine-tune spectrogram ConvNeXt checkpoints
episode.outcome: New best 0.24011 at v136

instance.goal: After disabling mel-spectrogram models improved the score to 0.24021, is there further gain from cleaning up the dead code and fine-tuning which checkpoint epochs are loaded for the remaining ConvNeXt spectrogram models?
instance.context: The mel-spectrogram model family was disabled in v134 yielding a new best (0.24021). Its code still existed in the notebook, adding complexity. The ConvNeXt spectrogram models had multiple saved checkpoints per fold from different training epochs.
instance.action: First, fully removed all mel-spectrogram model code (loads, transforms, prediction loops, buffers) to simplify the pipeline. Then swapped the per-fold ConvNeXt checkpoint files to different epoch snapshots (e.g., fold_1 epoch_7→epoch_6, fold_3 epoch_7→epoch_4). This yielded a marginal improvement from 0.24021 to 0.24011.

general.goal: After removing a model family from an ensemble improved the score, can further small gains be extracted from the remaining models without adding new components?
general.context: An ensemble improved when a weaker model family was dropped. Multiple checkpoint snapshots (from different training epochs) exist for each fold of the surviving models.
general.action: First, delete all dead code for the removed model family to reduce complexity and runtime. Then systematically try different epoch checkpoints for each fold of the remaining models, submitting to see if a different combination yields a small score improvement. Expect only marginal gains (on the order of noise) from checkpoint swapping alone.

instance.goal: When an ensemble component (mel-spectrogram models) hurts the score, what is the right sequence of actions—disable, verify improvement, then clean up, or clean up immediately?
instance.context: In v134 the mel-spectrogram models were disabled (skipped) and the score improved to 0.24021. The code for those models still remained in the notebook.
instance.action: The author first confirmed the score improvement by submitting with the models disabled (v134), then in a separate step (v135) fully removed the code. This two-phase approach (disable → verify → remove) ensured the improvement was real before permanently deleting code.

general.goal: When removing an ensemble component appears beneficial, how should the removal be staged to avoid losing the ability to revert?
general.context: A component was disabled (but not deleted) and the score improved. The code is still present and could be re-enabled.
general.action: Use a two-phase approach: first disable the component and submit to confirm the improvement on the leaderboard, then in a follow-up commit fully remove the dead code. This preserves the option to revert if the improvement was spurious, while eventually reducing complexity and runtime.

episode.objective: Add 50/30/10s spectrogram feature extraction and MaxViT+ConvNeXt models, rebalance blend
episode.outcome: New best 0.23959 at v139

instance.goal: Can adding multi-resolution spectrogram features (50s/30s/10s windows) as a new model input improve the ensemble beyond the existing single-resolution spectrogram and raw EEG models?
instance.context: The ensemble already blends raw EEG 2D models and single-resolution spectrogram models at LB 0.24011. The author has access to trained MaxViT and ConvNeXt checkpoints on multi-resolution spectrograms.
instance.action: First add the feature extraction code and one MaxViT model (v137, LB 0.25352 — worse because other models were skipped). Then add a ConvNeXt model for the same features (v138, LB 0.25665 — still incomplete). Finally re-enable all skipped model loops, include the new model group in the blend, rebalance weights across all groups, and submit the full blend (v139, LB 0.23959 — new best).

general.goal: Can extracting features at multiple temporal resolutions from the same signal and feeding them to additional models improve an ensemble that already uses a single resolution?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse backbones on one feature representation has plateaued; the underlying signal contains information at multiple time scales that a single resolution may not fully capture.
general.action: Create multi-resolution feature extraction (e.g., spectrograms at several window lengths), train or load models on these features, and blend their predictions into the existing ensemble. Rebalance blend weights to accommodate the new model group.

instance.goal: Why does adding a seemingly beneficial new model cause the leaderboard score to regress before eventually improving?
instance.context: Adding the 50/30/10s MaxViT model alone (v137) worsened the score from 0.24011 to 0.25352. Adding ConvNeXt on top (v138) gave 0.25665. Only after removing stray 'continue' statements that were skipping other model inference loops and rebalancing blend weights (v139) did the score reach a new best of 0.23959.
instance.action: When integrating a new model into a complex inference notebook, check that all existing model loops still execute (no accidental skips from debug statements). After confirming all models run, rebalance blend weights across all groups before evaluating the combined ensemble.

general.goal: How can temporary score regressions during incremental model integration be diagnosed and resolved?
general.context: Adding a new model to an inference pipeline sometimes accidentally disables or skips existing models (e.g., leftover debug statements), making the new addition appear harmful when the real issue is that the rest of the ensemble is broken.
general.action: After each integration step, verify that every model in the pipeline actually produces predictions (check for stray early-exit or skip statements). Only evaluate the new model's contribution after confirming the full ensemble runs end-to-end, then rebalance blend weights.

episode.objective: Try pseudo-labeled spectrogram MaxViT checkpoints and sweep checkpoint variants
episode.outcome: Regressed to 0.25994–0.26137; abandoned

instance.goal: Can pseudo-labeled checkpoints for the spectrogram MaxViT model improve the ensemble score beyond the current best of 0.23959?
instance.context: The author had reached a new best LB of 0.23959 with a multi-model ensemble. Pseudo-labeled checkpoints (trained on unlabeled data with model-generated labels) were available for the spectrogram MaxViT model family.
instance.action: Isolated the pseudo-labeled spectrogram MaxViT model by disabling all other model groups (inserting 'continue' statements), submitted its standalone predictions (LB 0.25994), then swept different per-fold checkpoint files across two more submissions (LB 0.25930, 0.26137). All three results were substantially worse than the prior ensemble best, indicating the pseudo-labeled checkpoints alone did not help.

general.goal: Will models trained with pseudo-labels on unlabeled data outperform or complement models trained only on labeled data?
general.context: An ensemble has reached a strong baseline score. Checkpoints from a semi-supervised (pseudo-label) training run are available for one model family in the ensemble.
general.action: First evaluate the pseudo-labeled model in isolation (disable other ensemble members) to measure its standalone quality. If it underperforms the existing ensemble substantially, sweeping checkpoint variants is unlikely to close the gap. Avoid blending it in until its standalone quality is competitive with the component it would replace.

instance.goal: Which per-fold checkpoint files yield the best inference performance for the spectrogram MaxViT model?
instance.context: Multiple saved checkpoints per fold exist (different epochs, different validation KL-divergence values in filenames). The author tested three different checkpoint combinations across v140–v142, getting LB scores of 0.25994, 0.25930, and 0.26137—all close together and all far from the ensemble best.
instance.action: Swapped checkpoint filenames fold-by-fold across two iterations, observing only marginal differences (±0.002). The small variation confirmed that checkpoint selection within this model family was not the bottleneck; the model family itself was weaker than the existing ensemble components.

general.goal: How much score variation can be expected from swapping saved checkpoints (different epochs or validation scores) for the same model architecture?
general.context: A model family is being evaluated in isolation and multiple checkpoint files per fold are available, each saved at different training epochs with slightly different validation metrics.
general.action: Swap checkpoints across two or three submissions. If the score varies only marginally (small fraction of the gap to the target), conclude that checkpoint selection is not the limiting factor and redirect effort to model architecture, training strategy, or ensemble composition instead.

episode.objective: Add multitaper spectrogram models with new transforms/TTA, then clean up unused models and transforms
episode.outcome: New best 0.23482 at v148 after cleanup

instance.goal: Can adding multitaper spectrogram features and new model families improve the ensemble beyond the current best of 0.23959?
instance.context: The author had a well-tuned ensemble at LB 0.23959. They introduced multitaper spectrogram computation, new transforms (FlipAlongAxis, FlipHemispheres, EEG3Dto2D), parallel I/O, and new MaxViT/ConvNeXt models trained on these features. The initial submission scored 0.66363, indicating severe bugs or misalignment.
instance.action: Iteratively debugged the new pipeline: fixed spectrogram input to use differenced EEG signals (v144, v145), re-ran to get 0.27167 (v146), tried adding ConvNeXt and blending (v147, 0.28616), then stripped out the underperforming new models and unused transforms (v148) to reach 0.23482, a new best. The cleanup of failed additions was key to recovering and surpassing the prior best.

general.goal: When adding a new feature extraction pipeline and model family to an existing ensemble, how can one recover if the addition degrades performance?
general.context: A new feature type and associated models are added to a mature ensemble but cause a large score regression, indicating bugs or poor-quality predictions contaminating the blend.
general.action: First fix obvious data-flow bugs (e.g., wrong input variable fed to feature extraction). Then submit to confirm partial recovery. If the new component still underperforms, remove it and its associated transforms/models entirely rather than continuing to tune it. The cleanup itself can yield a new best if it also removes previously-accumulated dead code that was subtly interfering.

instance.goal: Why did the score jump from 0.26137 to 0.66363 after adding multitaper spectrogram models and new transforms?
instance.context: The v143 submission introduced many new components simultaneously: multitaper spectrogram generation, new image transforms, new model checkpoints, parallel I/O changes, and updated blending. The massive score regression (0.66 vs prior 0.26) indicated a bug rather than a modeling issue.
instance.action: The author identified that the spectrogram was computed from raw EEG instead of differenced EEG (fixed in v144-v145), then re-ran (v146) recovering to 0.27. This confirmed the input mismatch was the primary bug. The lesson: when adding a complex new pipeline, a single wrong variable reference can catastrophically degrade results.

general.goal: What is the most likely cause when adding a new feature pipeline causes a catastrophic score regression rather than a modest change?
general.context: A large new feature extraction module is integrated and the score degrades by an order of magnitude, far beyond what a poor-but-valid model would produce.
general.action: Check that the correct intermediate data is being fed into the new feature extraction (e.g., preprocessed vs. raw signals). A single variable name error at the input of the pipeline is the most common cause of catastrophic regression. Fix the input wiring first before evaluating whether the new features help.

instance.goal: After fixing bugs, the multitaper spectrogram models score 0.27-0.29 standalone — should they be kept in the ensemble or removed?
instance.context: The existing ensemble without multitaper models scored 0.23959. After bug fixes, the multitaper MaxViT scored ~0.27 and adding ConvNeXt blend scored 0.286. These components were weaker than the existing ensemble members.
instance.action: The author removed the multitaper spectrogram models, their transforms, and associated loading code (v148), achieving 0.23482 — a new best. Removing weak ensemble members that dilute strong predictions improved the final score.

general.goal: When a new model component scores substantially worse than existing ensemble members, does including it help or hurt the blend?
general.context: A new model family produces predictions that are individually much worse than the current ensemble's score. Blending it in with any positive weight would pull the ensemble toward its weaker predictions.
general.action: Remove the weaker component entirely from the ensemble rather than trying to down-weight it. Even small blend weights on a substantially worse model can hurt, and removing dead code paths may also eliminate subtle side effects on shared data structures or preprocessing.

episode.objective: Sweep checkpoint variants and model group selections across raw EEG and spectrogram models to find optimal ensemble composition
episode.lever: ensemble member selection and checkpoint tuning
episode.outcome: New best 0.23032 at v158 with all models enabled

instance.goal: How can the best combination of model groups and checkpoints be identified for the ensemble when there are multiple model families (MaxViT, ConvNeXt) and input types (raw EEG, spectrograms)?
instance.context: The author had achieved 0.23482 after a cleanup. Multiple model groups (raw EEG 50s, raw EEG 50_10s, spectrogram 50s, spectrogram 50_10s) with MaxViT and ConvNeXt variants were available, each with multiple checkpoint options per fold.
instance.action: Systematically isolated individual model groups by inserting 'continue' statements to skip other groups, submitted each alone to get its standalone LB score, swapped checkpoint filenames within groups, then re-enabled all models and submitted the blended ensemble. The best single-model scores guided which checkpoints to keep. Final step (v158) removed all skips and used the blend, achieving 0.23032.

general.goal: How can the best combination of model groups and checkpoints be identified when building a multi-model ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of several model families is available, each with multiple saved checkpoint variants per fold. The combined blend has been performing well but individual component quality is uncertain.
general.action: Isolate each model group by disabling all others, submit to get its standalone score, and swap checkpoint files within each group to find the best variant. Once the best checkpoint per group is identified, re-enable all groups and submit the full blend. This confirms each component's contribution and avoids carrying weak members.

instance.goal: After tuning individual model groups, does the full blended ensemble outperform the best single model group?
instance.context: Individual model groups scored between 0.242 and 0.267 when submitted alone. The previous best blend was 0.23482. The author had updated checkpoints for several groups during the isolation sweep.
instance.action: After finding the best checkpoints per group via isolation, removed all 'continue' statements and switched submission to use blend_prediction_columns. The resulting blend scored 0.23032, substantially better than any single group, confirming the ensemble benefit and that the sweep improved component quality.

general.goal: After individually optimizing ensemble components, does recombining them into a blend recover or exceed the previous best ensemble score?
general.context: Individual components have been tuned via isolated evaluation and each scores worse than the prior full blend, but their checkpoint selections have been updated.
general.action: Re-enable all optimized components and submit the full weighted blend. Expect the blend to outperform every individual component and potentially beat the prior best, since each member is now individually stronger. If the blend does not improve, a component may be hurting diversity and should be removed.

episode.objective: Test individual model groups (MaxViT, ConvNeXt) vs full blend to confirm blend is best
episode.outcome: New best 0.22875 at v162 with full blend enabled

instance.goal: Is the full blended ensemble actually better than any individual model group (MaxViT or ConvNeXt alone)?
instance.context: The best score so far (0.23032) came from the full blend at v158. The author had been frequently toggling between single-model submissions and blended submissions without systematically confirming the blend's superiority with the current checkpoint set.
instance.action: Tested MaxViT alone (0.23961), ConvNeXt alone (0.24241), MaxViT with different checkpoints (0.24034), then re-enabled all models and submitted the blend (0.22875, new best). This confirmed the blend outperforms every individual component and yielded a meaningful improvement.

general.goal: How can one verify that a multi-model ensemble is actually better than its individual components rather than being dragged down by a weak member?
general.context: After assembling a blend of several model groups, the ensemble score has improved but it is unclear whether every member contributes positively or whether a single strong member alone would suffice.
general.action: Systematically submit each model group in isolation, record its standalone score, then submit the full blend. If the blend beats every individual member, keep it; if a member scores worse than the blend margin, consider dropping it. This ablation should be repeated whenever checkpoints or members change.

instance.goal: After updating checkpoints for individual model groups, does the previously-optimal blend still hold or does it need re-verification?
instance.context: Between v158 and v162, new MaxViT and ConvNeXt checkpoints were swapped in. The individual model scores changed (MaxViT: 0.23961→0.24034 with different checkpoints; ConvNeXt: 0.24241), so the blend composition may have shifted.
instance.action: After testing updated individual checkpoints, re-enabled all models and re-submitted the blend, achieving 0.22875 — a new best that surpassed the previous blend (0.23032). This confirms that after checkpoint updates, the blend must be re-evaluated end-to-end.

general.goal: When component models in an ensemble are retrained or their checkpoints are updated, does the ensemble automatically improve or must it be re-validated?
general.context: Individual model weights have been updated (new training runs or different epoch selections), and the ensemble was previously the best submission strategy.
general.action: After any checkpoint change, re-run the full ensemble and submit it rather than assuming the old blend weights and composition remain optimal. Even if individual components score slightly differently, the blend can still improve if the components remain diverse.

episode.objective: Add 30/10s spectrogram models (MaxViT, ConvNeXt variants), sweep checkpoints, and finalize ensemble blend weights
episode.lever: 30/10s spectrogram models and final blend tuning
episode.outcome: New best 0.22780 at v170 with expanded blend

instance.goal: How much can adding a new spectrogram resolution (30/10s) with additional model architectures (MaxViT, ConvNeXt, ConvNeXt-Base) improve the ensemble beyond the current best of 0.22875?
instance.context: The author had an ensemble of 50s and 50/10s spectrogram models plus raw EEG models achieving 0.22875. They hypothesized that a different temporal resolution (30/10s spectrograms) could provide complementary signal.
instance.action: First isolated the new model by disabling existing ensemble members (v162→v163), tested it standalone (v164→v165, LB 0.23667), then added MaxViT and ConvNeXt variants for the new resolution (v166–v169), and finally re-enabled all models and tuned blend weights to produce the full ensemble (v170, LB 0.22780 new best).

general.goal: How much can a new input representation at a different temporal/spatial resolution improve an existing ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of models operating at one or two resolutions has plateaued, and there is reason to believe a different resolution captures complementary information.
general.action: First evaluate the new-resolution model in isolation by disabling other ensemble members to confirm it has reasonable standalone performance. Then try multiple backbone architectures for that resolution. Finally re-enable all members and tune blend weights. Only adopt the new member if the full blend improves over the previous best.

instance.goal: What is the most effective way to integrate new model groups into an existing multi-model ensemble without regressing the score?
instance.context: The author's workflow involved toggling 'continue' statements to skip/enable model inference loops, testing individual models' predictions as the submission, then switching back to blended predictions. Standalone scores of new models (0.236–0.242) were worse than the existing ensemble (0.228), but the blend improved to 0.227.
instance.action: Used a disable-all-but-one pattern: insert 'continue' in loops to skip existing models, submit the new model alone, iterate on its checkpoints/architecture, then remove the 'continue' statements to re-enable all models and submit the blend. The final blend beat both the old ensemble and any individual model.

general.goal: How can a new model component be safely tested and integrated into a production ensemble without risking score regression?
general.context: The ensemble has many model groups whose inference is expensive; running all of them for every experiment is slow, and a bad new member could hurt the blend.
general.action: Gate each model's inference loop with a skip flag. To evaluate a candidate, disable all other members and submit the candidate alone to gauge its standalone quality. Iterate on its checkpoints or backbone variants in isolation. Once satisfied, re-enable all members, adjust blend weights, and verify the full ensemble improves over the previous best before adopting the change.

episode.objective: Build initial pipeline with Conv1D wave block, EEG filtering, spectrogram normalization and verify baseline performance.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.37463 at v6 after iterative fixes and reruns.

instance.goal: How much improvement can be gained by adding a 1D convolutional wave block for raw EEG processing, adjusting bandpass filter ranges, and changing spectrogram normalization from per-image to whole-sample?
instance.context: Baseline pipeline using spectrograms with a CNN scored 0.42923 on KL-divergence leaderboard. EEG signals were being filtered but not processed through dedicated temporal convolution layers.
instance.action: Added a Conv1D wave block module for EEG feature extraction, switched from per-image standardization to whole-sample standardization for spectrograms, adjusted the butter filter range, and increased epochs from 4 to 5. This yielded LB 0.40619 (−0.023 improvement).

general.goal: How much can a spectrogram-only pipeline be improved by adding a dedicated temporal convolution branch for the raw time-series signal?
general.context: A baseline that only uses frequency-domain representations (spectrograms) of physiological signals fed to an image backbone has plateaued.
general.action: Add a 1D convolutional branch that processes the raw time-series in parallel with the spectrogram branch. Also switch normalization from per-patch to per-sample scope, and verify the bandpass filter design matches the frequency range of interest. Expect a meaningful but not dramatic first-step gain.

instance.goal: How much further improvement comes from fixing spectrogram clipping/cropping bugs, correcting the filter design for different filter types, and adding L2 normalization to embeddings?
instance.context: After adding the wave block the score was 0.40619. Inspection revealed the butter filter was misusing list vs scalar for lowpass/highpass, spectrogram lower clip at exp(−4) was too aggressive, and cropping/resizing logic had placement issues.
instance.action: Made filter design conditional (lowpass/highpass/bandpass) to handle scalar vs list correctly, lowered spectrogram clip floor from exp(−4) to exp(−6), reworked cropping/resizing/centering logic, and added L2 normalization to embeddings. Score improved to 0.37463 (−0.032 improvement).

general.goal: After adding a new feature branch, where should one look for the next round of gains—architecture changes or fixing preprocessing details?
general.context: A multi-branch model has been assembled and shows improvement, but preprocessing steps (signal filtering, spectrogram clipping, spatial alignment of inputs) were written quickly and may contain subtle bugs or overly aggressive truncation.
general.action: Audit each preprocessing step for correctness: verify filter design handles edge cases (e.g., different filter types requiring different parameter shapes), relax aggressive clipping thresholds that discard useful dynamic range, and fix spatial alignment (crop/resize/center) of inputs. These bug fixes and tuning of preprocessing can yield gains comparable to or larger than the architectural addition itself.

episode.objective: Refactor data loading, add einops/Rearrange, fix EEG time indexing, increase EEG channels, and adjust model input dimensions.
episode.lever: EEG input channels and time indexing
episode.outcome: Score 0.37612 at v12, slight regression from v6 best 0.37463.

instance.goal: Can expanding the EEG input representation (more channels, fixed time indexing, better normalization) improve the model's score beyond 0.37463?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.37463. The EEG data generator used 4 channels and had a time-index bug (not multiplying by sampling rate). The author also wanted to add einops Rearrange and per-sample normalization.
instance.action: Fixed time_start/time_stop by multiplying by 200 (sampling rate), increased EEG channels from 4 to 6, added tf.image.resize and per-sample normalization, imported einops (then commented it out when it caused dependency issues), pointed to a different model checkpoint directory. Final submission scored 0.37612, slightly worse than the 0.37463 baseline.

general.goal: Will enriching the raw signal input (more derived channels, corrected indexing, additional normalization) improve a model that already performs well on spectral features?
general.context: A pipeline combining spectrograms and raw time-series signals has reached a strong baseline. The time-series branch uses fewer derived channels than available and has a suspected indexing bug in how signal windows are extracted.
general.action: Fix the window extraction to use the correct sampling rate, increase the number of derived input channels, and add per-sample normalization. After making these changes, retrain or load updated checkpoints and compare the leaderboard score. If the score does not improve, the additional channels or normalization may be adding noise or the checkpoint was not properly retrained on the new inputs.

instance.goal: How can dependency and infrastructure issues (missing einops, wrong pip syntax, wrong model path) be resolved quickly in a Kaggle notebook environment?
instance.context: After a major code change (v7→v8), the notebook failed to run: pip install lacked '!' prefix, einops was not available in the Kaggle environment, and the model checkpoint path was incorrect. Three consecutive micro-fixes were needed (v8→v9, v9→v10, v10→v11).
instance.action: Added '!' to the pip install line, commented out the einops import that wasn't available, and corrected the model directory name. Each fix was a separate commit/version, iterating until the notebook ran successfully.

general.goal: How can a series of runtime failures after a large refactor be debugged efficiently in a cloud notebook environment?
general.context: A major code change introduced multiple small breakages simultaneously: a shell command syntax error, a missing third-party library, and an incorrect file path. Each failure only surfaces after the previous one is fixed.
general.action: Fix one infrastructure issue per run, starting with the earliest failure in execution order (package installation syntax, then missing imports, then file paths). Keep each fix minimal so the next error is clearly attributable. Avoid bundling large feature changes with environment changes to reduce the number of debug iterations.

episode.objective: Major refactor of preprocessing, spectrogram/EEG sizing, add early stopping, switch to EfficientNetB0, fold-averaged predictions, and cosine scheduler.
episode.lever: model backbone and training pipeline overhaul
episode.outcome: New best 0.36216 at v22 after switching to B0 and fold averaging.

instance.goal: After a large refactor (new preprocessing, EfficientNetB0, cosine scheduler, fold averaging), the LB regressed from 0.37612 to 0.42974 — how to diagnose and recover?
instance.context: v12→v14 introduced many simultaneous changes (SFREQ 200→100, HIGH 128→512, early stopping, new EEG cropping, model changes) and LB worsened by ~0.05. The author could not isolate which change caused the regression because too many things changed at once.
instance.action: The author iteratively reverted and re-applied subsets of changes across v15–v21: first restoring SFREQ to 200 and HIGH to 128 (v15), fixing dependency issues (v16–v17), testing that config (v18: 0.37934, close to baseline), then trying the alternative config again (v19–v20: 0.41352, still worse), and finally combining the better preprocessing settings with the new model backbone (EfficientNetB0) and fold-averaged predictions (v21–v22: 0.36216, new best).

general.goal: A large multi-factor refactor caused a score regression — how to recover and find which changes help versus hurt?
general.context: When many changes (data preprocessing, model architecture, training schedule) are applied simultaneously and the metric worsens, the root cause is ambiguous.
general.action: Revert to the last known-good configuration, then re-introduce changes in smaller groups, submitting after each group. First restore the data pipeline settings that were known to work, verify the score recovers, then layer on architecture and training changes one group at a time. This isolates which factor caused the regression and which additions actually improve the score.

instance.goal: The best single-fold EfficientNet predictions scored 0.37612; can fold-averaged predictions improve the score further?
instance.context: In v21 the author switched to EfficientNetB0 and added fold-averaged (ensembled) predictions across K-fold models, combined with the preprocessing settings (SFREQ=200, HIGH=128) that had previously worked well.
instance.action: Average predictions across all fold models at inference time instead of using a single fold's prediction. This, combined with the backbone and preprocessing refinements, achieved 0.36216 — a new best, improving by ~0.014 over the previous best of 0.37463.

general.goal: Single-model inference has plateaued — can the submission score be improved without changing the training procedure?
general.context: Multiple fold models are available from cross-validation training, and the metric rewards well-calibrated probability distributions.
general.action: Average the predicted probability distributions from all fold models for each test sample. This reduces prediction variance and typically improves calibration, yielding a better score on distribution-matching metrics like KL divergence.

instance.goal: Two different spectrogram frequency resolutions (HIGH=128 vs HIGH=512) and sampling rates (SFREQ=200 vs 100) were tried — which combination works better for this EEG classification task?
instance.context: v14 used SFREQ=100, HIGH=512 and scored 0.42974. v18 restored SFREQ=200, HIGH=128 and scored 0.37934. v20 tried SFREQ=100, HIGH=512 again and scored 0.41352. The lower-resolution spectrogram with higher sampling rate consistently scored better.
instance.action: Kept SFREQ=200 and HIGH=128 (lower spectrogram frequency bins, higher temporal sampling rate) in the final best submission (v22: 0.36216). The higher-resolution spectrogram setting was abandoned after two failed attempts.

general.goal: What resolution and sampling rate for input spectrograms yields the best classification performance?
general.context: Higher frequency resolution in spectrograms increases input dimensionality but may add noise or exceed the model's capacity to exploit, while a higher temporal sampling rate preserves more temporal detail in the raw signal.
general.action: Test both high-frequency-resolution and low-frequency-resolution spectrogram settings with corresponding sampling rates. If the higher-resolution setting degrades the score on two separate attempts while the lower-resolution setting consistently performs better, commit to the lower-resolution setting and move on to other improvements.

episode.objective: Convert spectrograms to RGB colormapped images and add ImageNet-style per-channel normalization for pretrained backbone.
episode.outcome: Score 0.36532 at v26, did not beat v22 best of 0.36216.

instance.goal: Can converting single-channel log-spectrograms to RGB via a jet colormap improve a pretrained EfficientNet backbone's performance on EEG spectrograms?
instance.context: The best LB score was 0.36216 using grayscale/4-channel spectrogram input to EfficientNetB0. Pretrained ImageNet backbones expect 3-channel RGB input and their learned filters are tuned for natural color images.
instance.action: Applied a jet colormap to map log-scaled spectrogram values into 3-channel RGB images, adjusting the data generator output shape from (H,L,4) to (H,L,3,4). Submitted and got 0.37436, which was worse than the previous best 0.36216, indicating the colormap conversion alone did not help.

general.goal: Will converting single-channel spectrograms to pseudo-color RGB images improve a pretrained image classification backbone?
general.context: A pretrained backbone trained on natural RGB images is being fed non-RGB input (e.g., grayscale or multi-channel spectrograms). The hypothesis is that colormap-based RGB conversion better matches the pretrained feature detectors.
general.action: Apply a standard colormap (e.g., jet) to map scalar spectrogram values to 3-channel RGB, then feed to the pretrained backbone. Compare against the baseline input format on the leaderboard or validation. Be aware this may not help and can even hurt if the original channel encoding already carries useful information.

instance.goal: After converting spectrograms to RGB colormap images, does adding ImageNet per-channel normalization (mean=[0.485,0.456,0.406], std=[0.229,0.224,0.225]) recover or improve performance?
instance.context: The jet-colormap RGB approach scored 0.37436, worse than the 0.36216 baseline. The RGB values were not yet normalized to match ImageNet statistics that the pretrained EfficientNet expects. Also adjusted cmin/cmax from (-6,8) to (-4,6) to change the dynamic range mapping.
instance.action: Added explicit per-channel normalization using ImageNet mean and std² in the data generator, and tightened the spectrogram clipping range. Submitted and got 0.36532, which improved over the unnormalized colormap version (0.37436) but still did not beat the original best (0.36216).

general.goal: When feeding transformed images to a pretrained backbone, how much does matching the original training normalization statistics matter?
general.context: A pretrained backbone receives inputs that have been transformed (e.g., colormapped) but not yet normalized to the statistics the backbone was trained with. The unnormalized version underperforms the baseline.
general.action: Apply the exact per-channel mean and standard deviation normalization that the pretrained backbone was trained with. This typically recovers a significant portion of the performance gap, but may not fully close it if the underlying representation change (e.g., colormap vs. original channels) is suboptimal. Evaluate and compare against both the unnormalized variant and the original baseline to decide whether to keep the transformation.

episode.objective: Try EfficientNetV2 backbone variants and adjust learning rates, batch sizes, and class-balanced sampling.
episode.outcome: V2 regressed (0.38683 v29, 0.43849 v32); reverted to B0/B2 and got 0.36890 at v34.

instance.goal: Will switching from EfficientNetB0 to EfficientNetV2B0 as the spectrogram backbone improve the KL divergence score?
instance.context: The best score so far was 0.36216 with EfficientNetB0. The author tried EfficientNetV2B0 with matching pretrained weights and got 0.38683, a regression of ~0.025.
instance.action: Swapped the backbone to EfficientNetV2B0, submitted, observed the score regressed, then reverted back to EfficientNetB0 in subsequent steps.

general.goal: When a newer variant of the same model family is available, will it improve performance as a drop-in replacement for the current backbone?
general.context: A working pipeline with a specific pretrained backbone has an established baseline score. A newer architecture variant exists but the rest of the pipeline (input sizes, normalization, learning rate) was tuned for the original backbone.
general.action: Swap the backbone and submit without changing other hyperparameters to get a quick signal. If the score regresses, revert rather than investing time tuning around the new backbone, unless there is a strong prior that the new variant is superior and the regression is likely due to mismatched settings.

instance.goal: Can class-balanced sampling per batch, a lower learning rate (1e-4), and adjusted batch sizes improve the score?
instance.context: After reverting to EfficientNetB0, the author added per-batch class-balanced sampling (~batch_size/6 per class), reduced LR from 1e-3 to 1e-4, and changed batch sizes (16→18). This scored 0.43849, a severe regression from the 0.36216 baseline.
instance.action: Observed the large regression, then in the next step reverted: removed class-balanced sampling, restored LR to 1e-3, restored original batch sizes, and tried a larger EEG backbone (B2). The resulting score of 0.36890 was close to the original baseline, confirming the class-balanced sampling and low LR were harmful.

general.goal: How should multiple training changes (sampling strategy, learning rate, batch size) be evaluated to identify which ones help or hurt?
general.context: Several changes were applied simultaneously and the score regressed severely. Without isolated experiments, it is unclear which change caused the regression.
general.action: When a bundle of changes causes a large regression, revert all of them at once to recover the baseline, then re-introduce changes one at a time. Avoid combining a new sampling strategy with a large learning-rate reduction and batch-size change in a single experiment, as the confounded result wastes a submission and delays diagnosis.

episode.objective: Sweep spectrogram height, EEG channel count (4/6/8), and EfficientNet variant (B0/B2) for the EEG branch.
episode.lever: EEG input dimensions and backbone size
episode.outcome: Scores ranged 0.36596–0.39003; best 0.36596 at v36, no improvement over v22.

instance.goal: What combination of spectrogram height, EEG channel count, and EfficientNet backbone size yields the best score for the EEG branch?
instance.context: Best LB was 0.36216 (v22) with EfficientNetB0. Recent attempts with B2 (v33-34) scored 0.36890. The author now sweeps spectrogram height (64 vs 128), EEG channels (4, 6, 8), and backbone (B0 vs B2) across v34-v41.
instance.action: Systematically varied three axes: reduced spectrogram height from 128→64 (v35, scored 0.366), reverted to 128 but changed LENGTH (v37, scored 0.370), swapped B2→B0 (v38, scored 0.382), expanded EEG channels 6→8 with B2 (v39-40, scored 0.384), then reduced to 4 channels (v41, scored 0.390). The best configuration in this sweep was the first (height=64, 6 channels, B2) at 0.366, but none beat the prior best 0.362.

general.goal: How should multiple interacting architectural dimensions (input resolution, number of input channels, backbone capacity) be explored efficiently?
general.context: Several design axes interact: input spatial resolution, number of signal channels fed to the model, and backbone size. Changing one may require re-training and re-evaluating on the leaderboard.
general.action: Change one axis at a time and submit to measure its isolated effect. Start from the best-known configuration, vary one dimension, record the score, then revert if it worsens before trying the next axis. When a larger backbone paired with more input channels does not improve over a smaller backbone with fewer channels, prefer the simpler configuration.
