instance.goal: Does increasing the EEG channel count (from 6 to 8) paired with a larger backbone (B2) improve the score?
instance.context: With 6 EEG channels and EfficientNetB2, the score was 0.366-0.370. Switching to B0 with 6 channels worsened to 0.382. The author then tried 8 channels with B2 (v39-40, 0.384) and 4 channels with B2 (v41, 0.390).
instance.action: Expanding EEG channels from 6→8 and reducing to 4 both worsened the score compared to the 6-channel baseline. The original 6-channel configuration remained best, suggesting the default channel grouping was already near-optimal and adding or removing channels introduces noise or loses information.

general.goal: Does feeding more raw signal channels into a pretrained image backbone improve classification when the backbone was designed for 3-channel images?
general.context: A pretrained image backbone processes multi-channel signal data arranged as image rows. The number of signal channels can be varied (e.g., 4, 6, 8) but must be mapped into the backbone's expected input format.
general.action: Test a small range of channel counts (fewer and more than the current default) while keeping other settings fixed. If both increasing and decreasing the channel count worsen the score, the current count is likely near-optimal. Avoid assuming more channels always help—redundant or noisy channels can hurt when the backbone capacity is fixed.

episode.objective: Add mel-spectrogram branch via librosa, replace colormap with log-clipping, introduce custom loss, and fix tensor concatenation axis.
episode.lever: mel-spectrogram input branch and loss function
episode.outcome: New best 0.35728 at v49 after fixing concat axis and adjusting LENGTH.

instance.goal: Can adding a mel-spectrogram branch (via librosa) to the existing spectrogram+EEG model improve the KL-divergence score?
instance.context: Best LB was 0.36216. The author added a librosa mel-spectrogram branch in v42 (scored 0.36435), removed it in v44 (scored 0.40123), re-added it in v46 (scored 0.39316), then removed it again in v48 (scored 0.38574). None of these mel-branch variants beat the previous best.
instance.action: After three attempts adding/removing the mel-spectrogram branch with no improvement, the author abandoned it in v48 and instead focused on fixing tensor concatenation axis, input length, and validation logic in v49, which achieved a new best of 0.35728.

general.goal: When adding a new input modality branch to a multi-input model, how many attempts should be made before concluding the modality does not help?
general.context: A new input branch is added to a multi-branch model but repeated attempts (add, remove, re-add with different preprocessing) consistently fail to improve the validation metric over the baseline without that branch.
general.action: After two or three cycles of adding and removing the branch with no improvement, abandon the new modality and redirect effort to fixing existing architecture issues (tensor shapes, concatenation axes, input dimensions) which are more likely to yield gains.

instance.goal: What is preventing the model from reaching a new best score despite multiple architectural changes?
instance.context: Across v41–v48, the author tried mel branches, backbone upgrades (B0→B2), different input shapes, and preprocessing changes, but scores ranged 0.36435–0.40123 without beating the 0.36216 best. A Concatenate axis bug (axis=2 instead of axis=1) and wrong LENGTH (32 instead of 256) were present.
instance.action: In v49, the author fixed the Concatenate axis from 2 to 1, restored LENGTH to 256, made validation sampling deterministic, and added loss-curve plotting for diagnosis. This yielded a new best of 0.35728, suggesting the tensor shape bug had been silently degrading all recent experiments.

general.goal: Why do multiple feature-engineering and architecture changes fail to improve the score over a known baseline?
general.context: Several successive experiments with new input branches, backbone sizes, and preprocessing each fail to beat a prior best, suggesting a latent bug may be masking any gains from the new changes.
general.action: Before continuing to iterate on features or architecture, audit the tensor shapes and concatenation operations in the model graph for silent shape mismatches. Fix any axis or dimension bugs first, add diagnostic plots (e.g., training loss curves), and re-evaluate. A single shape bug can nullify many rounds of experimentation.

episode.objective: Iterate on mel-spectrogram branch configuration, spectrogram preprocessing, and sampling frequency.
episode.outcome: Scores 0.36844–0.38197; did not beat v49 best of 0.35728.

instance.goal: Does adding a mel-spectrogram branch (via librosa) alongside the existing spectrogram and EEG branches improve the score beyond the current best of 0.35728?
instance.context: v49 achieved a new best LB of 0.35728 without a mel-spectrogram branch. The author added a mel branch, changed HEIGHT from 128→64, removed RGB colormap mapping, and switched to single-channel spectrogram processing.
instance.action: Added the mel-spectrogram branch and simplified spectrogram preprocessing. LB regressed to 0.36844. Then removed the mel branch in v51, restored RGB colormap mapping, but also changed SFREQ (200→50) and filter range (0.5–40→0.5–20), which further regressed to 0.38197. In v52, reverted SFREQ to 200 and filter range to [0.5, 40], recovering to 0.37019 — still worse than v49's best.

general.goal: When a new input branch or feature source is added to a multi-input model, how can one tell whether the new branch helps versus other simultaneous changes hurting?
general.context: A new best score was just achieved. The practitioner wants to push further by adding a new input modality or feature branch, but also changes preprocessing parameters at the same time.
general.action: Change only one variable at a time: add the new branch while keeping all other preprocessing (image size, sampling rate, filter range, colormap) identical. If the score regresses, revert the branch addition before adjusting other parameters. Bundling a new branch with preprocessing changes makes it impossible to attribute the regression and wastes iterations.

instance.goal: What EEG sampling frequency and bandpass filter range produce the best features for this EEG classification pipeline?
instance.context: v49 (best, 0.35728) used SFREQ=200 and filter_range [0.5, 40]. v51 changed to SFREQ=50 and [0.5, 20], scoring 0.38197. v52 reverted to SFREQ=200 and [0.5, 40], improving to 0.37019, confirming the higher sampling rate and wider bandpass are better.
instance.action: Compared SFREQ=50/filter [0.5,20] vs SFREQ=200/filter [0.5,40]. The higher sampling frequency and wider bandpass consistently scored better (0.37019 vs 0.38197). Kept SFREQ=200 and [0.5, 40] going forward.

general.goal: How does the signal sampling rate and bandpass filter bandwidth affect classification performance on physiological time-series data?
general.context: Reducing the sampling rate and narrowing the bandpass filter saves computation but may discard informative high-frequency content. A prior best result used the higher rate and wider band.
general.action: Test the lower sampling rate and narrower filter as a pair against the original settings. If the score degrades, revert both. Physiological signals (especially brain activity) can carry discriminative information in higher frequency bands, so do not aggressively downsample or narrow the filter without empirical validation.

episode.objective: Add class-balanced mixup augmentation, label-aware cropping, cosine scheduler, and early stopping to improve training robustness.
episode.outcome: Regressed badly to 0.45357 at v55; mixup/sampling changes hurt.

instance.goal: Can adding class-balanced mixup augmentation, label-aware cropping, cosine scheduling, and early stopping improve the current best score of 0.357?
instance.context: The previous best LB was 0.357 with a simpler data pipeline. The author introduced multiple changes at once: lowered SFREQ from 200→100, added class-balanced sampling with mixup in the data generator, replaced random cropping with label-aware cropping, added cosine LR scheduler and early stopping, and changed the model checkpoint path.
instance.action: Bundled all changes together (v52→v53→v54), submitted at v55, and got LB 0.454 — a large regression from 0.357. Then tried switching backbones to EfficientNetV2 variants at v56, which worsened further to 0.509. The author subsequently reverted/simplified in v57.

general.goal: Will combining several training improvements (augmentation, scheduling, sampling strategy, preprocessing changes) in one step yield a net gain?
general.context: A pipeline has reached a competitive score and the practitioner wants to add multiple enhancements (data augmentation, learning-rate scheduling, class-balanced sampling, input resolution changes) simultaneously.
general.action: Avoid bundling many changes in a single iteration: if the combined result regresses, it is impossible to identify which change caused the harm. Instead, add one change at a time, verify each on the leaderboard or a reliable local validation, and only keep changes that individually help or are neutral.

instance.goal: After a large regression from bundled changes, can switching to a larger/newer backbone (EfficientNetV2S / V2B0) recover the lost performance?
instance.context: LB worsened from 0.357 to 0.454 after augmentation and preprocessing changes. The author tried upgrading backbones from EfficientNetB0/B2 to EfficientNetV2S/V2B0 without reverting the other changes, and the score worsened further to 0.509.
instance.action: Swapped backbone architecture and pretrained weights while keeping the already-regressed pipeline. The result was a further degradation, suggesting the backbone change compounded existing issues rather than compensating for them.

general.goal: When performance has regressed due to recent changes, is upgrading the model backbone a good recovery strategy?
general.context: A pipeline has regressed after multiple simultaneous changes to data processing and training. The practitioner considers switching to a larger or newer backbone to compensate.
general.action: Do not layer additional architectural changes on top of an already-regressed pipeline. First revert to the last known-good configuration to isolate the regression cause, then try the backbone upgrade from that stable baseline. Compounding changes on a broken pipeline makes diagnosis harder and typically worsens results.

episode.objective: Replace backbones with EfficientNetV2 variants and add three-sample mixup augmentation.
episode.lever: backbone swap to V2 and multi-sample mixup
episode.outcome: V2 regressed to 0.50856 at v56; three-sample mixup gave 0.41959 at v60; both worse.

instance.goal: Will switching from EfficientNetV2 back to a smaller EfficientNet backbone, simplifying spectrogram preprocessing (per-sample normalization instead of ImageNet constants), and adding three-sample mixup recover or improve performance after a large regression (0.50856)?
instance.context: v55→v56 switched to EfficientNetV2 variants and scored 0.50856, a massive regression from the best of 0.35728. The author's best results came from simpler EfficientNet B0/B2 backbones with direct preprocessing.
instance.action: Reverted to a smaller EfficientNet backbone, replaced per-channel ImageNet normalization with per-sample mean/std normalization, removed colormap-based 3-channel mapping in favor of direct slicing+resize, added intra-batch shuffling, then extended mixup from 2-sample to 3-sample weighted mixup with NaN handling. Submitted and got 0.41959 — better than 0.50856 but still far from the 0.35728 best.

general.goal: How to recover from a large score regression caused by switching to a newer or larger backbone architecture?
general.context: A backbone swap produced a dramatic performance drop, suggesting the new architecture's preprocessing requirements or capacity don't match the current pipeline and data scale.
general.action: Revert to the previously successful smaller backbone, simplify preprocessing to per-sample normalization rather than architecture-specific constants, and verify recovery before layering additional changes. Expect that the regression is only partially recovered if multiple changes are bundled together.

instance.goal: Does extending mixup from two samples to three samples improve generalization for this EEG/spectrogram classification task?
instance.context: The pipeline already used a fixed two-sample mixup (alpha=0.3). The author's best score (0.35728) used a simpler pipeline. The current run bundles three-sample mixup with backbone and preprocessing changes, making it hard to isolate the mixup effect. Final score was 0.41959.
instance.action: Replaced two-sample mixup with three-sample weighted mixup: first sample weight fixed at 0.8, second weight drawn randomly from remaining 0.2, third gets the rest. Applied to both inputs and soft labels, with np.nan_to_num on all input slices. The bundled changes did not reach the previous best, so the isolated benefit of three-sample mixup remains unclear.

general.goal: Can multi-sample (more than two) mixup augmentation improve generalization over standard two-sample mixup?
general.context: Standard two-sample mixup is already in use. The task involves soft/vote-based labels where blending multiple examples is natural, but the effect is hard to measure when changed simultaneously with other components.
general.action: Extend mixup to blend three samples with a dominant weight on the primary sample (e.g., 0.8) and split the remainder randomly between two other samples. Ensure NaN values in inputs are zeroed before mixing. Evaluate in isolation or with minimal other changes to attribute any score change correctly.

episode.objective: Switch to soft-label KL training, rework EEG slicing/filtering, remove spectrogram branch, add step LR scheduler, and refine data generator.
episode.outcome: New best 0.35346 at v70 after removing spectrogram branch and using KL loss.

instance.goal: Can switching from cross-entropy to KL-divergence loss improve performance when labels are soft vote distributions?
instance.context: The competition metric is KL divergence and labels are expert vote distributions (soft labels). Previous best LB was 0.35728 using cross-entropy-style training. The author had been iterating on augmentation and architecture without breaking through.
instance.action: Switched the training loss to KL-divergence to directly optimize the competition metric, combined with removing the spectrogram branch (EEG+image only), increasing sampling frequency to 200 Hz, enabling proper EEG time-window slicing/filtering, and adding a step LR scheduler. This yielded a new best LB of 0.35346.

general.goal: Can aligning the training loss with the evaluation metric improve leaderboard performance when the metric measures distributional similarity?
general.context: The evaluation metric compares predicted probability distributions against soft label distributions, but training uses a surrogate classification loss (e.g., cross-entropy on hard or soft labels).
general.action: Replace the surrogate loss with the actual evaluation metric (or its differentiable equivalent) as the training objective. When the metric is a divergence between distributions and labels are already soft distributions, train directly with that divergence as the loss function.

instance.goal: After a major pipeline refactor (new loss, new preprocessing, removed branch), how many bug-fix iterations should be expected before the pipeline runs correctly and scores well?
instance.context: The author made a large refactor in v60→v61 (KL loss, SFREQ change, soft labels, mixup, new slicing). The first submission scored 0.43066 (worse than best 0.35728). It took 8 more versions—fixing test-mode DataGenerator init (v63→v64), fixing patient_id column name (v64→v65), reducing resolution and adding spectrogram branch (v66→v67), then re-removing spectrogram and re-raising SFREQ (v68→v69)—before achieving a new best of 0.35346.
instance.action: After a major refactor, submit early to get a baseline score, then systematically fix bugs (runtime errors, column mismatches, missing test-mode paths) one at a time, submitting periodically. Expect several iterations of small fixes before the refactored pipeline surpasses the previous best. Don't abandon the approach after the first poor score.

general.goal: How should a large pipeline refactor be validated and debugged when initial results regress?
general.context: A major change to loss function, preprocessing, and model inputs is introduced simultaneously. The first evaluation score is significantly worse than the previous best, but the changes are theoretically sound.
general.action: Submit immediately after the refactor to establish a baseline, then fix one bug per iteration (data loading errors, column name mismatches, missing test-mode logic). Submit periodically to track whether fixes are recovering performance. Expect multiple fix iterations before the refactored pipeline matches or exceeds the prior best; do not revert the entire refactor based on the first poor score alone.

instance.goal: Does simplifying the model by removing the spectrogram input branch and relying on EEG+image help or hurt?
instance.context: At v67 the author added a scipy spectrogram branch and reduced image resolution (HIGH 64), scoring 0.37990. At v69 they removed the spectrogram branch, restored HIGH to 128, and increased SFREQ to 200, scoring a new best 0.35346.
instance.action: Removed the spectrogram computation branch from the data generator and model, restoring the simpler EEG+image pipeline with higher resolution inputs. The simpler pipeline with better raw signal processing outperformed the more complex multi-branch version.

general.goal: When adding a new input branch to a multi-input model does not improve results, what alternative should be tried?
general.context: A newly added feature-extraction branch (e.g., a hand-crafted spectral representation) was expected to help but the score did not improve or worsened compared to the simpler pipeline.
general.action: Remove the underperforming branch and instead invest the computational budget in improving the quality of existing inputs (higher resolution, better filtering, correct time-window alignment). A simpler model with higher-fidelity inputs often outperforms a more complex model with redundant or noisy additional branches.

episode.objective: Refine per-fold training (per-fold LR schedule, class balancing, memory cleanup), add image modality, set deterministic seeds, and rework train-set grouping.
episode.lever: per-fold training and image modality addition
episode.outcome: New best 0.34054 at v76 after adding image modality and deterministic ops.

instance.goal: After achieving a new best score (0.35346), what changes to the training loop and data handling could yield further improvement?
instance.context: The best LB was 0.35346 at v70. The author had been iterating on EEG preprocessing, model backbones, and loss functions. Per-fold training details (LR schedule, class balancing, memory cleanup) and data grouping/aggregation had not been fully optimized.
instance.action: In v70→v71, moved optimizer/compile into per-fold scope with explicit LR schedule and class-balanced undersampling. This regressed to 0.40939. In v72→v73, changed sampling frequency, image sizing, and class-balanced overlapping sampling — regressed further to 0.49443. In v74→v75, reverted some changes, added an image modality branch, set deterministic seeds, reworked eeg_id grouping/aggregation with target normalization, and restored HIGH=128. This achieved a new best of 0.34054.

general.goal: When a pipeline has plateaued, how can restructuring the training loop and adding a new input modality improve performance?
general.context: A multi-input model is already performing well on one or two modalities. Per-fold training details and data grouping have not been carefully tuned, and an additional available modality has not yet been incorporated.
general.action: Add the new modality as a separate input branch, ensure per-sample grouping and target normalization are consistent across modalities, set deterministic seeds for reproducibility, and restore proven preprocessing parameters (e.g., resolution) that may have been inadvertently changed. If intermediate changes regress, revert the harmful parts while keeping the beneficial additions.

instance.goal: After a large regression (0.35→0.41→0.49), how can the author diagnose which changes caused the degradation and recover?
instance.context: v70→v71 introduced per-fold LR scheduling, class-balanced undersampling, and moved compile into fold scope — score regressed from 0.35 to 0.41. v72→v73 changed SFREQ from 200→100, HIGH from 128→96, and replaced train-set construction with overlapping class-balanced sampling — score worsened to 0.49. The author needed to identify which changes helped vs. hurt.
instance.action: In v74→v75, the author reverted harmful preprocessing changes (restored HIGH to 128), kept the deterministic-seed and grouping improvements, and added a genuinely new feature (image modality). The combined result was a new best (0.34), suggesting the resolution reduction and sampling-frequency change were the culprits, while the new modality and better grouping helped.

general.goal: When multiple simultaneous changes cause a large score regression, how can one recover without losing all experimental progress?
general.context: Several changes were bundled together (preprocessing parameters, data sampling strategy, training loop restructuring) and the score regressed significantly across two iterations.
general.action: Revert the preprocessing parameters that differ most from the last known-good configuration (especially resolution and sampling rate), retain structural improvements that are unlikely to cause regression (deterministic seeds, cleaner data grouping), and layer in one genuinely new improvement (e.g., an additional input modality). Submit to confirm recovery before further iteration.

episode.objective: Switch to a newer model checkpoint directory for inference.
episode.outcome: New best 0.32680 at v78.

instance.goal: Can a newer set of trained model checkpoints improve the leaderboard score beyond the current best of 0.34054?
instance.context: The pipeline and preprocessing were unchanged from the previous best submission (v76, LB 0.34054). A new checkpoint directory (models2024022702) was available, presumably trained with the same or refined configuration offline.
instance.action: Changed only the LOAD_MODELS_FROM path variable from 'models2024022701' to 'models2024022702', then re-ran inference. The result improved to 0.32680, a new best by 0.01374.

general.goal: How much can improved or further-trained checkpoints improve the final score without changing the inference pipeline?
general.context: The inference code, preprocessing, and ensembling logic are stable and already producing competitive results. New checkpoints have been trained offline (possibly with longer training, different seeds, or refined hyperparameters).
general.action: Swap only the checkpoint directory path and re-run inference to isolate the effect of the new weights. Compare the leaderboard score to the previous best to confirm the new checkpoints are strictly better before making any other changes.

episode.objective: Enable stagewise training (STAGE variable), create non-overlapping class-balanced train set, add cached train.csv, and iterate on stage configuration.
episode.outcome: New best 0.27931 at v83 with stage-based training.

instance.goal: Can creating a non-overlapping, class-balanced EEG-level training set and introducing stagewise training improve the KL-divergence score beyond 0.32680?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.32680. The training data had overlapping EEG segments across folds and imbalanced class distributions. The author had already iterated extensively on backbones, preprocessing, and augmentation.
instance.action: Built a pipeline that deduplicates EEG segments to create non-overlapping training examples, balances classes during selection, caches the result as train.csv, and introduces a STAGE variable for multi-stage training. This yielded LB 0.27977, a large improvement of ~0.047.

general.goal: Can deduplicating and class-balancing the training set at the sample-group level improve performance when samples overlap across groups?
general.context: The dataset contains repeated or overlapping observation windows from the same recording sessions, causing data leakage or redundancy in training. Class imbalance is also present.
general.action: Aggregate labels to the unique observation level, remove overlapping windows so each appears once, balance the resulting set across classes, and cache the cleaned dataset for reproducibility. This reduces noise from duplicates and ensures the model sees a representative class distribution.

instance.goal: After the large gain from data deduplication and stage-1 training, can skipping stage-1 and running only stage-2 with adjusted learning rate and epochs squeeze out further improvement?
instance.context: LB was 0.27977 with the two-stage pipeline. The author had pre-saved stage-1 weights and wanted to iterate faster on stage-2 configuration without re-running stage-1 each time.
instance.action: Commented out the entire stage-1 training block, pointed to saved stage-1 checkpoints, changed stage-2 to use the stage-1 learning rate (LR1) and epoch count (EPOCHS1), and re-submitted. This gave a marginal improvement to 0.27931.

general.goal: How can the later stage of a multi-stage training pipeline be iterated on efficiently without re-running expensive earlier stages?
general.context: A multi-stage training pipeline exists where the first stage is expensive and its weights are already saved. The practitioner wants to tune the second stage's schedule independently.
general.action: Save checkpoints after each stage, gate each stage behind a flag so it can be skipped, and load the saved weights directly into the later stage. This allows rapid iteration on later-stage hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, callbacks) without redundant computation.

episode.objective: Iterate on which training stages to skip/enable, fold gating, data filtering (stage1 vs stage2, Other class), and checkpoint selection.
episode.outcome: New best 0.27366 at v90 after fixing Other-class filter and using correct checkpoints.

instance.goal: Which combination of training stage, data filtering (e.g., excluding 'Other' class), and checkpoint produces the best leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author had a best score of 0.27931 from a two-stage training pipeline. They could toggle stage-1 vs stage-2 training, filter by expert_consensus class, change which folds run, and swap model checkpoints. No validation logs are visible, so they relied on LB submissions to evaluate.
instance.action: Systematically tried: (1) skip stage-2, use stage-1 filtering → LB 0.28584 (worse); (2) switch to stage-2 filtering with 'Other'-only data → LB 0.40640 (much worse); (3) fix filter to exclude 'Other' → LB 0.31761 (better but not best); (4) remove the 'Other' filter entirely, use new checkpoints → LB 0.27366 (new best). Kept the configuration that included all classes.

general.goal: Which data subset and training-stage configuration yields the best test performance when multiple stages and class filters are available?
general.context: A multi-stage training pipeline allows skipping stages or filtering training data by class label. Without reliable offline validation, leaderboard feedback is the primary signal.
general.action: Sweep one variable at a time: first toggle which training stage is active, then vary the class filter (include all classes, exclude one class, include only one class), submitting each to get feedback. When filtering out a class degrades the score substantially, revert to using all data. Keep the combination that achieves the best score.

instance.goal: Was the dramatic score regression (0.28584 → 0.40640) caused by a data filtering bug or a genuine modeling choice?
instance.context: In v86→v87 the author switched stage selection logic and filtered to expert_consensus=='Other' only, producing LB 0.40640. The next edit (v87→v88) flipped the filter to != 'Other', recovering to 0.31761, suggesting the == 'Other' filter was a bug.
instance.action: Identified the inverted filter condition as the cause, fixed it in the next version, and then in v88→v89 removed the class filter entirely, ultimately achieving a new best of 0.27366.

general.goal: How can a sudden large score regression be diagnosed when multiple changes were made simultaneously?
general.context: A version that changed both the data filtering logic and other settings produced a large regression. The filter selected only one minority class instead of excluding it.
general.action: When a large regression appears after multiple changes, first check data filtering and selection logic for accidental inversions (e.g., == vs !=). Fix the suspected bug in isolation and resubmit before reverting other changes. If the fix partially recovers the score, also try removing the filter entirely to see if the full dataset performs best.

episode.objective: Switch between stage1/stage2 weights and tighten train/valid filtering (AND vs OR conditions for event count and KLD).
episode.lever: checkpoint stage and sample filtering criteria
episode.outcome: Regressed to 0.32367 at v95; AND-filtering too restrictive.

instance.goal: Which training stage's weights (stage1 vs stage2) and which checkpoint directory yield the best leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author had achieved a new best LB of 0.27366 using stage1 weights from one checkpoint directory. Multiple checkpoint directories existed from different training runs, and both stage1 and stage2 weight files were available.
instance.action: Switched from stage1 to stage2 weights and updated the checkpoint directory path (v90→v91→v92), then submitted (v93) to get LB 0.26921, a new best. This confirmed stage2 weights from the newer directory were superior.

general.goal: Which checkpoint from a multi-stage training pipeline produces the best test-time predictions?
general.context: A multi-stage fine-tuning pipeline saves weights after each stage. Later-stage weights are fine-tuned on a curated subset but may overfit, while earlier-stage weights are more general.
general.action: Systematically try weights from each training stage and each saved checkpoint directory, submitting each to the leaderboard. Pick the combination that scores best. Do not assume the final stage is always superior.

instance.goal: Will tightening the sample filtering from OR (high event count OR low KLD) to AND (high event count AND low KLD) improve the score?
instance.context: After achieving LB 0.26921 with the current filtering, the author changed the train/validation selection mask from an OR condition to an AND condition, expecting a cleaner subset of high-confidence samples to improve fine-tuning.
instance.action: Changed the filtering logic to require both conditions simultaneously and submitted (v95), but the score regressed sharply to 0.32367. The stricter filter likely reduced the training set too aggressively, hurting generalization.

general.goal: How aggressively should training samples be filtered by quality criteria when fine-tuning on a curated subset?
general.context: A fine-tuning stage selects high-quality samples using multiple quality indicators (e.g., annotator agreement and prediction confidence). Using a union (OR) of criteria keeps more samples; using an intersection (AND) keeps fewer but supposedly cleaner ones.
general.action: Test both union and intersection filtering and compare on the leaderboard. Be cautious with intersection filtering: it can reduce the training set too much, causing underfitting or poor generalization, especially when individual criteria are already selective.

episode.objective: Add STFT modality to the pipeline, compute and save/load STFT features, adjust batch size and stage control.
episode.outcome: Score 0.27844 at v100, close to but not beating best 0.27366.

instance.goal: Can adding an STFT-based spectral modality to the existing EEG+spectrogram+image pipeline improve the score beyond 0.26921?
instance.context: The best score so far was 0.26921. The pipeline already used EEG waveforms, Kaggle spectrograms, and images. The author added STFT computation (scipy.signal.spectrogram) as a new input branch, but the first submission with STFT included scored 0.32109 (worse). After removing STFT from DATATYPE, adjusting augmentation/batch size, and fixing a residual concatenation bug, the score recovered to 0.27844.
instance.action: Added STFT as a new modality, submitted, saw degradation (0.32109 vs 0.26921), then removed STFT from the active input types while keeping the code infrastructure, fixed a conditional concatenation bug for when STFT is absent, and re-submitted to recover near-best performance (0.27844).

general.goal: Will adding a new derived spectral input modality improve a multi-input classification model?
general.context: A multi-modal pipeline already combines several input representations and has reached a strong baseline score. A new frequency-domain feature (e.g., short-time spectral transform) is computed and concatenated as an additional branch.
general.action: Add the new modality behind a feature flag, submit quickly to measure impact, and if the score degrades, disable the modality while keeping the code infrastructure for future experiments. Ensure that data assembly (e.g., concatenation) is guarded by the flag so removing the modality doesn't leave dead-code bugs.

instance.goal: After adding and then removing the STFT branch, why doesn't the score return to the previous best of 0.26921?
instance.context: The best LB was 0.26921 (v93). Adding STFT degraded to 0.32109 (v97). After removing STFT and fixing the concatenation bug, the score was 0.27844 (v100) — better than with STFT but still worse than v93. Other changes (batch size 12→16, augmentation/windowing tweaks, different model checkpoint path) were also made alongside the STFT removal.
instance.action: The author changed multiple things simultaneously (modality, batch size, augmentation, checkpoint path), making it impossible to isolate the STFT effect cleanly. The residual gap (0.27844 vs 0.26921) likely comes from these confounded changes. Lesson: when testing a new modality, change only the modality flag and keep all other hyperparameters fixed to get a clean A/B comparison.

general.goal: How can the effect of adding or removing a single input modality be measured reliably?
general.context: Multiple changes (batch size, augmentation strategy, checkpoint version, and the new modality) are bundled into one submission, so the score change cannot be attributed to any single factor.
general.action: Toggle only the modality flag between two otherwise identical runs. Keep batch size, augmentation, learning rate schedule, and model checkpoint fixed. Submit both versions to get a clean comparison before making further adjustments.

episode.objective: Simplify pipeline by removing STFT, clean up augmentation/dependencies, enable early stopping, and average fold predictions.
episode.outcome: Score 0.27969 at v107; marginal, did not beat 0.27366.

instance.goal: Does removing the truncation of pooled feature vectors ([:,:128] slicing after GlobalAveragePooling2D) and enabling spectrogram masking augmentation improve the score?
instance.context: v103 scored 0.27315 (near best). In v104, the author removed the [:,:128] truncation after pooling and re-enabled spectrogram masking augmentation. The resulting v105 scored 0.28170, which is worse.
instance.action: The author tested removing the feature truncation and adding masking augmentation. The score regressed by ~0.009. They then reverted/simplified in v106, removing unused code and averaging fold predictions, recovering to 0.27969.

general.goal: Will using the full-dimensional pooled feature vector from a pretrained backbone (instead of truncating it) improve downstream classification?
general.context: A truncated pooled representation is already performing well. Removing the truncation increases the number of parameters feeding into the classification head.
general.action: Test with and without truncation on the leaderboard. If the full-dimensional vector degrades the score, revert to the truncated version — the extra dimensions may introduce noise or overfitting when the classification head is small relative to the feature dimension.

instance.goal: After a change worsened the score, how can the pipeline be cleaned up and partially recovered without reverting entirely?
instance.context: v105 scored 0.28170 (regression from 0.27315). The author cleaned up: removed unused imports (librosa, albumentations), removed dead mel-spectrogram code, simplified augmentation, added early stopping, and averaged fold predictions. v107 scored 0.27969, partially recovering.
instance.action: Rather than a full revert, the author simplified the pipeline (removed unused dependencies and dead code), added fold-prediction averaging and early stopping, and pointed to a new checkpoint. This recovered most of the regression (0.28170 → 0.27969) though not fully to 0.27315.

general.goal: When a set of changes caused a score regression, how can the pipeline be stabilized without fully reverting to the old version?
general.context: Multiple changes were bundled (augmentation, architecture tweak, checkpoint) and the combined effect was negative. A full revert would lose any beneficial sub-changes.
general.action: Remove dead code and unused dependencies to reduce noise, add robustness measures like early stopping and averaging predictions across cross-validation folds, and re-submit. Fold averaging smooths out variance and can partially compensate for a suboptimal single-fold configuration.

episode.objective: Refine data preprocessing/augmentation, add staged KL-loss scheduling, rework class-balanced sampling, and restrict to image-only modality.
episode.outcome: Regressed to 0.35418 at v113 with image-only; bugs in test loading.

instance.goal: Can restricting the model to only the image modality (dropping EEG and spectrogram inputs) improve or simplify performance?
instance.context: The best LB score was 0.26921 with a multi-input model (EEG + spectrogram + image). The author changed DATATYPE to only ['img'] in v110, trained/inferred with image-only, and submitted at v113 getting 0.35418 — much worse than the multi-input baseline.
instance.action: Set DATATYPE to image-only, reworked class-balanced sampling, and submitted. The score regressed by ~0.08. In the next version (v114, after episode), the author re-enabled EEG and spectrogram inputs, confirming the image-only approach was abandoned.

general.goal: Will dropping input modalities from a multi-modal model simplify the pipeline without hurting accuracy?
general.context: A multi-modal model combining several input types has achieved the current best score. One modality alone seems potentially sufficient.
general.action: Test single-modality ablations by disabling other input branches. If the score degrades substantially, the dropped modalities carry complementary information and should be retained. Revert quickly if the ablation shows a large regression.

instance.goal: After a large refactor (new augmentation, staged KL loss, class-balanced sampling, modality changes), how can indentation/control-flow bugs in the inference path be caught before wasting a submission?
instance.context: In v110 the author made a major rewrite. Steps v111 and v112 were both micro-fixes correcting indentation so that the test CSV was loaded correctly on Kaggle — the inference path was broken by the refactor.
instance.action: The author needed two successive micro-fixes (v111, v112) to correct platform-conditional CSV loading before the pipeline could run on Kaggle. This delayed the submission and the eventual score (v113) was poor, partly because the image-only choice was bad but also because debugging consumed iterations.

general.goal: How can inference-path breakage be avoided when making large refactors to a training+inference notebook?
general.context: A notebook serves both training and inference; a major rewrite of data loading and branching logic can silently break the inference code path, which is only exercised at submission time.
general.action: After any large refactor, do a dry-run of the inference code path locally (or with a small test set) before submitting. Check every platform-conditional branch and ensure indentation/scoping is correct for all modes. This avoids burning submission attempts on trivial bugs.

episode.objective: Re-enable EEG+spectrogram modalities, switch image backbone to B0, refine spectrogram preprocessing (windowing, nfft, frequency cutoff, colormap), and adjust CV splitting.
episode.lever: spectrogram preprocessing and CV split strategy
episode.outcome: New best 0.26861 at v125 after switching to cividis colormap and pure GroupKFold.

instance.goal: After an image-only approach regressed to 0.35418, how can the multimodal pipeline (EEG + spectrogram + image) be restored to beat the previous best of 0.26921?
instance.context: v112 removed EEG and spectrogram modalities, keeping only images, and LB worsened from 0.26921 to 0.35418. The author's best scores came from multimodal setups with all three input types.
instance.action: Re-enabled EEG and spectrogram in DATATYPE, switched image backbone from EfficientNetB4 to B0, then iteratively refined spectrogram preprocessing (Hann window, nfft=512, frequency cutoff 20→40 Hz, mel-spectrogram via librosa, colormap jet→cividis) and switched GroupKFold from stratified-by-target to pure group-by-patient. Achieved new best 0.26861.

general.goal: After removing input modalities caused a regression, how can the multimodal pipeline be restored and improved beyond the previous best?
general.context: A multimodal model (raw signal + spectrogram + image branches) previously scored well, but an ablation to a single modality regressed significantly, confirming all modalities contribute.
general.action: Restore all modalities, then systematically refine the spectrogram branch (windowing function, FFT size, frequency range, colormap for rendered spectrograms) and the cross-validation split strategy (pure group-based instead of stratified). Change one or two preprocessing details per iteration and submit to track which changes help.

instance.goal: Does switching from stratified GroupKFold (using expert_consensus as y) to plain GroupKFold (y=None, groups=patient_id) improve the leaderboard score?
instance.context: Previous CV used StratifiedGroupKFold with expert_consensus as the stratification target. The author changed to gkf.split(train, None, train.patient_id) in v124, and the subsequent submission (v125) achieved a new best of 0.26861, improving over 0.27372.
instance.action: Removed the stratification variable from the GroupKFold split call so folds are formed purely by patient grouping without forcing class balance across folds. Combined with a colormap change (jet→cividis), this yielded the best score of the episode.

general.goal: When using group-based cross-validation, does adding stratification by label help or hurt generalization?
general.context: Labels are soft distributions from multiple annotators, and the consensus label used for stratification may not represent the true distribution well. Forcing balanced class proportions across folds can create splits that don't reflect the natural test distribution.
general.action: Try pure group-based splitting (without stratification) alongside the stratified variant and compare leaderboard or held-out scores. When labels are noisy or soft, pure grouping may generalize better because it avoids artificially balancing uncertain labels.

instance.goal: What spectrogram frequency range and rendering colormap produce the best input features for the EEG classification model?
instance.context: The author tried frequency cutoffs of 20 Hz (v116, LB 0.27372) and 40 Hz (v118, LB 0.28050), and colormaps jet vs cividis. The 20 Hz cutoff scored better than 40 Hz; cividis combined with other changes achieved the best score (0.26861).
instance.action: Tested narrower (≤20 Hz) vs wider (≤40 Hz) frequency bands for self-generated spectrograms. The narrower band performed better, suggesting higher frequencies added noise. Also switched the colormap from jet to cividis for the rendered spectrogram images fed to the CNN, which contributed to the best result.

general.goal: How should the frequency range and visual rendering of self-generated spectrograms be tuned for a CNN-based classifier?
general.context: Self-generated spectrograms are rendered as color images and fed to a pretrained image backbone. The frequency range determines signal-to-noise ratio, and the colormap affects how the backbone's pretrained filters respond to the input.
general.action: Experiment with restricting the spectrogram to the informative frequency band (removing high-frequency noise) and try perceptually uniform colormaps instead of rainbow-type ones. Evaluate each change on the leaderboard or a robust validation split, as both frequency range and colormap can materially affect CNN performance on rendered spectrograms.

episode.objective: Improve training data quality: shuffle rows, filter out 'Other'/low-confidence examples, add class-balanced sampling with temporal dedup, enable mixed precision and label smoothing.
episode.lever: training data filtering and label smoothing
episode.outcome: New best 0.26637 at v131 with simplified dedup and label smoothing.

instance.goal: Will filtering out 'Other' (low-confidence) class examples and shuffling training rows improve the KL-divergence score beyond 0.26861?
instance.context: Best LB was 0.26861. The author tried excluding 'Other' expert_consensus rows and shuffling the dataframe before GroupKFold splitting, also passing expert_consensus as y to GroupKFold.
instance.action: Filtered out rows with expert_consensus == 'Other', randomly permuted the training dataframe, and passed expert_consensus as y to GroupKFold. Score worsened to 0.27932, so this filtering alone was not beneficial.

general.goal: Will removing ambiguous/low-confidence class samples from training improve a soft-label classification metric?
general.context: A multi-class model trained with soft labels (vote distributions) where one class represents an ambiguous catch-all category.
general.action: Try excluding the ambiguous class from training. If the metric worsens, the model likely benefits from seeing those examples — possibly because they regularize predictions or because test data contains such cases. Revert the exclusion and instead try combining it with other improvements.

instance.goal: After an initial filtering attempt hurt the score, can combining class-balanced sampling with temporal deduplication, mixed precision, label smoothing, and simplified data selection recover and surpass the previous best of 0.26861?
instance.context: v127 scored 0.27932 (worse than 0.26861 baseline). The author then tried complex per-class temporal dedup sampling (v128, scored 0.30897 — even worse), then simplified the sampling, added label smoothing, mixed precision, and early stopping (v130), which achieved 0.26637 — a new best.
instance.action: Rather than reverting all changes after the first regression, the author iterated: first tried elaborate class-balanced temporal dedup (which worsened further to 0.30897), then simplified the dedup, added label smoothing and mixed precision training, and obtained a new best 0.26637. The key was bundling multiple complementary improvements and simplifying the data selection.

general.goal: When an initial data-filtering change worsens the score, how should one proceed — revert entirely or iterate further?
general.context: A data selection change caused a regression, and a more complex version of the same idea caused an even larger regression. The practitioner suspects the core idea has merit but the implementation needs refinement.
general.action: Instead of reverting completely, simplify the data selection logic and combine it with complementary training improvements (label smoothing, mixed-precision training, early stopping). Test the bundle together. If the combined changes beat the original baseline, keep them; the synergy of multiple small improvements can overcome the regression from any single change.

episode.objective: Add Transformer block, adjust EEG windowing to full 50s segment, try removing modalities (spe-only, img-only) to find best combination.
episode.outcome: Scores 0.28049–0.31300; all worse than 0.26637 best.

instance.goal: Which combination of input modalities (EEG, spectrogram, image) gives the best score for this multi-modal brain activity classification model?
instance.context: The best score so far (0.26637) used all three modalities (eeg, spe, img). The author added a Transformer block and changed EEG windowing, scoring 0.28049 with all three. They then tried spe+img (0.28034) and img-only (0.31300), both worse than the previous best.
instance.action: Ablated modalities one at a time: first removed EEG (spe+img → 0.28034), then removed spectrogram too (img-only → 0.31300). Each removal degraded the score, confirming all three modalities contribute. The author later reverted to including EEG in v139.

general.goal: Which subset of available input modalities contributes most to performance in a multi-modal pipeline?
general.context: A multi-modal model uses several input branches and has achieved a strong baseline score. It is unclear whether all branches help or some add noise.
general.action: Run a systematic ablation: remove one modality at a time and score each variant on the leaderboard or a held-out set. If every removal hurts, keep all modalities. If removing one improves or is neutral, drop it to reduce complexity. Compare each ablation against the full-modality baseline, not against each other.

instance.goal: Can adding a Transformer block and switching to a full 50-second EEG window improve the classification score beyond the current best of 0.26637?
instance.context: Previous best (0.26637) used multi-slice EEG stacking with CNN-only architecture. The author introduced a TransformerBlock class, changed EEG input to a single full 50s segment, and added per-sample normalization.
instance.action: Added the Transformer block and full-window EEG representation in one commit, then scored 0.28049 — worse than the 0.26637 baseline. The author later removed the Transformer block in v139, indicating it did not help.

general.goal: Will adding a self-attention mechanism to a convolutional feature pipeline improve performance on a sequential classification task?
general.context: A CNN-based pipeline has a strong baseline. The practitioner hypothesizes that global context modeling via attention could capture longer-range dependencies.
general.action: Add the attention block and test on the leaderboard or validation set. If the score regresses, revert the change rather than trying to tune it extensively — the added complexity may not suit the data scale or the existing feature representation. Isolate architectural changes from preprocessing changes to attribute effects correctly.

episode.objective: Switch to EEG-only with modified CNN, add GPU spectrogram via CuPy, then fix CuPy issues and fall back to SciPy, re-enable multimodal with STFT.
episode.lever: EEG CNN architecture and STFT/spectrogram computation backend
episode.outcome: Score 0.27393 at v150 after fixing CuPy→SciPy; close to but not beating 0.26637.

instance.goal: Can switching to EEG-only input with a modified CNN branch improve the score over the image-only pipeline?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.26637 with multimodal inputs. The author switched DATATYPE to ['eeg'] only, removed a Transformer block, modified conv layers, and disabled mixed precision. The resulting LB was 0.38984, a large regression.
instance.action: After seeing the EEG-only score regress badly (0.389 vs 0.266 best), the author immediately re-enabled multimodal inputs (eeg+spe+img) in the next version and added STFT features, recovering to 0.2885 and eventually 0.2739 with the full multimodal pipeline plus STFT.

general.goal: Will dropping modalities and relying on a single input branch improve or simplify the model without hurting performance?
general.context: A multimodal pipeline combining several input types has achieved the current best score. One branch alone seems simpler to optimize.
general.action: Test the single-modality ablation, but if the score regresses substantially, immediately restore all modalities. Treat the ablation as a diagnostic, not a permanent simplification. Gains are more likely from adding or refining modalities than from removing them once the fusion is working.

instance.goal: Can GPU-accelerated spectrogram computation via CuPy replace the CPU-based SciPy/librosa path for generating STFT features?
instance.context: The author tried CuPy's internal spectrogram function (cupyx.scipy.signal.spectrogram) but hit import and API issues across multiple versions (v141→v148), requiring repeated fixes to the import path, conditional checks, and .get() calls.
instance.action: After three failed attempts to fix the CuPy spectrogram call (v142 import fix, v147 conditional fix, v148 fallback), the author fell back to SciPy's signal.spectrogram on CPU. The final working version (v150, LB 0.27393) used the CPU path. The STFT modality was later dropped entirely in v151.

general.goal: How reliably can a GPU-accelerated library replace a CPU signal-processing routine in a competition notebook environment?
general.context: The environment may have version mismatches or incomplete GPU library installations. The GPU library's internal API paths can change between versions, causing repeated import and type errors.
general.action: When porting a CPU signal-processing step to a GPU library, have the CPU fallback ready and test the GPU path in isolation first. If the GPU call requires more than one fix iteration, fall back to the CPU version immediately to avoid wasting submission attempts on infrastructure bugs rather than modeling improvements.

episode.objective: Expand extra training data, drop STFT modality, increase batch size, and fix matplotlib backend for headless environment.
episode.lever: extra data inclusion and batch size

instance.goal: Can adding extra labeled training data (with filtering for quality) improve the model's leaderboard score beyond the current best of 0.27393?
instance.context: The pipeline had reached LB 0.27393. Extra labeled data was available but not yet incorporated. The author enabled READ_EXTRA flags, filtered extra data by removing rows with other_vote_raw != 0, deduplicated by spectrogram_id, and increased batch size from 12 to 16.
instance.action: Added extra data with quality filtering (keep only rows with positive target votes, no 'other' votes), dropped the STFT modality, increased batch size, and pointed to new checkpoints. The result was LB 0.27719, worse than the previous 0.27393, so the extra data in this form did not help.

general.goal: Will incorporating additional labeled data with quality filtering improve a model that has plateaued?
general.context: A model has reached a competitive score and additional labeled examples are available but may contain noisy or ambiguous labels (e.g., low agreement among annotators).
general.action: Filter extra data to keep only high-confidence examples (e.g., those where the dominant class has positive votes and the catch-all/ambiguous class has zero votes), deduplicate by sample identifier, and evaluate on the leaderboard. If the score worsens, the extra data may introduce distribution shift or noise; revert and try stricter filtering or a separate training stage for the extra data.

instance.goal: How should extra data be incorporated across multi-stage training to avoid hurting performance?
instance.context: Simply adding filtered extra data in one shot (v151→v152) worsened LB from 0.27393 to 0.27719. The author then tried adding stage 1 back (STAGETRAIN [1,2,3]) with stricter filtering (keep only rows with any positive target), guarded empty-data loading, and used a newer checkpoint. This gave LB 0.27455, still worse than baseline. Then removing stage 1 again, reducing signal length to 128, and re-enabling the Agg backend yielded LB 0.27394, essentially matching the original best.
instance.action: Iterated through: (1) adding an extra training stage for the new data → worse; (2) reverting to fewer stages with reduced signal length and tighter config → recovered to baseline. The episode showed that naively adding extra data or stages did not improve the score, and the best outcome was recovering the original performance.

general.goal: When adding auxiliary data degrades performance, how can the training pipeline be adjusted to recover or improve?
general.context: A multi-stage training pipeline's score worsened after incorporating extra data. Adding more training stages or changing filtering did not surpass the original score.
general.action: Try isolating the extra data in a dedicated early training stage so it does not contaminate fine-tuning on clean data. If that still hurts, revert the extra data inclusion entirely and reduce other changed hyperparameters (e.g., input resolution, batch size) back to their proven values. Accept that the extra data may not help in its current form and move on to other levers.

episode.objective: Add spectrogram temporal masking augmentation, restore time-cropping, switch to librosa mel-spectrogram replacing CuPy, and adjust training config (optimizer, mixed precision, early stopping).
episode.outcome: New best 0.26603 at v168 after switching to librosa mel-spectrograms.

instance.goal: Can replacing the CuPy GPU-based spectrogram with a librosa mel-spectrogram improve the score or reliability of the pipeline?
instance.context: The pipeline used CuPy-based GPU spectrograms which had required multiple bug fixes (v147-v149). The best LB was 0.26637. After several augmentation experiments (time-cropping, blackout masking, image-region augmentation) scores stayed around 0.27-0.28, not beating the best.
instance.action: Replaced the CuPy spectrogram with librosa mel-spectrogram (power-to-dB), adjusted concatenation axis, updated optimizer/mixed-precision/early-stopping config, and retrained. This yielded a new best LB of 0.26603.

general.goal: Can switching the spectrogram computation backend or representation improve model performance or pipeline reliability?
general.context: A GPU-accelerated spectrogram library has required repeated bug fixes and the pipeline score has plateaued despite augmentation experiments.
general.action: Replace the fragile GPU spectrogram with a well-tested CPU library's mel-spectrogram (log-scaled), which produces a perceptually-motivated and more compact frequency representation. Combine this change with training config adjustments (optimizer choice, mixed precision, early stopping) and evaluate end-to-end.

instance.goal: Does adding spectrogram temporal masking (blackout) augmentation during training improve the EEG classification score?
instance.context: The previous best LB was 0.26637. The author added random zeroing of two spectrogram time regions with 50% probability during training, along with image-region augmentation and GroupKFold split changes.
instance.action: Enabled spectrogram blackout augmentation (zeroing random time segments) and tested across multiple submissions (v159: 0.27857, v161: 0.27427, v163: 0.27691). None beat the previous best, suggesting these augmentations alone were insufficient or slightly harmful.

general.goal: Does random temporal masking of spectrogram inputs during training act as effective regularization for a classification model?
general.context: The model uses spectrogram inputs processed by a convolutional backbone and the score has plateaued.
general.action: Add random zeroing of contiguous time-frequency regions in the spectrogram (applied stochastically per sample during training only). Test across multiple runs. If the score does not improve after several attempts, the augmentation is not beneficial for this input representation and should be reverted or combined with other changes.

instance.goal: How should multiple incremental changes (augmentation, normalization, window length, model features) be evaluated when individual submissions don't improve the score?
instance.context: Over steps v157-v166, the author tried time-cropping, spectrogram blackout, image-region augmentation, EEG normalization changes, window length 128→256, and second EEG branch — all scoring 0.274-0.285, worse than the 0.26637 best. Then a single combined change (librosa mel + training config) achieved 0.26603.
instance.action: After several incremental augmentation/preprocessing changes failed individually, the author bundled a representation change (mel-spectrogram backend) with training config adjustments (optimizer, mixed precision, early stopping) into one commit and achieved a new best. The pattern: when small tweaks plateau, try a qualitative change to the input representation rather than continuing to iterate on augmentation details.

general.goal: When incremental augmentation and preprocessing tweaks stop improving the score, where should effort be redirected?
general.context: Multiple small changes to augmentation strategy and input normalization have been tested individually over several iterations without beating the best score.
general.action: Instead of continuing to iterate on augmentation details, make a qualitative change to the input representation itself (e.g., switching the spectral transform type or scaling). Bundle it with aligned training configuration changes and evaluate. A representation-level change can unlock gains that augmentation tweaks on a suboptimal representation cannot.

episode.objective: Sweep STAGETEST parameter (stage 2 vs 3) to find which training stage produces best test predictions.
episode.outcome: Stage 2 gave 0.28251/0.28320; stage 3 better at 0.26603. Reverted.

instance.goal: Which training stage's checkpoint produces the best test-time predictions in a multi-stage training pipeline?
instance.context: The pipeline has at least 3 training stages (e.g., stage 1, 2, 3). The best LB so far (0.26603) was obtained with STAGETEST=3. The author wants to know if stage 2 or stage 3 yields better predictions.
instance.action: Sweep the STAGETEST parameter: set it to 2 (v169, LB 0.28251 — worse), then back to 3 with extra data added (v171, LB 0.26488 — new best), then try 2 again (v172, LB 0.28320 — worse). Concluded stage 3 is consistently better than stage 2 for inference.

general.goal: Which checkpoint from a multi-stage fine-tuning pipeline should be used at test time?
general.context: A model is trained in successive stages (e.g., broad data then curated data). Later stages may overfit or may capture better signal; the best stage for inference is not obvious a priori.
general.action: Run inference with each stage's checkpoint separately and compare leaderboard or validation scores. Test at least two stages, and if results are consistent across multiple runs (including when the training data changes), trust the pattern. Pick the stage that reliably scores best.

instance.goal: Can adding extra labeled data from an external source improve the model's leaderboard score?
instance.context: Best LB was 0.26603 with stage 3 and no extra data. The author has an external CSV (df_extra_data.csv) with additional labeled EEG/spectrogram samples that can be merged into training.
instance.action: Load the extra data CSV, construct target columns, load corresponding .npy feature arrays, pad/truncate them to expected shapes, and concatenate with the training dataframe. Re-run with STAGETEST=3. This yielded a new best LB of 0.26488, confirming the extra data helps.

general.goal: Will augmenting the training set with additional labeled examples from a secondary source improve generalization?
general.context: The model has plateaued on the primary training set. Additional labeled samples are available but may have different preprocessing or array shapes.
general.action: Merge the extra samples into the training pipeline, ensuring all feature arrays are padded or truncated to match the expected input dimensions. Evaluate on the held-out metric. If the score improves, keep the extra data; otherwise revert.

episode.objective: Add extra labeled data from external source with padding/truncation, then remove it and simplify; try multi-stage test weighting and different checkpoints.
episode.lever: extra data ingestion and multi-stage test weighting
episode.outcome: New best 0.26166 at v180 after removing extra data and using clean checkpoint.

instance.goal: Does adding extra labeled data from an external source improve the leaderboard score for this EEG classification task?
instance.context: The best score so far was 0.26488 (v171) using extra data with padding/truncation. After removing extra data and simplifying (v173→v174), score was 0.27151. Re-adding extra data (v175→v178) gave 0.27560. Finally removing extra data again and using a different checkpoint (v179→v180) achieved 0.26166, a new best.
instance.action: Tried adding external labeled data (loading CSV, mapping labels, deduplicating, concatenating, loading .npy arrays), evaluated the score, then removed it and tested with a cleaner pipeline and different model checkpoint. The version without extra data and with the right checkpoint scored best, so the extra data was dropped.

general.goal: Does incorporating additional labeled data from an external source improve the final metric?
general.context: Extra data requires preprocessing (label mapping, deduplication, shape padding/truncation) that adds complexity and potential noise. The benefit depends on data quality and compatibility with the main training distribution.
general.action: Add the external data, train, and evaluate on the leaderboard. Then remove it and evaluate with the same or updated checkpoint. Compare both scores. If the extra data does not improve or hurts the score, remove it and keep the simpler pipeline. The cleaner pipeline may generalize better if the external labels are noisy or distribution-shifted.

instance.goal: Which model checkpoint produces the best leaderboard score when the data pipeline is held constant?
instance.context: Throughout the episode, the author toggled between different model directories (model20240701, model2024040701, and others) while also changing data pipeline settings. The final best score (0.26166) came after settling on a specific checkpoint with the simplified (no extra data) pipeline.
instance.action: Systematically changed LOAD_MODELS_FROM to point to different saved model folders across versions, submitted each configuration, and kept the checkpoint that yielded the best leaderboard result.

general.goal: How can the best-performing saved checkpoint be identified when multiple candidates exist?
general.context: Multiple model checkpoints are available from different training runs or stages, and the data pipeline may also be changing simultaneously, making attribution difficult.
general.action: Isolate checkpoint selection from other changes: fix the data pipeline first, then swap checkpoints one at a time and submit. Compare leaderboard scores to identify the best checkpoint. Avoid changing both the data pipeline and the checkpoint simultaneously, as this confounds the comparison.

episode.objective: Test stage 2 instead of stage 3 for evaluation.
episode.outcome: Stage 2 gave 0.27700 at v181; worse than 0.26166. Abandoned.

instance.goal: Which training stage's checkpoint produces the best leaderboard score for this pipeline?
instance.context: The author has a multi-stage training pipeline. Stage 3 (STAGETEST=3) gave the best score so far (0.26166). Previously, switching from stage 3 to stage 2 hurt the score (v171→v172: 0.26488→0.28320), but the model checkpoints have since changed substantially (new model folder in v178-v179).
instance.action: Changed STAGETEST from 3 to 2 to re-evaluate stage 2 with the new checkpoints. The score worsened from 0.26166 to 0.27700, confirming stage 3 remains better for these checkpoints. The author reverted back to stage 3 in subsequent versions.

general.goal: Which checkpoint or training stage yields the best test-time predictions when the training pipeline has changed?
general.context: A multi-stage training pipeline exists and the model weights or data pipeline have been updated since the last time different stages were compared. A previously inferior stage might now be better with the new weights.
general.action: Re-probe each candidate stage after any significant change to the training setup or checkpoints. Compare the resulting metric against the current best. If the alternative is worse, revert to the previously best stage. Do not assume earlier comparisons still hold after pipeline changes.

episode.objective: Add a second EEG-derived input branch (x_eeg2) with different sampling/shape, adjust deduplication, add spectrogram temporal masking, and tune LR schedule.
episode.lever: additional EEG input branch and augmentation
episode.outcome: New best 0.25555 at v183; final score 0.25639 at v185.

instance.goal: Can adding a second EEG-derived input branch with different temporal sampling/shape improve the KL-divergence score beyond the current best of 0.26166?
instance.context: The pipeline already used spectrograms and one EEG branch. The author had been iterating on multi-modal inputs for many versions. Previous best was 0.26166.
instance.action: Added a new x_eeg2 input array with different sampling/shape from the existing EEG branch, normalized it, created a corresponding Keras Input and convolutional blocks, and merged it into the multi-branch model. Also changed deduplication to use multiple vote columns. This yielded 0.25555, a large improvement.

general.goal: Can extracting a second representation from the same raw signal modality (different resolution or windowing) provide complementary information that improves the model?
general.context: A multi-branch model already ingests one representation of a time-series modality alongside other modalities, and performance has plateaued.
general.action: Create a parallel input branch from the same raw signal but with different temporal sampling, window length, or frequency resolution. Give it its own convolutional feature extractor and merge its embeddings with the existing branches before the classification head. Evaluate on the leaderboard to confirm the gain.

instance.goal: Will adding spectrogram temporal masking augmentation and adjusting the LR schedule further improve the score beyond 0.25555?
instance.context: After adding the second EEG branch the score improved substantially to 0.25555. The author then added spectrogram temporal masking (zeroing random time intervals), changed EEG offset sampling logic, and extended the learning rate at 1e-4 for more epochs.
instance.action: Added temporal masking augmentation on spectrograms during training, randomized EEG offset selection within each eeg_id, and flattened the LR schedule to hold at 1e-4 longer. The score slightly regressed from 0.25555 to 0.25639, suggesting these changes did not help or were not yet tuned.

general.goal: After a large architectural gain, will additional augmentation and learning-rate schedule changes compound the improvement?
general.context: A significant score jump was just achieved by adding a new input branch. The practitioner wants to push further with training-time augmentation (temporal masking) and schedule tuning.
general.action: Test augmentation and schedule changes in a separate submission rather than bundling them with the architectural change. If the score regresses even slightly, revert and test each modification independently to isolate which helps and which hurts.

episode.objective: Build the initial inference pipeline (parquet→npy conversion, checkpoint loading, submission generation) and verify it produces a valid submission.
episode.outcome: First score obtained at v4: LB 0.35973.

instance.goal: How to set up a working inference pipeline that converts raw parquet EEG data to the format expected by the model and produces a valid submission?
instance.context: Starting from scratch with a pre-trained checkpoint and external scripts for parquet-to-npy conversion and model inference. The Kaggle environment requires specific paths and the model's pretrained flag must be set to False during inference to avoid downloading weights.
instance.action: Defined DATA_PATH and OUT_PATH variables, ran an external script to convert parquet files to npy format, then invoked the test/inference script with the checkpoint path and model.pretrained=False. Verified the output by displaying the head of the generated submission.csv. Re-ran the unchanged notebook to confirm reproducibility before submitting, achieving LB 0.35973.

general.goal: How to verify that a newly assembled inference pipeline produces valid predictions before iterating on model quality?
general.context: When building an inference notebook from a trained checkpoint and preprocessing scripts, silent failures (wrong paths, missing conversions, pretrained-weight downloads) can produce garbage output without raising errors.
general.action: After wiring up the pipeline, inspect the output file (e.g., print the first rows of the submission) to confirm it has the right shape and plausible values. Then do at least one identical re-run to confirm determinism and reproducibility before submitting. Only after a confirmed valid score, begin swapping checkpoints or changing settings.

episode.objective: Find the best single checkpoint for inference by swapping different saved checkpoints.
episode.outcome: Best single-checkpoint score at v8: LB 0.32858.

instance.goal: Which of several trained checkpoints yields the best leaderboard score for this EEG classification task?
instance.context: The author had multiple saved checkpoints from training runs with different hyperparameters (learning rate, weight decay, frequency filters, architecture blocks, epochs). The initial checkpoint scored 0.35973 on LB (KL divergence, lower is better).
instance.action: Swapped checkpoint paths one at a time in the inference command, submitting each to the leaderboard. Tested four checkpoints across the episode: the original (0.35973), a ResNet variant (0.36479, worse), an epoch-14 checkpoint with val_loss 0.4588 (0.34843, new best), and an epoch-14 checkpoint with val_loss 0.4944 (0.32858, new best). The checkpoint with the lower validation loss was not the best on LB; the one with higher val_loss (0.4944) scored best.

general.goal: Which saved checkpoint from training gives the best test-time performance when multiple candidates exist?
general.context: Multiple checkpoints are available from different training runs or epochs, and the validation metric recorded during training may not perfectly correlate with the public leaderboard metric.
general.action: Sweep checkpoints by substituting each into the inference pipeline and submitting. Do not rely solely on the validation loss recorded during training to pick the best checkpoint; instead, evaluate each on the actual test/leaderboard metric. A checkpoint with a slightly worse validation loss can outperform one with a better validation loss due to distribution shift or metric differences.

instance.goal: Why did the v5→v6 checkpoint swap not produce a valid submission (not submitted), while v6→v7 with the same checkpoint did (0.34843)?
instance.context: In v6 the author changed the checkpoint but the run was not submitted. In v7 the only change was adding 'hydra=test' to the command line, after which the same checkpoint produced a valid submission scoring 0.34843.
instance.action: Diagnosed that the inference script required a specific Hydra configuration override ('hydra=test') to run correctly in the Kaggle test environment. Added this argument, which fixed the pipeline and allowed the checkpoint to be properly evaluated.

general.goal: Why does the inference pipeline fail silently or produce no output when a new model file is swapped in?
general.context: A configuration-management framework controls the inference script, and switching model artifacts without updating the corresponding configuration can cause the run to fail or produce incorrect outputs without an obvious error.
general.action: When swapping model artifacts in a config-driven pipeline, verify that all required configuration overrides (e.g., environment mode, paths, runtime flags) are set correctly for the target execution context. If a run produces no submission, check the configuration layer before suspecting the model file itself.

episode.objective: Ensemble multiple fold checkpoints by averaging their predictions to improve the submission score.
episode.outcome: Best score at v13: LB 0.29157 with 5-fold pseudo_log checkpoint ensemble.

instance.goal: How much can averaging predictions from multiple checkpoints improve the KL-divergence score beyond the best single checkpoint?
instance.context: Best single checkpoint scored 0.32858. Multiple checkpoints from different epochs and folds were available from cross-validation training.
instance.action: Started by averaging 3 checkpoint predictions (score 0.30216), then expanded to 5 checkpoints (score 0.29768), then switched to pseudo-labeled fold checkpoints (score 0.29242). Each fold's submission was saved separately, then a merge function averaged probabilities across folds and re-normalized. Total improvement: 0.32858 → 0.29157.

general.goal: How much can combining predictions from multiple training checkpoints improve a probabilistic classification metric beyond the best single model?
general.context: A single checkpoint gives a competitive score, and several checkpoints from different folds or training stages are available. The metric rewards well-calibrated probability distributions.
general.action: Run inference separately with each checkpoint, save per-checkpoint prediction files, then average the predicted probability vectors and re-normalize so they sum to one. Start with a small number of checkpoints to confirm improvement, then incrementally add more. Expect diminishing but consistent gains as ensemble size grows.

instance.goal: Which set of checkpoints produces the best ensemble — epoch-selected checkpoints or pseudo-label fine-tuned fold checkpoints?
instance.context: Ensembling 5 epoch-based checkpoints scored 0.29768. Pseudo-labeled fold checkpoints (fold0–fold4_pseudo_log.ckpt) were also available, trained with a two-stage pseudo-labeling procedure.
instance.action: Replaced all 5 ensemble members with the pseudo-label fine-tuned fold checkpoints. Score improved from 0.29768 to 0.29242, confirming pseudo-label checkpoints were stronger ensemble members.
