general.goal: When ensembling multiple checkpoints, does the choice of training procedure behind each checkpoint matter more than simply adding more members?
general.context: An ensemble of checkpoints from standard training already improves over a single model. Alternative checkpoints from a second-stage fine-tuning procedure (e.g., on high-confidence or pseudo-labeled data) are available.
general.action: Swap ensemble members to use checkpoints from the stronger training procedure rather than just adding more members from the weaker one. Compare the ensemble score before and after the swap to confirm the gain comes from checkpoint quality, not just quantity.

episode.objective: Try the conv1d_pseudo experiment config for fold inference instead of the default model.
episode.outcome: Marginal improvement at v14: LB 0.29146 (new best).

instance.goal: Can switching from the default ResNet-based model to a conv1d_pseudo experiment config improve the ensemble's leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author had already optimized checkpoint selection and fold averaging with ResNet checkpoints, reaching LB 0.29157. Pseudo-labeled conv1d checkpoints were available as an alternative backbone/config.
instance.action: Changed the Hydra experiment override to experiment=conv1d_pseudo in every fold's inference call while keeping the same ensemble-averaging pipeline. This yielded a marginal improvement from 0.29157 to 0.29146.

general.goal: After optimizing checkpoint selection and fold ensembling for one model architecture, where can the next incremental gain come from?
general.context: The current architecture's score has plateaued through checkpoint and ensemble tuning, and alternative trained model configs (different backbone or training regime) are available.
general.action: Swap the experiment/config to a different trained model family while keeping the rest of the inference and ensembling pipeline identical. Evaluate on the leaderboard; even a tiny gain confirms the alternative model captures complementary signal, which can later be combined with the original.

instance.goal: Is the marginal gain from conv1d_pseudo real or noise, and is it worth building on?
instance.context: Switching from ResNet to conv1d_pseudo improved LB by only 0.00011. In hindsight, the next version (re-run) scored worse (0.29328), and a two-variant conv1d ensemble scored 0.31220, suggesting the conv1d alone was not reliably better.
instance.action: The author submitted the conv1d_pseudo result and observed the tiny improvement. Hindsight shows the gain was fragile: re-running regressed, and ensembling two conv1d variants hurt. This suggests the improvement was within noise.

general.goal: How can one distinguish a genuine leaderboard improvement from noise when the gain is extremely small?
general.context: A model swap produced a barely measurable improvement on the public leaderboard, with no local validation delta visible.
general.action: Treat very small single-submission gains (on the order of the fourth decimal place) as tentative. Verify by re-running the same pipeline and checking consistency. If a re-run or a natural extension (e.g., ensembling variants of the new model) regresses, treat the original gain as noise rather than building further on it.

episode.objective: Build a multi-version ensemble blending predictions from different model variants (conv1d_pseudo v0, conv1d_resv2 v1, pseudo_resv2 v2) across folds.
episode.outcome: Best at v21: LB 0.27185 with v2 only; adding v0 hurt (v22: 0.27950).

instance.goal: How much does averaging predictions from two different conv1d model variants (conv1d_pseudo v0 and conv1d_resv2 v1) improve over using either alone?
instance.context: Single-model v0 scored 0.29146; v1 alone scored 0.31220. The author needed to determine whether combining them helps despite v1 being individually worse.
instance.action: Ran inference for each model variant across all folds, saved per-fold CSVs with version suffixes, then averaged and renormalized predictions. The v0+v1 blend (0.28947) beat v0 alone (0.29146), confirming that even a weaker model variant improves the ensemble. A third variant v2 alone scored 0.27185, and v0+v2 scored 0.27950 (worse than v2 alone), showing diminishing or negative returns when adding a much weaker member.

general.goal: When combining predictions from multiple model variants, how can one tell whether adding a weaker variant helps or hurts the ensemble?
general.context: Several model variants are available, each with different standalone scores. Simple averaging gives equal weight to all members.
general.action: Test each variant alone first, then add variants one at a time to the ensemble and check the metric. A weaker variant can still help if it is diverse, but if the gap is large, equal-weight averaging may dilute the best model. When adding a member worsens the score, either drop it or move to weighted blending that down-weights the weaker member.

instance.goal: The merge loop was producing incorrect averages — why were not all fold/version predictions being included?
instance.context: In v18, the preds.append() call was outside the inner loop, so only the last fold/version prediction was appended per iteration, silently producing wrong averages. The submission scored 0.31220, same as v1 alone, hinting the merge was broken.
instance.action: In v19, fixed indentation so preds.append() was inside the loop body. After the fix, the two-version ensemble (v20) scored 0.28947, beating both individual models, confirming the bug had prevented proper averaging.

general.goal: How can one detect that an ensemble averaging loop is silently dropping some members' predictions?
general.context: An ensemble of multiple models scores identically to one of its members, suggesting the merge code is not actually combining all inputs.
general.action: Verify that the append/accumulate step is inside the correct loop scope. A quick sanity check: the number of accumulated arrays should equal the number of models × folds. If the ensemble score equals one member's score, inspect the loop for off-by-one or indentation bugs before concluding the models are redundant.

episode.objective: Switch from unweighted averaging to weighted blending of ensemble members.
episode.outcome: v23: LB 0.27421, improvement over v22 but not best overall.

instance.goal: Can weighting ensemble members by perceived quality improve the submission score over a simple average?
instance.context: In v21, averaging only v2 predictions scored 0.27185 (best). In v22, adding v0 predictions with equal weight worsened the score to 0.27950, suggesting v0 is weaker than v2.
instance.action: Replaced the unweighted average with a weighted blend using weights [0.2, 0.8] for [v0, v2], multiplying each version's predictions by its weight, summing, and row-normalizing. The result (0.27421) improved over equal weighting (0.27950) but did not beat v2-only (0.27185).

general.goal: When adding a weaker model to an ensemble hurts the score under equal weighting, can a weighted blend recover the benefit?
general.context: An ensemble of two prediction sources where one is clearly stronger: equal-weight averaging degraded the score compared to using the stronger source alone.
general.action: Assign a high weight (e.g., 0.8) to the stronger source and a low weight to the weaker one, multiply predictions by weights, sum, and renormalize to valid distributions. Compare the weighted blend against both the equal-weight ensemble and the single-source baseline. If the weighted blend still underperforms the single source, the weaker member adds only noise and should be dropped entirely.

instance.goal: What is the right balance between including diverse models for ensemble gain and excluding weak models that add noise?
instance.context: v21 (v2 only) scored 0.27185; v22 (v0+v2 equal weight) scored 0.27950; v23 (v0 at 0.2 + v2 at 0.8) scored 0.27421. The weaker v0 model hurt even at low weight, never beating the v2-only submission.
instance.action: The trajectory shows that when a weaker member degrades even a heavily down-weighted blend, the practitioner should drop it and instead seek a qualitatively different model (the next version introduced a transformer-based model). Diversity in architecture matters more than adding another variant of the same family.

general.goal: When does adding a second model to an ensemble help versus hurt, and what should be tried next if weighting fails?
general.context: A single strong model outperforms both equal-weight and skewed-weight blends that include a weaker model of similar type.
general.action: If down-weighting the weaker model still cannot match the single-model baseline, remove it entirely. To regain ensemble diversity, introduce a model from a different architecture family rather than another checkpoint or variant of the same family, because uncorrelated errors are what make ensembles effective.

episode.objective: Add LeViT/transformer-based checkpoints (and their pseudo variants) to the ensemble and tune blend weights to improve score.
episode.outcome: Best at v28: LB 0.25703 with v0+v2 at 0.5/0.5 weights after adding pseudo LeViT.

instance.goal: Can adding a structurally different model (LeViT/transformer) to an ensemble of conv1d models further reduce KL divergence?
instance.context: The best score so far (0.27185) came from ensembling conv1d-based fold predictions. A transformer-based architecture (LeViT) was trained on the same data and checkpoints were available.
instance.action: Replaced conv1d_pseudo fold checkpoints with LeViT checkpoints, ran inference for all folds, and blended with existing predictions. Score improved from 0.27421 to 0.26613, confirming the diverse architecture helps. Then swapped to pseudo-labeled LeViT checkpoints, gaining another improvement to 0.26010.

general.goal: Can ensembling predictions from an architecturally different model family improve the blended score beyond what same-family ensembles achieve?
general.context: An ensemble of models from one architecture family has plateaued, and checkpoints from a structurally different architecture (e.g., convolutional vs. transformer) trained on the same task are available.
general.action: Add the new architecture's fold predictions as an additional ensemble member. Start with a moderate weight for the new member (e.g., 30%) and adjust. Architecturally diverse members typically reduce ensemble error more than additional same-family members because their errors are less correlated.

instance.goal: What blend weight between the conv1d pseudo model (v0) and the LeViT pseudo model (v2) minimizes KL divergence?
instance.context: With weights [0.3, 0.7] favoring v2 (LeViT pseudo), score was 0.26010. Both model families had comparable individual quality after pseudo-label training.
instance.action: Changed weights from [0.3, 0.7] to [0.5, 0.5] (equal weighting). Score improved to 0.25703. Later attempt to add a third model (v29, LB 0.27662) hurt, suggesting equal weighting of two strong diverse models was optimal here.

general.goal: How should blend weights be set when combining two diverse model families of similar individual strength?
general.context: Two architecturally different models are being blended; one was initially given higher weight, but both have comparable quality after the same training regimen (e.g., pseudo-labeling).
general.action: Try equal weighting when both members are similarly strong. Iteratively adjust weights in small increments (e.g., 0.1 steps) and submit. When individual model qualities converge after similar training procedures, equal blending often outperforms skewed weights because it maximizes diversity benefit. Adding a third weaker or correlated member can hurt; verify each addition improves the score before keeping it.

instance.goal: Does switching from base-trained checkpoints to pseudo-label-trained checkpoints improve the LeViT ensemble member's contribution?
instance.context: LeViT (conv1d_tfm2d) fold checkpoints scored 0.26613 in the blend. Pseudo-labeled versions of the same architecture were available, and pseudo-labeling had already improved the conv1d model in earlier episodes.
instance.action: Swapped foldX_levit.ckpt to foldX_levit_pseudo.ckpt and changed experiment config to conv1d_tfm2d_pseudo. Score improved from 0.26613 to 0.26010, confirming pseudo-label training benefits transfer across architectures.

general.goal: If a semi-supervised training technique improved one model family, will it also improve a different architecture used in the same ensemble?
general.context: A training technique (e.g., pseudo-labeling or knowledge distillation) already boosted one ensemble member. Checkpoints from a second, architecturally different model trained with and without the same technique are available.
general.action: Swap in the enhanced-training checkpoints for the second architecture and measure the ensemble score. Techniques that leverage unlabeled data or soft labels tend to generalize across architectures on the same task, so the upgrade is usually beneficial and worth testing early.

episode.objective: Add EfficientNet-B1 v3 (and its pseudo variant, plus effv2) as a third ensemble member and tune blend weights/membership to beat 0.25703.
episode.outcome: Best at v43: LB 0.25606 with v0+v2+v3 at [0.3,0.3,0.4]. Many intermediate regressions and reverts.

instance.goal: How much does adding a third model variant (EfficientNet-B1 v3) to an existing two-model ensemble improve the KL-divergence score?
instance.context: The best score was 0.25703 with a 0.5/0.5 blend of two model versions (v0 conv1d_pseudo and v2 pseudo_resv2). A new EfficientNet-B1-based model (v3) was available as a candidate ensemble member.
instance.action: Added v3 predictions with weights [0.4, 0.4, 0.2], which worsened the score to 0.27662. Then tried removing v3 and reverting, tried pseudo-labeled v3 with weights [0.3, 0.3, 0.4], tried v3 alone (0.27261), tried effv2_pseudo alone (0.26549), and finally blended all three versions [0.3, 0.3, 0.4] achieving 0.25606 — a new best. The key was iterating over both membership and weights.

general.goal: How should a new candidate model be integrated into an existing weighted ensemble without degrading the score?
general.context: An ensemble of two diverse models already achieves a strong score. A third model from a different architecture family is available but its standalone quality is uncertain.
general.action: First test the new model in isolation to gauge its standalone quality. Then try adding it to the blend at a small weight while keeping existing members' relative weights similar. If the blend worsens, try the pseudo-labeled or fine-tuned variant of the new model. Iterate over weight allocations, giving the new member progressively more weight only if the score improves. Expect several rounds of weight tuning before finding the optimal combination.

instance.goal: When a new ensemble member hurts the blended score, what is the most informative diagnostic step?
instance.context: Adding v3 at weight 0.2 to the existing v0+v2 blend worsened the score from 0.25703 to 0.27662. It was unclear whether v3 predictions were bad or just poorly weighted.
instance.action: Submitted v3 alone (weight 1.0) to get its standalone score (0.27261), then submitted the alternative effv2_pseudo alone (0.26549). This revealed both were weaker than the existing blend but not terrible, confirming they could help at a small weight. The final blend [0.3, 0.3, 0.4] with the pseudo variant achieved 0.25606, beating the previous best.

general.goal: How can one determine whether a new ensemble component is fundamentally weak or just poorly weighted in the blend?
general.context: Adding a new model to an existing blend worsened the combined score. The new model's standalone quality on the leaderboard is unknown.
general.action: Submit the new model's predictions alone (weight 1.0) to establish its standalone leaderboard score. Compare this to the existing blend's score. If the standalone score is within a reasonable margin, the model likely adds diversity and should be blended at a low weight. If it is much worse, consider using a retrained or pseudo-labeled variant before blending.

instance.goal: Does switching from base checkpoints to pseudo-labeled checkpoints for the new EfficientNet-B1 v3 model improve its contribution to the ensemble?
instance.context: The non-pseudo v3 model worsened the blend (0.27662 vs 0.25703 baseline). Previous experience in this notebook showed pseudo-labeled checkpoints consistently improved scores for other model variants (v0, v2).
instance.action: Switched v3 inference to conv1d_effb1_v3_pseudo checkpoints and increased v3's blend weight to 0.4 (from 0.2). The three-way blend with pseudo v3 at [0.3, 0.3, 0.4] achieved 0.25606, a new best, confirming pseudo-labeling improved the new member enough to benefit the ensemble.

general.goal: When a new ensemble member trained on labeled data alone is too weak to help the blend, what training-side improvement is most likely to make it viable?
general.context: A model trained only on labeled data degrades the ensemble. The same semi-supervised or self-training procedure that improved other ensemble members is available.
general.action: Retrain the weak member using the same semi-supervised (pseudo-labeling) pipeline that benefited existing members. If pseudo-labeling consistently helped other architectures in the same competition, it is likely to help the new architecture as well, making it a viable ensemble component.

episode.objective: Add codebase-v2 models (xcit, effb1 clean/corr pseudo) as new ensemble members (v4, v5) and tune the blend to incorporate them.
episode.outcome: v4+v5 alone worse (v48: 0.27952); blending all four versions (v49: 0.25988); corrected pseudo variants tried (v50); final score v52: LB 0.25829, did not beat v43's 0.25606.

instance.goal: How much do new model families (xcit, effb1) from a second codebase contribute when added to an already-strong ensemble of conv1d and other models?
instance.context: The existing ensemble of v0/v2/v3 models scored 0.25606. Two new architectures (xcit pseudo, effb1 pseudo) were trained with a different codebase (hms-mk-codesv2) and available as fold checkpoints.
instance.action: First tested the new models alone (v4+v5 at equal weights → 0.27952, much worse than existing best). Then blended them with existing models (v0,v3,v4,v5 at 0.3,0.3,0.2,0.2 → 0.25988, still worse than 0.25606). Tried corrected pseudo variants with equal weights → 0.25829, still not beating the previous best. The new models did not improve the ensemble.

general.goal: Will adding predictions from a new model family improve an existing ensemble?
general.context: An ensemble of several diverse models already achieves a strong score. New model architectures trained on the same data are available but have not been validated individually against the current best.
general.action: First evaluate the new models in isolation to gauge their standalone quality. If they score substantially worse than the current ensemble, expect limited or no gain from blending. Add them with small weights and compare against the baseline ensemble. If no improvement appears after trying several weight configurations, drop the new members rather than diluting the ensemble.

instance.goal: When integrating models from a separate codebase with different data preprocessing, what is the right workflow to avoid errors and isolate their contribution?
instance.context: The author needed to add xcit and effb1 models from 'hms-mk-codesv2' which required different sys.path, data conversion (parquet→npy with v2 code), and a different test dataset class. Multiple folds and two model variants needed to run.
instance.action: Added a second output path, switched sys.path to the new codebase, ran data conversion with v2 code, executed inference for all folds of both model variants saving to distinctly named files (submission_fold{n}_v4/v5.csv), then tested the new predictions alone before blending with existing ones. This isolated integration issues from ensemble-weight tuning.

general.goal: How to safely integrate predictions from a different training pipeline or codebase into an existing ensemble workflow?
general.context: A new set of models was trained with a different codebase that has its own data preprocessing and inference API, and predictions must be merged with those from the original pipeline.
general.action: Set up a separate output directory and import path for the new codebase. Run data conversion and inference independently, saving outputs with distinct version-tagged filenames. Verify the new predictions in isolation (submit or validate alone) before blending, so any integration bugs are caught before they corrupt the ensemble.

episode.objective: Set up initial inference pipeline with image preprocessing and pretrained model configuration.
episode.outcome: First submission baseline at v2 LB 0.65796.

instance.goal: How should spectrogram images be preprocessed and the pretrained model configured to produce a valid first submission?
instance.context: Starting from scratch with a timm-based FastViT model and spectrogram inputs for EEG classification. The checkpoint was trained without ImageNet pretrained weights, so the model must be instantiated with pretrained=False to match.
instance.action: Added albumentations-based resize/normalize transforms as a preprocessing chain applied to spectrogram images before inference. Set the timm model's pretrained flag to False so architecture weights match the provided checkpoint. This yielded LB 0.65796 as a baseline.

general.goal: How should input preprocessing and model initialization be set up to get a working first inference baseline?
general.context: Building an initial inference pipeline with a pretrained-backbone image classifier and image-like inputs (e.g., spectrograms). A fine-tuned checkpoint is available but was trained with specific preprocessing and without the default pretrained initialization.
general.action: Ensure the image resize, normalization, and channel formatting in the inference pipeline exactly match what was used during training. When loading a fine-tuned checkpoint, instantiate the backbone with pretrained=False so the architecture matches the saved weights and no pretrained weights are loaded underneath. Verify with a submission that the pipeline produces valid predictions.

episode.objective: Replace single FastViT model with an ensemble of EEG CNN-RNN models and filtering-based spectrogram features.
episode.outcome: Large improvement to LB 0.37116 at v3, new best.

instance.goal: How much can the score improve by replacing a single vision-transformer model with an ensemble of specialized EEG models and better feature engineering?
instance.context: The baseline FastViT model scored 0.65796 on the KL-divergence leaderboard. The competition data includes raw EEG signals and spectrograms; strong solutions are known to use CNN-RNN architectures on EEG with signal-processing features and ensembles.
instance.action: Replaced the single FastViT pipeline with multiple pretrained EEG CNN-RNN model checkpoints loaded from disk, added Butterworth filtering and custom spectrogram computation from raw EEG, and averaged predictions across all models. This dropped the score from 0.658 to 0.371 (a 0.287 improvement).

general.goal: How much can the score improve by switching from a generic pretrained image model to domain-specific architectures with proper signal-processing features?
general.context: A generic vision backbone applied to spectrograms gives a weak baseline on a physiological time-series classification task. The raw signals are available and domain knowledge suggests filtering and specialized temporal models are far more effective.
general.action: Replace the generic image backbone with an ensemble of domain-specific models (e.g., CNN-RNN on raw signals) that incorporate proper signal preprocessing (bandpass filtering, custom spectrograms). Load multiple fold checkpoints and average their predictions. Expect a large score jump—potentially halving the error or more—because the architecture and features now match the data modality.

instance.goal: What is the most impactful first move when a vision-only spectrogram baseline underperforms on an EEG classification task?
instance.context: The competition metric is KL divergence on soft label distributions. A single FastViT model on Kaggle-provided spectrograms scored 0.658. Known strong solutions use raw EEG features with Butterworth filtering and multi-fold ensembles of CNN-RNN models.
instance.action: In one large refactor, simultaneously switched the model family (FastViT → EEG CNN-RNN), added signal-processing features (Butterworth filtering, custom spectrogram generation from raw EEG), and introduced multi-checkpoint ensembling. All three changes were bundled together rather than tested incrementally, yielding a 44% relative improvement in one step.

general.goal: When a weak baseline needs a large improvement, is it better to make incremental changes or bundle multiple high-confidence improvements together?
general.context: The baseline is far from competitive, and several improvements (domain-appropriate architecture, proper signal preprocessing, ensembling) are each individually well-supported by known strong solutions. Testing each one separately would be slow.
general.action: When the gap to competitive performance is large and multiple improvements are each strongly motivated by domain knowledge or known solutions, bundle them into a single refactor. Verify the combined effect on the leaderboard. Reserve incremental ablation for later fine-tuning once the score is in a competitive range.

episode.objective: Tune ensemble composition by swapping/removing members and switching checkpoint selection to improve score.

instance.goal: Which checkpoint selection strategy (final vs best-validation) and which subset of ensemble members yields the best KL divergence?
instance.context: Starting from LB 0.37116 with an ensemble of EEG CNN-RNN models using 'model_final.pt' checkpoints. Multiple model directories and fold checkpoints are available.
instance.action: Switched from 'model_final.pt' to 'model_best_test.pt' checkpoints, removed one model directory from the ensemble, and added output normalization (divide by sum). This worsened the score slightly to 0.37553. Then swapped another model directory (stage_3 → simple stage_2), recovering partially to 0.37494. Neither change beat the original 0.37116.

general.goal: How should checkpoint selection and ensemble member composition be tuned to improve a probability-distribution prediction metric?
general.context: An ensemble of neural network folds is already producing a competitive score. Both last-epoch and best-validation checkpoints are available, and multiple trained model variants exist.
general.action: Try swapping checkpoint selection (last-epoch vs best-validation) and toggling individual ensemble members one at a time, submitting after each change. If switching to best-validation checkpoints does not help, the final-epoch checkpoints may have been better regularized or the validation metric may not align with the test metric. Revert changes that hurt and only keep those that improve.

instance.goal: Are the raw averaged ensemble outputs valid probability distributions, and does normalizing them matter for KL divergence scoring?
instance.context: Ensemble predictions were averaged across models and folds but not explicitly normalized to sum to 1. The competition metric is KL divergence, which requires proper probability distributions.
instance.action: Added a normalization step (divide each row by its sum) before outputting predictions. Despite this fix, the score worsened (0.37116 → 0.37553), likely because the normalization was confounded with simultaneously removing an ensemble member and changing checkpoints.

general.goal: Does post-hoc normalization of averaged ensemble outputs affect a divergence-based scoring metric?
general.context: When averaging probability outputs from multiple models, the result may not sum exactly to 1 due to floating-point issues or if individual models output unnormalized logits. The evaluation metric penalizes invalid distributions.
general.action: Always normalize averaged probability predictions to sum to 1 before submission when the metric is a divergence or log-likelihood. However, change only one thing at a time so the effect of normalization can be isolated from other modifications.

episode.objective: Try different model variants (softmax, base EegModel) with adjusted preprocessing and checkpoints to improve score.
episode.outcome: v6 regressed to 0.43363, v7 achieved new best 0.32513.

instance.goal: Which model variant and checkpoint combination yields the best score when swapping components in the EEG ensemble?
instance.context: Score plateaued around 0.37 with CNN-RNN ensemble. Multiple trained checkpoints exist: softmax-trained, base EegModel with different selection criteria (model_final.pt, model_best_test.pt, model_best_val_g10.pt). Switching to softmax model with model_final.pt worsened score to 0.43.
instance.action: Tried EegModelSoftmax with model_final.pt checkpoint first (v6, score worsened to 0.43). Then switched to base EegModel with model_best_val_g10.pt checkpoint plus corrected preprocessing (bandpass filtering, binning, NaN handling, exp of log-probs), achieving new best 0.32513.

general.goal: Which checkpoint selection criterion produces the best inference quality when multiple saved checkpoints exist from training?
general.context: Multiple checkpoints are available from training (final epoch, best on full validation, best on high-confidence validation subset). The model architecture and its output format (log-probabilities vs. probabilities) must match the checkpoint.
general.action: Try checkpoints selected on the high-confidence validation subset (e.g., best score on samples with many annotator votes) rather than final-epoch or full-validation-best checkpoints. Ensure the output conversion (e.g., exponentiating log-probabilities) matches what the checkpoint was trained to produce.

instance.goal: Why did the softmax model variant score much worse than expected despite using the same architecture family?
instance.context: Switching from base EegModel to EegModelSoftmax with model_final.pt and different preprocessing (mean-centering instead of bandpass+binning) degraded score from 0.37 to 0.43. Reverting to base EegModel with bandpass filtering, binning, NaN handling, and proper log-prob→prob conversion recovered to 0.32.
instance.action: Ensured preprocessing pipeline (bandpass filtering + temporal binning for downsampling, NaN/inf handling) matched what the model was trained with, and used the correct output transformation (exp of log-probs). The preprocessing mismatch was likely the dominant cause of the v6 regression.

general.goal: What causes a large score regression when substituting a model variant that should perform comparably?
general.context: A model swap caused unexpected degradation. The new variant used different input normalization and a different checkpoint selection, making it unclear whether the architecture or the preprocessing was at fault.
general.action: When a model swap degrades performance, check that the inference-time preprocessing (filtering, normalization, downsampling) exactly matches what the checkpoint was trained with, and that the output transformation (e.g., softmax vs. log-softmax) is correct. Fix preprocessing alignment before concluding the architecture is worse.

episode.objective: Try KNN-augmented model variant and then revert to simpler baseline CNN-RNN checkpoint.
episode.outcome: Both v8 (0.35391) and v9 (0.36957) worse than v7; abandoned.

instance.goal: Can a KNN-augmented variant of the CNN-RNN model outperform the baseline CNN-RNN checkpoint that achieved the current best score?
instance.context: The baseline eeg_cnn_rnn model with a specific checkpoint achieved LB 0.32513 (best so far). A KNN-augmented variant (eeg_cnn_rnn_knn) with its own checkpoints and a different prediction method (knn_predict) was available.
instance.action: Swapped to the KNN variant (v8, LB 0.35391), observed it was worse, then reverted to the baseline CNN-RNN with a single checkpoint (v9, LB 0.36957). Neither beat the v7 best of 0.32513, confirming the original baseline was superior to both alternatives tried.

general.goal: When a baseline model holds the best score, is a more complex variant (e.g., adding a retrieval-based prediction layer) likely to improve it?
general.context: A simpler model variant already achieves a strong score. A more complex variant exists that changes the prediction pathway but uses the same backbone.
general.action: Test the complex variant on the leaderboard. If it scores worse, revert promptly. Do not assume added complexity helps; treat it as a probe and keep the simpler model as the default unless the complex one clearly wins.

instance.goal: After the KNN variant failed, can a single-fold baseline checkpoint recover the previous best performance?
instance.context: The KNN multi-fold ensemble scored 0.35391. The previous best (0.32513) used a specific baseline checkpoint. Reverting to a single baseline checkpoint yielded 0.36957, still worse than v7.
instance.action: Loaded a single baseline CNN-RNN checkpoint instead of the multi-fold KNN ensemble. The score (0.36957) did not recover the v7 best, suggesting the exact checkpoint or fold combination matters, not just the model class. The author later (v10) returned to multi-fold ensembling to recover performance.

general.goal: Why might reverting a model class change not recover the previous best score?
general.context: A model variant swap degraded the score. Reverting the model class but using a different checkpoint or fewer folds than the original best submission still underperforms.
general.action: When reverting an unsuccessful change, replicate the exact configuration (checkpoint paths, number of folds, preprocessing) of the previous best, not just the model class. Differences in checkpoint selection or ensemble size can account for meaningful score gaps even within the same architecture.

episode.objective: Build a multi-family ensemble by combining different EEG model variants with fold averaging to improve predictions.
episode.outcome: Progressively improved: v10 0.33179, v11 0.30250 (best), v12 regressed 0.32099, v13 0.30219 new best.

instance.goal: How much can combining two different EEG model architectures (eeg_cnn_rnn_w1 and baseline_eeg_diff) with separate preprocessing improve KL divergence over any single model family?
instance.context: Single-model submissions plateaued around 0.32–0.37. The author had multiple trained model families with different architectures and input normalization schemes, each with fold checkpoints.
instance.action: First loaded one model family with fold averaging (v10, 0.33179). Then added a second model family with its own preprocessing and averaged both families' outputs (v11, 0.30250). Tested the newer checkpoints alone (v12, 0.32099, worse). Re-added the second family to get the best score (v13, 0.30219). The two-family ensemble consistently beat either family alone.

general.goal: How much does ensembling architecturally diverse models improve predictions compared to using the best single model family?
general.context: Multiple model families have been trained independently with different architectures and input preprocessing, each achieving similar but not identical single-model scores.
general.action: Load each model family with its own preprocessing pipeline, run inference separately, and average their output probabilities. Verify the ensemble beats each family alone by also submitting each family individually. If one family alone scores worse than the ensemble, keep both; the diversity gain typically exceeds what any single family achieves.

instance.goal: When combining model families, is it better to swap in newer/distilled checkpoints or to keep the original checkpoints and add a complementary model?
instance.context: v11 achieved 0.30250 with two model families. v12 replaced the first family's checkpoints with 'new_distil' and dropped the second family, scoring 0.32099 (worse). v13 restored the two-family ensemble with the distilled checkpoints plus the second family, scoring 0.30219 (best).
instance.action: Test checkpoint upgrades in isolation (single-family submission) to measure their standalone quality, but always re-test the full ensemble afterward. Do not permanently drop a complementary model family just because a new checkpoint seems promising alone—the diversity benefit of the second family may outweigh the checkpoint improvement.

general.goal: When upgrading one component of a multi-model ensemble, how can one tell whether the upgrade helps or whether removing ensemble diversity hurts more?
general.context: An ensemble of two model families scores better than either alone. A new checkpoint is available for one family, and testing it requires deciding whether to also keep the other family.
general.action: Evaluate the new checkpoint both in isolation and within the full ensemble. If the isolated score is worse than the ensemble, the diversity contribution of the other family is confirmed. Always restore the full ensemble after testing a component swap, and only drop a family if the ensemble without it scores better than the ensemble with it.

episode.objective: Add test-time augmentation (spatial flips) to improve inference robustness.

instance.goal: Can test-time augmentation (spatial flips) on spectrogram/EEG inputs improve the ensemble's KL-divergence score beyond the current best of 0.30219?
instance.context: The author had just achieved a new best LB score (0.30219) by ensembling two model families on EEG spectrograms. The competition metric is KL divergence (lower is better), and the inputs are 2D spectrogram-like representations amenable to spatial flips.
instance.action: Added horizontal flip, vertical flip, and combined flip as TTA variants. For each sample, generated all TTA versions, ran both model families on each variant, averaged predictions across all TTA variants and models, then renormalized. Score worsened from 0.30219 to 0.31017.

general.goal: Can test-time augmentation with spatial flips improve predictions when ensembling models on 2D spectral representations?
general.context: An ensemble of multiple model families has reached a new best score on a probabilistic classification task. The inputs are 2D time-frequency representations where spatial axes encode time and frequency.
general.action: Apply horizontal and vertical flips as TTA, average predictions across all augmented views and models, then renormalize. Monitor the leaderboard: if the score worsens, the augmentations likely break meaningful spatial structure (e.g., frequency ordering or temporal direction) and should be removed. Spectrograms typically have non-symmetric axes, so geometric TTA that worked on natural images may hurt.

episode.objective: Add spectrogram-based model to ensemble and then simplify by removing TTA and trimming members.
episode.outcome: v15 regressed badly (0.43907), v16 recovered to 0.31128 by removing spec model and TTA; abandoned.

instance.goal: Can adding a spectrogram-based model to an EEG-only ensemble improve the score?
instance.context: The best LB so far (0.30219) came from ensembling two EEG model families. A spectrogram modality was available but not yet used in the current ensemble.
instance.action: Added a SpectrogramModel with a new spectrogram feature pipeline (scipy.signal, butter filter, MAD normalization) alongside existing EEG models. The initial integration scored 0.43907 (much worse), so in the next step the author removed TTA overhead and trimmed one model source from the ensemble, recovering to 0.31128. The spectrogram model was kept but the ensemble was simplified.

general.goal: Will introducing a new input modality into an existing ensemble improve predictions?
general.context: An ensemble of models from one modality has reached a plateau. A second modality is available and could provide complementary signal, but integrating it changes the averaging balance.
general.action: Add the new-modality model and submit. If the score degrades substantially, diagnose whether the new model's predictions are miscalibrated or the ensemble weighting is off. Simplify by removing weaker members or test-time augmentation overhead, then re-submit. If the new modality still hurts, remove it and try again with better-trained checkpoints before concluding the modality is unhelpful.

instance.goal: Why did the ensemble score degrade so sharply after adding the spectrogram model (0.30219 → 0.43907)?
instance.context: The spectrogram model was new and possibly poorly calibrated or undertrained. TTA was also active, adding complexity. The large regression suggested the new component dominated or corrupted the average.
instance.action: Removed TTA and excluded one model folder from the ensemble to reduce noise and rebalance contributions. This recovered most of the loss (0.43907 → 0.31128), confirming the issue was ensemble composition rather than the core pipeline.

general.goal: How to recover when adding a new ensemble member causes a large score regression?
general.context: A newly added model caused the ensemble score to worsen dramatically, suggesting miscalibration or an imbalanced contribution from the new member.
general.action: Isolate the effect by removing other recent changes (e.g., test-time augmentation) and trimming weaker or redundant ensemble members. Submit the simplified version to determine whether the new model itself is harmful or whether the regression was caused by interaction with other components.

episode.objective: Replace ensemble with a newer EEG model (EegModel3) and add spatial-flip TTA to improve score.
episode.lever: new EEG model variant with TTA
episode.outcome: v17 new best 0.28185, v18 slight improvement 0.28137 new best.

instance.goal: Can a single newer model (EegModel3) with robust preprocessing outperform the previous multi-model ensemble?
instance.context: The best ensemble of models_0, models_1, and models_2 scored 0.30219. A new EegModel3 checkpoint was available with a different architecture and training stage. The author disabled all previous models and spectrogram pipelines.
instance.action: Replaced the entire ensemble with EegModel3 only, using robust normalization (MAD-based std, NaN/Inf handling, clipping) matched to the new model's expected input format. This single-model approach scored 0.28185, a new best by a large margin.

general.goal: When a stronger single model becomes available, is it worth replacing an existing multi-model ensemble with it alone?
general.context: An ensemble of several weaker models holds the current best score, but a newer model trained with improved methodology is available.
general.action: Test the new model in isolation first, disabling all other ensemble members. If it already beats the full ensemble, use it as the new baseline and build future ensembles around it. A stronger single model often outperforms an ensemble of weaker ones.

instance.goal: Can exploiting the spatial symmetry of EEG channel layouts via test-time augmentation further improve predictions?
instance.context: EegModel3 alone scored 0.28185. EEG data has a spatial channel layout (left-right hemisphere symmetry) that can be flipped horizontally and vertically. Earlier TTA attempts on a different model (v14, 0.31017) had hurt the score.
instance.action: Generated three spatial flips of the EEG input (horizontal, vertical, both) using simple array reversal, ran each through every fold model, and averaged all predictions together. This yielded 0.28137, a small but consistent improvement over no-TTA.

general.goal: How much can spatial test-time augmentation improve predictions when the input has a natural spatial symmetry?
general.context: A single strong model is the current baseline. The input data has an inherent spatial structure (e.g., symmetric sensor layout) that permits meaningful geometric flips. Previous TTA on weaker models was not beneficial.
general.action: Apply spatial flips (horizontal, vertical, combined) as test-time augmentations and average predictions across all augmented views and folds. When the base model is already strong and the flips respect the data's physical symmetry, expect a small but reliable gain. If the base model is weak, TTA may add noise rather than help.

episode.objective: Introduce attention-model with midline/EKG derived channels to improve predictions.
episode.lever: attention model with new EEG channels
episode.outcome: v19 LB 0.28876, worse than v18 0.28137; abandoned.

instance.goal: Can adding derived EEG channels (midline Fz/Cz/Pz and EKG) and a new attention-based model architecture improve the ensemble's KL divergence score?
instance.context: The best score so far (0.28137) was achieved with an EEG CNN-RNN ensemble plus test-time spatial augmentations. The existing pipeline used 18 bipolar EEG channels; midline and EKG channels were unused.
instance.action: Added a new EegModel variant with attention, extended the feature pipeline to compute 19 channels (18 bipolar + midline/EKG derived), applied MAD normalization and clipping, loaded new checkpoints, and included the new model's predictions in the ensemble. Score worsened from 0.28137 to 0.28876.

general.goal: Will enriching the input feature set with additional derived channels and switching to a more expressive model variant improve predictions?
general.context: An ensemble of simpler models on a subset of available input channels has reached a strong baseline. Additional channels derivable from the raw signals have not yet been exploited.
general.action: Derive the new channels, add appropriate normalization (e.g., robust statistics, clipping), train or load a model that accepts the expanded input, and include it in the ensemble. If the leaderboard score worsens, the new component may be adding noise or the model checkpoint may not be well-calibrated; revert or reduce its ensemble weight before iterating further.

instance.goal: When swapping in a new model family (attention-based with 19-channel input) for an existing one (CNN-RNN with 18-channel input), how should the ensemble be managed to avoid regression?
instance.context: The author commented out the previous best model group (models_3) and replaced it with the new attention model (models_4), rather than adding it alongside. The score regressed by ~0.007.
instance.action: Replaced the previous model group entirely with the new one. The regression suggests the new model alone was weaker than the replaced one. A safer approach would have been to add the new model alongside the existing best models and verify the combined ensemble improves before removing any component.

general.goal: How should a new model component be integrated into an existing ensemble to minimize the risk of score regression?
general.context: The current ensemble has a known strong score. A new model variant with different input features is available but untested on the leaderboard.
general.action: Add the new model as an additional ensemble member rather than replacing an existing one. Submit to verify the combined ensemble improves. Only then consider removing weaker members. Replacing a proven component with an unproven one risks regression even if the new model is individually strong.

episode.objective: Integrate spectrogram CNN models into the ensemble using different spectrogram preprocessing approaches.
episode.outcome: v20 badly regressed (0.51146), v21 improved but still poor (0.33979); abandoned.

instance.goal: Can adding a spectrogram-based CNN model to the existing EEG-only ensemble improve the KL divergence score?
instance.context: The best score so far (0.28137) came from EEG-based models with TTA. A previous attempt to add spectrogram models (v15, 0.43907) had failed badly. The author tries again with different spectrogram preprocessing approaches.
instance.action: First tried scipy-based spectrogram preprocessing with a spectrogram CNN model alone (v20, score 0.51146—much worse). Then switched to torchaudio-based spectrogram computation with different normalization and a different pretrained model set (v21, score 0.33979—still worse than EEG-only baseline). Neither spectrogram-only approach beat the EEG ensemble; the author later combined both modalities (v22, 0.29324).

general.goal: When introducing a new input modality into an ensemble, how can one tell whether the modality adds value versus hurts performance?
general.context: An ensemble using one modality has a strong baseline score. A second modality is available but previous attempts to use it alone or naïvely scored much worse.
general.action: First verify the new-modality model works standalone at a reasonable level before adding it to the ensemble. If standalone performance is far below the existing baseline, do not replace existing models; instead add the new modality alongside existing ones so the ensemble can benefit from complementary signal without losing the strong baseline. Iterate on the new modality's preprocessing until standalone quality is acceptable, then combine.

instance.goal: Why does the spectrogram model score so poorly (0.51) when used alone, and can a different spectrogram computation method fix it?
instance.context: v20 used scipy-based spectrogram extraction with albumentations resize and scored 0.51146. The author suspects the preprocessing pipeline or spectrogram parameters are mismatched with the pretrained model.
instance.action: Switched from scipy spectrogram to torchaudio.Spectrogram with different n_fft/window/hop settings, abs→log→mean normalization, and frequency-axis slicing. Also switched to a different pretrained checkpoint folder. This improved from 0.51 to 0.34 but still fell short of the EEG-only 0.28 baseline.

general.goal: When a pretrained model produces poor predictions at inference time, how much of the gap is due to mismatched input preprocessing versus model quality?
general.context: A pretrained model loaded with one preprocessing pipeline scores far below expectations. The model was trained with a specific spectral transform and normalization that may differ from what is applied at inference.
general.action: Ensure the inference-time feature extraction (spectral transform parameters, normalization, cropping/resizing) exactly matches what was used during training. When the training pipeline is uncertain, try the most likely transform library and parameters, and measure the score change. A large improvement from just changing preprocessing confirms mismatch was the dominant issue; a modest improvement suggests the model itself may also be weak.

episode.objective: Re-add raw EEG model to the ensemble alongside spectrogram models to recover performance.
episode.outcome: v22 LB 0.29324, partial recovery but not best.

instance.goal: How can the score be recovered after a regression caused by switching to spectrogram-only models?
instance.context: v17-v18 achieved 0.28137 with raw EEG models. v20-v21 replaced them with spectrogram-based models, regressing to 0.33979-0.51146. The raw EEG pipeline and checkpoints were still available.
instance.action: Re-added the EegModel instances and their raw EEG preprocessing (compute_eeg_from_file, NaN/Inf zeroing, tensor conversion) back into the ensemble alongside the spectrogram models. This recovered to 0.29324, much closer to the previous best of 0.28137.

general.goal: How can performance be recovered after a regression caused by replacing a proven model family with a new one?
general.context: A new model modality (e.g., spectrogram-based) was tried as a replacement for an existing strong model (e.g., raw-signal-based), but the swap caused a large score regression. The original model code and checkpoints remain available.
general.action: Rather than replacing the proven model, add the new model alongside it in the ensemble. Re-include the original model's preprocessing and inference path so both modalities contribute predictions. This recovers most of the lost performance and may eventually surpass the original when the new modality is properly tuned.

instance.goal: What is the safest way to evaluate whether spectrogram models add value to an EEG-based ensemble?
instance.context: The author tried spectrogram-only inference (v20, v21) and saw large regressions (0.51, 0.34 vs best 0.28). Only after re-adding EEG models (v22, 0.29) could the spectrogram contribution be assessed without confounding the loss of the EEG signal.
instance.action: Kept the best-performing EEG models as a fixed baseline in the ensemble and added spectrogram models on top, rather than swapping them in. The combined result (0.29324) showed the spectrogram models were not yet helping enough to offset any noise they introduced.

general.goal: How should a new model modality be tested when an existing ensemble already performs well?
general.context: An ensemble of one modality has a strong baseline score. A second modality is available but untested in combination.
general.action: Never remove the existing strong models when testing a new modality. Add the new modality's predictions to the existing ensemble so the incremental effect can be measured cleanly. If the combined score regresses or barely improves, the new modality needs further tuning before inclusion.

episode.objective: Switch to multimodal model checkpoints and sweep different checkpoint sets to find the best ensemble.
episode.outcome: v23 0.28499, v24 regressed 0.33446, v25 recovered 0.28686, v26 0.28546; none beat v18 best of 0.28137.

instance.goal: Which set of multimodal model checkpoints produces the best leaderboard score when used in the ensemble?
instance.context: The author had a best LB of 0.28137 from EEG-only models with TTA. A new MultimodalModel architecture was available with multiple checkpoint directories (final_multimodal_sanity, final_multimodal_s1, stage_6). No local validation scores are visible.
instance.action: Swept through checkpoint directories one at a time: first final_multimodal_sanity (0.28499), then final_multimodal_s1 (0.33446), then stage_6 (0.28686), then combined final_multimodal_sanity + stage_6 (0.28546). The first directory tried (final_multimodal_sanity alone) gave the best result among these, but none beat the prior best of 0.28137.

general.goal: Which checkpoint set from a new model architecture should be included in an inference ensemble?
general.context: Multiple checkpoint directories exist from different training stages or configurations of a newly available model architecture, and no reliable local validation is available to pre-screen them.
general.action: Sweep checkpoint directories one at a time on the leaderboard, starting with the most promising (e.g., a sanity-checked or final-stage set). If none improves over the current best, try combining the top two directories. Stop when combinations also fail to improve, and revert to the previous best ensemble.

instance.goal: When switching to a multimodal model, does changing spectrogram resize interpolation affect score?
instance.context: In v23→v24, the author simultaneously switched checkpoint directories (final_multimodal_sanity → final_multimodal_s1) and changed spectrogram resize to use cubic interpolation. The score worsened from 0.28499 to 0.33446.
instance.action: The confounded change made it impossible to attribute the regression. In the next step (v24→v25), only the checkpoint directory was changed (to stage_6), recovering to 0.28686, suggesting the checkpoint switch in v24 was the main cause of regression, not the interpolation change.

general.goal: How can the effect of a preprocessing change be isolated when it was introduced alongside a model change?
general.context: A submission that changed both the checkpoint source and a preprocessing parameter regressed significantly, making attribution ambiguous.
general.action: In the next iteration, change only one variable (revert or swap just the checkpoint) to isolate which factor caused the regression. Avoid bundling unrelated changes in a single submission when doing a sweep, so each leaderboard probe tests exactly one hypothesis.

episode.objective: Set up a multi-member ensemble and tune blending weights between two prediction populations.
episode.outcome: Best score 0.30010 at v4; v5 not submitted. Weights adjusted from 0.45/0.15/0.40 to 0.45/0.15/0.40.

instance.goal: How should multiple model predictions (predss_1, predss_2, predss_3) be weighted to minimize KL divergence on the leaderboard?
instance.context: The author has three prediction populations from different checkpoints. Initial weights (0.45, 0.15, 0.40) scored 0.34106. Removing one checkpoint and rebalancing to (0.5, 0.1, 0.40) improved to 0.30010.
instance.action: Iteratively adjusted blend weights in small increments (0.05 steps), submitted to leaderboard, observed the score change, and continued tuning. Disabling a weak ensemble member and redistributing its weight yielded the biggest single improvement (~0.04 KL reduction).

general.goal: How should blending weights across ensemble members be tuned when only leaderboard feedback is available?
general.context: Multiple model predictions are combined via weighted averaging for a probabilistic prediction task, and no reliable local validation is set up to guide weight selection.
general.action: Sweep blend weights in small increments (e.g., 0.05), submitting each configuration. Also try removing individual members entirely: dropping a weak member and redistributing its weight often gives a larger gain than fine-tuning weights among all members.

instance.goal: Does adding a second checkpoint population (pop_1) to the ensemble improve or hurt the KL divergence score?
instance.context: The author started with fewer ensemble members and added a new checkpoint with its own blending coefficient (koef_2=1.0). The first submission after adding it scored 0.34106, which was worse than the eventual score after removing it (0.30010).
instance.action: Added the checkpoint, submitted, observed degradation, then commented it out in the next version. This confirmed the member was harmful and led to the best score of the episode.

general.goal: When is adding another model to an ensemble counterproductive?
general.context: A new model checkpoint is available for ensembling, but its individual quality relative to existing members is uncertain.
general.action: Add the candidate member, submit or validate, and compare the metric to the baseline ensemble. If the score worsens, remove the member rather than trying to down-weight it; a weak or redundant member can hurt even at low weight, and removing it is the cleanest fix.

episode.objective: Swap in a different Resnet1d+GRU checkpoint and tune its kernel size to improve single-model quality.
episode.outcome: Kernel size 9 scored 0.40866 at v7, a large regression from 0.30010.

instance.goal: Will swapping in a different Resnet1d+GRU checkpoint and changing its kernel size from 5 to 9 improve the ensemble's leaderboard score?
instance.context: Previous ensemble blend scored 0.30010. The author pointed one ensemble member to a new checkpoint ('Resnet1d GRU ver 82.pth') and changed fixed_kernel_size from 5 to 9, but the score worsened dramatically to 0.40866.
instance.action: Replaced the checkpoint file path and changed the 1D CNN kernel size in a single probe. The large regression (0.30010 → 0.40866) indicates the new checkpoint or kernel size was incompatible with the rest of the pipeline or ensemble weights. The author subsequently abandoned this direction.

general.goal: When substituting a different pretrained checkpoint into an inference pipeline, how can one avoid silent architecture mismatches that degrade the score?
general.context: A checkpoint trained with one set of architecture hyperparameters (e.g., convolution kernel size) is being loaded into an inference script whose architecture definition may not match.
general.action: Always verify that every architecture hyperparameter in the inference code exactly matches the configuration used during training of the checkpoint. Change the architecture definition and the checkpoint together, not separately. After swapping, compare a few sample outputs against the old model before submitting, to catch gross mismatches early.

instance.goal: How much risk is there in changing both the checkpoint and a key hyperparameter at the same time?
instance.context: The author changed the checkpoint file in one step and the kernel size in the next, without an intermediate submission to isolate effects. The final score regressed by +0.108, making it impossible to tell which change caused the degradation.
instance.action: The two changes were made in rapid succession without submitting after the first. The large regression could not be attributed to either change individually, wasting diagnostic information.

general.goal: How should multiple interacting changes to a model be sequenced to preserve diagnostic clarity?
general.context: Two changes that interact (a new set of pretrained weights and an architecture hyperparameter) are being applied to an inference pipeline scored only via a leaderboard.
general.action: Submit after each individual change so the effect of each can be measured independently. When only leaderboard feedback is available (no local validation), isolating one variable per submission is especially important to avoid confounding regressions.

episode.objective: Test whether a single model prediction outperforms the blended ensemble.
episode.outcome: Single-model submission scored 0.68408 at v8, a severe regression.

instance.goal: After a large score regression from changing a kernel size (0.30 → 0.41), is the ensemble blend masking a problem, or is one component model actually better alone?
instance.context: The author had a best LB of 0.30 with a weighted blend of three models. After modifying the 1D CNN kernel size, the score regressed to 0.41. They suspected the blend might be dragging performance down or hiding which component was responsible.
instance.action: Replaced the weighted ensemble (0.45/0.15/0.40) with predictions from a single model (predss_1) only. The result was far worse (0.68), confirming the ensemble was beneficial and the single model alone was insufficient. The author returned to blending in subsequent versions.

general.goal: After a score regression following a component change in a multi-model blend, how can the source of the regression be isolated?
general.context: An ensemble of several models had a good score, but after modifying one component the blended score worsened. It is unclear whether the blend itself or the modified component is at fault.
general.action: Submit each component model's predictions individually to measure its standalone quality. If a single component scores much worse than the blend, the ensemble is providing significant value and the regression likely comes from the modified component. Use this diagnostic to decide which component to fix rather than dismantling the blend.

instance.goal: How much does the ensemble contribute beyond the best single model in this EEG classification task?
instance.context: Best blended score was 0.30 (KL divergence). The author tested predss_1 alone and got 0.68, more than doubling the error.
instance.action: Submitted the single-model prediction and observed a 0.38-point degradation, demonstrating the ensemble provided roughly half the final score quality. This motivated restoring and re-tuning the blend in later versions.

general.goal: How much of the current performance comes from blending versus from the strongest individual model?
general.context: A weighted blend of multiple models achieves a good score, but the contribution of blending versus individual model strength is unknown.
general.action: Submit the single best component's raw predictions as an ablation. Compare the gap to the blended score. If the gap is large (e.g., error more than doubles), the ensemble synergy is critical and effort should go into maintaining or improving the blend rather than relying on any single model.

episode.objective: Major refactor of the data/model pipeline to reorganize spectrogram, montage, and validation components.
episode.outcome: Score improved to 0.36230 at v9 (from 0.68408) but still worse than earlier best 0.30010.

instance.goal: After a single-model submission scored very poorly (0.68), how can the pipeline be restructured to recover and improve performance?
instance.context: The previous step (v8) isolated a single model's predictions (predss_1) for submission, which scored 0.68 — far worse than the earlier ensemble score of 0.30. This indicated the single model alone was inadequate and the pipeline needed fundamental changes.
instance.action: Performed a major refactor: disabled the existing Keras data generator, reorganized the feature pipeline to incorporate bandpass filtering, EEG montage features, and spectrogram features, switched validation to StratifiedGroupKFold with a custom metric, and restructured the OOF/inference flow. This recovered to LB 0.36, much better than the single-model 0.68 but not yet matching the best ensemble at 0.30.

general.goal: After isolating a single component reveals it performs far below the ensemble baseline, how should the pipeline be restructured to recover?
general.context: A diagnostic test (submitting one model alone) showed that the individual model is much weaker than the blended ensemble, indicating the pipeline's feature engineering and validation strategy need improvement rather than just re-tuning blend weights.
general.action: Refactor the data and feature pipeline: add domain-appropriate signal preprocessing (e.g., filtering, derived features), switch to a grouped stratified cross-validation scheme that respects the data's group structure, and rebuild the out-of-fold and inference flow before returning to ensemble tuning. This addresses root-cause weaknesses rather than superficial weight adjustments.

instance.goal: What is the actual standalone quality of each model in the ensemble, and is the ensemble masking a weak component?
instance.context: At v7 the ensemble scored 0.41, and earlier blends scored 0.30. The author submitted predss_1 alone at v8 and got 0.68, revealing that model was very weak on its own.
instance.action: Submitted a single model's raw predictions to the leaderboard to diagnose its standalone quality. The poor result (0.68 vs 0.30 ensemble) confirmed the model needed pipeline-level improvements, motivating the v9 refactor rather than further blend-weight tuning.

general.goal: How can the contribution and standalone quality of each ensemble member be assessed?
general.context: When ensemble blend weights are being tuned but scores fluctuate or degrade, it is unclear whether individual components are strong enough or if one is dragging performance down.
general.action: Submit each ensemble member's predictions individually to the leaderboard (or evaluate on a held-out fold). If a component scores far below the ensemble, prioritize improving that component's pipeline (features, preprocessing, validation) rather than continuing to tune blend coefficients.

episode.objective: Sweep ensemble blend weights across three model predictions (predss_1, predss_3, predss_4) to find optimal mix.
episode.outcome: v10 scored 0.39598; v11 and v12 not submitted. No improvement over 0.30010.

instance.goal: What blend weights across three model prediction streams (predss_1, predss_3, predss_4) minimize KL divergence on the public leaderboard?
instance.context: Starting blend was (0.35, 0.15, 0.50). The first submitted change to (0.45, 0.40, 0.15) worsened the score from 0.36230 to 0.39598, suggesting predss_4 was the strongest contributor. Subsequent unsubmitted versions shifted weight heavily toward predss_4 (0.65 then 0.80).
instance.action: Swept blend weights manually: first shifted weight away from predss_4 toward predss_1/predss_3, observed degradation, then reversed direction in two steps to concentrate weight on predss_4 (up to 0.80). Only the first change was submitted; the later two were not, likely awaiting a combined submission with other changes (v13 achieved 0.28438).

general.goal: How should blend weights be allocated across multiple model predictions when no local validation score is available to guide the search?
general.context: Multiple prediction streams are available for ensembling. A single leaderboard submission showed that reducing the weight of one stream hurt the score, implying that stream is strongest.
general.action: After one leaderboard probe reveals which model stream dominates, shift weight strongly toward it in subsequent iterations rather than continuing to explore balanced blends. Save leaderboard budget by batching the weight sweep with other changes before submitting again.

instance.goal: Is it worth submitting every incremental weight tweak to the leaderboard, or should multiple changes be bundled?
instance.context: v10 was submitted and scored 0.39598 (worse than v9's 0.36230). v11 and v12 were not submitted. The author eventually combined the weight shift with a checkpoint swap and kernel-size change in v13, which scored 0.28438—a large improvement.
instance.action: After the first probe showed the direction of improvement (more weight on predss_4), the author stopped submitting intermediate weight-only tweaks and instead bundled the weight change with model-level improvements before the next submission.

general.goal: When tuning ensemble weights with limited submission attempts, how can leaderboard budget be conserved?
general.context: Each leaderboard submission is costly (daily limits or information leakage risk). A single probe has already revealed which direction improves the blend.
general.action: Use one or two probes to identify the dominant model and the direction of improvement, then bundle the refined blend weights with other orthogonal improvements (e.g., better checkpoints or architecture tweaks) into a single submission rather than submitting each incremental weight change separately.

episode.objective: Revert kernel size to 5, swap checkpoint, and rebalance ensemble to fix regression and improve score.
episode.lever: kernel size, checkpoint, and blend weights together
episode.outcome: New best score 0.28438 at v13.

instance.goal: How can a regression in score caused by earlier changes to kernel size and checkpoint be recovered and surpassed?
instance.context: Changing the 1D CNN kernel size from 5 to 9 in v7 degraded LB from 0.30 to 0.41. Subsequent checkpoint and blend weight changes did not recover the original score. The best prior score was 0.30010.
instance.action: Reverted fixed_kernel_size from 9 back to 5, swapped the model checkpoint to a different one (pop_2_weight_oof), and rebalanced ensemble blend weights from (0.15, 0.05, 0.8) to (0.25, 0.35, 0.4). This achieved 0.28438, a new best.

general.goal: How can a score regression introduced by a hyperparameter change be diagnosed and fixed when multiple settings were changed afterward?
general.context: A single hyperparameter change (e.g., convolution kernel size) caused a clear score drop, but subsequent edits to other settings (checkpoints, blend weights) obscured the root cause and failed to recover performance.
general.action: Revert the specific hyperparameter that caused the initial regression to its previous value, then simultaneously adjust the other coupled settings (checkpoint selection, ensemble weights) that were tuned around the bad value. Bundling the revert with fresh tuning of dependent settings avoids intermediate broken states and can surpass the original score.

instance.goal: What combination of checkpoint and ensemble weights works best once the kernel size is corrected?
instance.context: After reverting kernel size to 5, the old blend weights (tuned for kernel=9 and a different checkpoint) were no longer optimal. Three model streams (predss_1, predss_3, predss_4) needed reweighting.
instance.action: Changed blend weights from heavily favoring one model (0.8) to a more balanced distribution (0.25, 0.35, 0.4), paired with a new checkpoint. The resulting 0.28438 beat all prior submissions.

general.goal: After changing a component in an ensemble pipeline, how should the blend weights be adjusted?
general.context: When one ensemble member's architecture or checkpoint changes, the previously tuned blend weights become stale because the relative quality of predictions shifts.
general.action: Re-distribute ensemble weights toward a more balanced allocation rather than keeping extreme weights tuned for the old configuration. Submit and compare; then fine-tune weights incrementally from the new balanced starting point.

episode.objective: Fine-tune ensemble blend weights around the new best to squeeze out further improvement.
episode.outcome: No improvement over 0.28438; closest was v17 at 0.28443. Best remained v13.

instance.goal: How much can the leaderboard score be improved by tuning ensemble blend weights around the current best configuration?
instance.context: v13 achieved a new best LB of 0.28438 with weights (0.25, 0.35, 0.40) for three model predictions. The author had no local validation signal visible and relied entirely on LB feedback.
instance.action: Swept blend weights across 4 submissions: shifted weight heavily toward predss_4 (0.60), then back toward equal (0.20/0.30/0.50), then toward predss_1+predss_3 (0.30/0.40/0.30), then toward predss_4 again (0.25/0.30/0.45). None of the 4 attempts beat the original v13 score of 0.28438; the best was v17 at 0.28443, essentially matching v13. The sweep showed the score surface was flat near the optimum.

general.goal: How much further improvement can be extracted by tuning the blending weights of a fixed set of model predictions?
general.context: An ensemble blend has just achieved a new best score, and the practitioner wants to know if the weighting is suboptimal enough to yield meaningful gains.
general.action: Sweep blend weights in several directions around the current best (shifting mass toward each component in turn). If multiple perturbations all produce scores within a narrow band of the original, conclude the weight surface is flat and stop tuning weights—further gains require changing the component models or adding new ones rather than reweighting.

instance.goal: Without local validation, how can the author efficiently search for better blend weights using only public leaderboard feedback?
instance.context: Each submission costs a leaderboard evaluation. The author tried 4 weight configurations in sequence, adjusting direction based on whether the previous attempt improved or worsened the score.
instance.action: Used a reactive grid search: first tried a large shift (predss_4 weight 0.40→0.60), saw degradation (0.28438→0.28656), then moved back partway (0.50), saw improvement (0.28468), shifted further away from predss_4 (0.30), saw degradation (0.28555), then tried an intermediate (0.45) which nearly matched the original. This bracketing pattern identified that the original weights were already near-optimal.

general.goal: How to search a one-dimensional weight space efficiently when the only feedback is a noisy leaderboard score?
general.context: No offline validation metric is available; each evaluation requires a full submission. The search space is a simplex of blend weights for a small number of models.
general.action: Use a bracketing strategy: make one large perturbation in a chosen direction, observe the result, then move in the opposite direction or halve the step. After a few trials that all land near the same score, conclude the optimum has been bracketed and stop. Limit total attempts to roughly four or five to avoid overfitting to public leaderboard noise.

episode.objective: Build a working inference/submission pipeline from training code, loading fold checkpoints and producing predictions via tf.data datasets.
episode.outcome: Pipeline functional at LB 0.34131 (v3), subsequent versions are refactoring with no score change through v8.

instance.goal: How to convert a training notebook into a reliable inference pipeline that loads multiple fold checkpoints and produces averaged predictions?
instance.context: The author had training code for EfficientNet (spectrogram) and 1D CNN (raw EEG) models with multiple K-fold checkpoints. The pipeline needed to handle multiple data types (spectrograms, EEG spectrograms, raw EEGs), load fold weights, and average predictions into a submission.
instance.action: Built incrementally over 7 versions: (1) stripped training code and added data I/O, (2) added model definitions and fold-loading logic achieving LB 0.34131, (3) refactored into BaseDataGenerator with ABC, (4) wrapped generators in tf.data.Dataset with explicit TensorSpec signatures, (5) added versioning constants and multi-replica batching, (6) made mode/data_type required arguments removing default-value bugs, (7) commented out strict assertion sanity checks that blocked submission. Each step was a small structural change, submitting periodically to verify no regression.

general.goal: How to safely convert a training notebook into an inference/submission pipeline without introducing bugs that change predictions?
general.context: Training code contains model building, compilation, learning rate schedules, augmentation, and validation logic that must be removed or disabled for inference, while data loading and model architecture definitions must be preserved exactly.
general.action: Refactor incrementally: first strip training-only code and reorganize data I/O, then add model loading and prediction averaging, then refactor shared utilities into base classes, then wrap data pipelines in the framework's dataset API with explicit type signatures. Submit after each major change to confirm predictions are unchanged (score should not regress). Remove or disable hard assertions that may block submission on edge cases.

instance.goal: When refactoring data generators and dataset creation functions, how to avoid subtle bugs from default arguments referencing outer-scope variables?
instance.context: The DataGenerator and create_dataset function had default parameter values that referenced outer-scope dictionaries (specs, eeg_specs, raw_eegs). This created fragile coupling and potential bugs when variables were renamed or reordered during refactoring (v4→v6).
instance.action: Changed DataGenerator.__init__ and create_dataset to require mode, data_type, and data dictionaries as explicit positional arguments with no defaults, eliminating reliance on outer-scope names. This made the API explicit and prevented silent bugs from stale references.

general.goal: How to prevent silent bugs when refactoring data-loading functions that reference global or outer-scope variables as default arguments?
general.context: Python evaluates default argument values at function definition time, so defaults referencing mutable outer-scope objects can silently point to stale or wrong data after renaming or restructuring.
