They introduced a new Net1db7 (EfficientNet-B7) class and integrated it alongside x3d and double-head models, also halving batch size to accommodate the larger model's memory.
instance.action: Defined a new model class with the larger backbone, halved the DataLoader batch size to fit it in GPU memory, loaded pretrained weights, and added its predictions to the ensemble average. The result (0.24428) was worse than the previous best (0.22944), suggesting the B7 weights were not well-trained or the ensemble balance was off.

general.goal: Does scaling up the backbone capacity in an ensemble member improve the final blended prediction?
general.context: An ensemble of moderate-capacity models has reached a plateau. A larger backbone variant is available but requires reduced batch size for inference and may not have been trained as thoroughly.
general.action: Introduce the larger backbone as an additional ensemble member, reduce batch size to fit memory, and compare the ensemble score. If the score worsens, the larger model's checkpoints may need more training or the ensemble weights need rebalancing before the capacity increase pays off.

episode.objective: Toggle Net1d vs Net1db7, enable/disable model runs, switch between mean and weighted blending, add butter-filtered double-head model.
episode.lever: model class selection and ensemble blending
episode.outcome: v187 achieved 0.22709, v192 achieved 0.22694. NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Which model variant (Net1d vs Net1db7) and which subset of ensemble members with what blend weights yields the best leaderboard score?
instance.context: The author had a best score of 0.22940 before this episode. Swapping between Net1d and Net1db7 model classes, toggling ensemble members on/off, and switching between simple mean vs weighted blend produced wildly varying scores (0.91 to 0.22694). The best results (0.22709, 0.22694) came from specific combinations of Net1d with particular ensemble compositions.
instance.action: Systematically toggled: (1) Net1d vs Net1db7 for two model instantiations, (2) which run_weight_* predictions to include, (3) simple mean vs weighted blend. After a catastrophic regression to 0.91 in v186, the author stripped back to fewer members (v187→0.22709 best), then iteratively re-added members and re-tuned weights, reaching 0.22694 in v192 with Net1d, multiple members enabled, and weighted blending.

general.goal: How to recover and find the best ensemble configuration after a large score regression caused by changing model variants and blend settings?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models is being tuned at inference time. A change that simultaneously alters model architecture variant, number of ensemble members, and aggregation method causes a catastrophic score regression.
general.action: Roll back to a minimal working configuration (fewer members, simpler averaging) to isolate which change caused the regression. Then re-introduce changes one at a time: first confirm the correct model variant, then incrementally add ensemble members, and finally switch from uniform averaging to weighted blending. Submit after each single change to attribute score movements.

instance.goal: Does adding a butter-filtered double-head model (combining spectrogram and raw EEG with Butterworth preprocessing) to the ensemble improve predictions?
instance.context: The ensemble already contained spectrogram-based, raw-EEG, and X3D models. A Butterworth bandpass filter variant had been tried earlier (v182-v183) with marginal benefit. The author created new model classes (Netdoubleheadbutterfilter) with dedicated spectrogram extraction and 0–20Hz cropping.
instance.action: Implemented a new double-head model variant using Butterworth-filtered EEG input, added its pretrained weights, and integrated its predictions into the ensemble. The butter-filtered model alone (v191, 0.23226) didn't beat the best, but when combined with the right ensemble composition and weighted blending (v192), it contributed to a new best of 0.22694.

general.goal: Can diversity in signal preprocessing (different filter types applied to the same raw input) improve an ensemble of neural models?
general.context: Multiple models already process the same underlying signal with one preprocessing pipeline. A different filtering approach produces slightly different input representations that may capture complementary information.
general.action: Create a model variant that uses an alternative signal filter for preprocessing, train it separately, and add its predictions to the ensemble. The variant alone need not outperform existing members; evaluate its contribution only within the full weighted ensemble, as diversity gains may only appear in combination.

episode.objective: Tune ensemble composition (enable/disable members), blend weights, spectrogram scaling/normalization, and short-window transforms.
episode.outcome: v200 achieved LB 0.22621. NEW BEST.

instance.goal: How should multiple diverse model predictions (spec, x3d, eeg_raw, butter_filter, double_head) be combined to minimize KL divergence on the leaderboard?
instance.context: The author had achieved 0.22694 with a weighted blend of multiple models. Over the episode, simple averaging (v193: 0.23360) and various subsets with equal or hand-tuned weights were tried. Adding all five models back with a carefully tuned weighted blend (v200: 0.22621) beat all other configurations.
instance.action: Systematically toggled ensemble members on/off and alternated between simple mean and hand-tuned weighted blends across 8 submissions. The best result used all five diverse models with unequal weights (0.1, 0.2, 0.175, 0.175, 0.35) rather than dropping members or equal-weighting. Fewer members with equal weights consistently scored worse.

general.goal: How should predictions from multiple heterogeneous models be aggregated to minimize a divergence-based metric?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models (different architectures, preprocessing pipelines) is available. Both the subset of members included and the blend weights affect the final score.
general.action: Sweep over ensemble subsets and weighting schemes by alternating between simple averaging and hand-tuned weighted blends. Include all diverse members rather than pruning to a small subset, and assign higher weight to the single strongest individual model. Evaluate each configuration on the leaderboard or a reliable validation set; revert when a change hurts.

instance.goal: Can changing spectrogram parameters (n_fft, win_length, hop_length) and normalization (log10 vs linear clipping) at inference time improve predictions from pretrained models?
instance.context: Models were already trained with specific spectrogram settings. The author changed n_fft from 1024→512, win_length from 512→128, replaced log10+clip with linear clip/scale, and added a short-window (10s) transform concatenated with a 50s transform—all at inference only. Every such change degraded the score (v196: 0.29780, v197: 0.27255, v198: 0.26546, v199: 0.25381) compared to the baseline (v195: 0.22795).
instance.action: Tried multiple spectrogram parameter and normalization changes at inference time without retraining. All degraded performance substantially. The author ultimately reverted these preprocessing changes and recovered the best score by returning to the original settings and re-tuning only ensemble weights (v200: 0.22621).

general.goal: Can input preprocessing parameters be changed at inference time to improve a pretrained model's predictions?
general.context: Models were trained with specific feature-extraction settings (e.g., spectral transform resolution, normalization scheme). Changing these settings at test time creates a train-test mismatch.
general.action: Avoid modifying feature-extraction or normalization parameters at inference time without retraining the model on identically processed data. Even seemingly reasonable adjustments (resolution, scaling) cause large score regressions due to distribution mismatch. If exploration is needed, treat each change as a hypothesis, submit quickly, and revert promptly when scores degrade.

episode.objective: Toggle ensemble members and switch between mean/weighted blending; tune spectrogram log/clip preprocessing.
episode.outcome: v206 re-run at 0.22628; essentially flat around best.

instance.goal: How should multiple model predictions be combined — simple mean or hand-tuned weighted blend — to minimize KL divergence on the leaderboard?
instance.context: v200 achieved a new best (0.22621) with a weighted blend of multiple models. The author then tried simplifying to mean (v201: 0.27024, worse), re-adding models with new weights (v202: 0.22738, close but not better), simplifying again (v203: 0.27238, worse), and finally restoring a weighted blend (v205/v206: 0.22628, near-best).
instance.action: Alternate between simple averaging and weighted blending while toggling ensemble members. Each time simple mean was tried with fewer models, the score degraded substantially. The best results consistently came from weighted blends with more diverse models included. Revert quickly when a simplification hurts by more than ~0.005.

general.goal: How should multiple model predictions be combined — equal averaging or learned/hand-tuned weighting — when optimizing a divergence-based metric?
general.context: An ensemble of diverse models (different architectures, preprocessing) has reached a strong score with weighted blending. The practitioner wants to know whether simplifying to equal-weight averaging could match or beat it.
general.action: Test both simple averaging and weighted blending on the leaderboard. When removing members and switching to equal averaging consistently degrades the score, keep the weighted blend with all diverse members. Revert immediately if a simplification worsens the metric by a noticeable margin, as the diversity of members matters more than blend simplicity.

instance.goal: What is the effect of changing spectrogram preprocessing (log transform, win_length, clipping, scaling) on inference quality when models were trained with specific preprocessing?
instance.context: Changing win_length from 128→256 and input scaling (v203) hurt the score (0.27238). Removing the log transform (v204) made it much worse (0.34797). These models were trained with particular spectrogram parameters, so mismatched inference preprocessing causes large degradations.
instance.action: When tuning spectrogram parameters at inference time, change only one parameter at a time and immediately revert if the score degrades. The author found that altering log/clip/scale or FFT window parameters away from training-time values caused 0.05–0.12 score regressions, confirming that inference preprocessing must match training preprocessing exactly.

general.goal: What happens when signal-to-spectrogram preprocessing parameters are changed at inference time relative to what was used during training?
general.context: Pretrained models were trained with specific spectrogram generation settings (window length, log scaling, clipping). The practitioner considers adjusting these at inference to potentially improve predictions.
general.action: Do not change spectrogram preprocessing parameters (window size, log transforms, normalization) at inference unless the model is retrained with the new settings. Even small mismatches between training and inference preprocessing cause large score regressions. Test one parameter at a time and revert immediately if the metric worsens.

episode.objective: Tune spectrogram normalization (log10 vs clip/scale), add HGNet backbone, and adjust ensemble members and Butterworth filter order.
episode.outcome: v211 at 0.23479, v212 at 0.23478; no improvement over 0.22621.

instance.goal: What spectrogram normalization (log10 vs linear clip-and-scale) works best for the CNN ensemble at inference time?
instance.context: Previous best LB was 0.22628 with clip-to-[0,10000]/divide-by-1000 normalization. The author tried log10 normalization (v207, LB 0.27069), then reverted to clip-to-[0,5000]/divide-by-100 (v208, LB 0.25986), both worse than baseline. The models were trained with specific preprocessing, so inference preprocessing must match.
instance.action: Tried log10 after clipping to [1e-4, 1e8], saw a large score regression. Reverted to linear clip-and-scale with adjusted range. Both were worse, so the author effectively abandoned the log10 direction and returned close to original preprocessing in later steps.

general.goal: How sensitive is a pretrained model's inference score to changes in input normalization applied only at test time?
general.context: Models were trained with a specific input normalization scheme. Changing normalization at inference without retraining creates a train-test mismatch.
general.action: When experimenting with input normalization at inference, keep changes small and consistent with training preprocessing. If a normalization change (e.g., switching from linear scaling to log scaling) causes a large score regression, revert immediately rather than trying to tune it further, because the mismatch with training conditions is the root cause.

instance.goal: Can adding a new backbone (HGNet-v2-b5) to the ensemble improve the score beyond the current best of ~0.22628?
instance.context: The ensemble already contained EfficientNet, X3D, raw-EEG 1D CNN, and double-head models. The author integrated HGNet with flip TTA (v211, LB 0.23479), then swapped it out for a butter-filtered raw-EEG model (v212, LB 0.23478). Neither improved over the best score of 0.22628.
instance.action: Implemented HGNet backbone, ran inference with flip TTA across multiple folds, appended predictions to ensemble. Score did not improve, so the author disabled HGNet and re-enabled a previously proven ensemble member. The new backbone was effectively rejected after one test.

general.goal: When does adding a new backbone architecture to an already-diverse ensemble yield diminishing returns?
general.context: An ensemble of several diverse model families (2D CNNs, 3D CNNs, 1D signal models) is already near its best score. A newly trained backbone is added but its individual quality or diversity contribution is uncertain.
general.action: Add the new backbone's predictions to the ensemble and evaluate on the leaderboard. If the score does not improve or barely changes, the new model likely does not add sufficient diversity or quality. Remove it and keep the simpler, proven ensemble. One submission is enough to decide if the backbone is not clearly beneficial.

instance.goal: Does increasing the Butterworth bandpass filter order from 2 to 4 for EEG preprocessing improve predictions?
instance.context: A 2nd-order Butterworth filter was used for EEG bandpass filtering. The author increased to 4th order (v209, LB 0.23481) alongside swapping ensemble members, then reverted to order 2 (v210, not submitted) when also enabling log transform on spectrograms.
instance.action: Tested order 4 in one version, observed no clear improvement over baseline. Reverted to order 2 in the next version. The change was small and bundled with other modifications, making attribution difficult, but the revert suggests order 2 was preferred.

general.goal: How aggressively should a bandpass filter be applied to physiological signals at inference time?
general.context: A low-order bandpass filter is already in use. Increasing filter order makes the frequency cutoff sharper but may remove signal content the model learned to use during training.
general.action: Test a higher filter order in one experiment. If the score does not clearly improve, revert to the lower order, since a sharper filter risks removing information the model expects. Keep the filter order consistent with what was used during training whenever possible.

episode.objective: Tune spectrogram clipping/scaling and batch size for inference loaders to improve throughput and predictions.
episode.outcome: v213 regressed (0.26971), v214 achieved LB 0.22478. NEW BEST.

instance.goal: Why did adding more ensemble members and changing spectrogram preprocessing (clip max 5000→10000, scaling /100→/1000, slice offset +2→+10) hurt the score from 0.234 to 0.270?
instance.context: v213 changed multiple things at once: spectrogram clipping/scaling, slice dimensions, enabled additional model runs, added HGNet, and switched from mean to weighted blend. The score regressed significantly.
instance.action: In v214, reverted the harmful changes implicitly by fixing the batch size (from CFG['batch_size']//2 to CFG['batch_size']) in both normal and flip-TTA DataLoaders, which achieved a new best of 0.22478. This suggests the halved batch size was causing incomplete or inconsistent inference batching that corrupted predictions.

general.goal: Could an inference-time batch size mismatch be silently degrading predictions?
general.context: When inference DataLoaders use a reduced batch size (e.g., half of the configured value), the last incomplete batch or padding behavior may differ from training, especially with batch-dependent normalization layers or when test-time augmentation paths use inconsistent batch sizes.
general.action: Ensure inference DataLoaders use the same batch size as configured/expected. When debugging a score regression caused by multiple simultaneous changes, isolate infrastructure settings (batch size, data loading) as a separate variable—they can have outsized, non-obvious effects on predictions.

instance.goal: How can the score be improved beyond the current plateau around 0.227–0.235?
instance.context: The author had been iterating on spectrogram preprocessing parameters (clip range, scaling, slice offsets) and ensemble composition for many versions with marginal gains. v212 scored 0.23478.
instance.action: Made a large multi-factor change in v213 (preprocessing + ensemble members + blend weights) which regressed to 0.270, then in v214 fixed only the batch size parameter, achieving a new best of 0.22478. The net episode gain came from a single infrastructure fix, not from the preprocessing/ensemble changes.

general.goal: When many modeling and preprocessing tweaks yield diminishing returns, where else might hidden score improvements lie?
general.context: After extensive tuning of input preprocessing and ensemble composition with only marginal gains, infrastructure details in the inference pipeline (data loading, batching, padding) may contain latent bugs or suboptimal defaults that silently degrade predictions.
general.action: Audit the full inference pipeline for consistency issues: check that batch sizes, data loader settings, and preprocessing paths match between training and inference, and between different test-time augmentation branches. Fix these before continuing to tune model or preprocessing hyperparameters.

episode.objective: Add hgnet-based single-image model, try 18-lead EEG input, and tune spectrogram/windowing parameters.

instance.goal: Can a new backbone (hgnet) and single-image model variant improve the ensemble beyond the current best of 0.22478?
instance.context: The author had reached LB 0.22478 with an ensemble of EfficientNet, X3D, raw-EEG, and double-head models. They introduced an hgnet-based single-image model with changed spectrogram preprocessing and windowing.
instance.action: Added hgnet backbone, changed spectrogram win_length/clipping/scaling, shifted inference window offset, and swapped ensemble members. Score worsened to 0.26249. Over next steps tried 18-lead EEG input (0.23945), frequency band narrowing (0.26072), and toggling ensemble members (0.24602). None beat the prior best. The author abandoned these changes in v219, reverting to the proven ensemble with weighted blending (0.22697).

general.goal: When introducing a new backbone or input representation into an inference ensemble, how can one tell quickly whether it helps?
general.context: A well-tuned ensemble has reached a strong baseline score. A new model variant is added alongside changes to preprocessing and input configuration, making it hard to isolate the effect of each change.
general.action: Introduce the new component in isolation first (one change at a time) and submit. If the score degrades substantially, revert and test the component differently rather than continuing to layer additional changes on top. When multiple exploratory submissions all score worse than the baseline, revert the entire batch and return to the known-good configuration.

instance.goal: Does expanding EEG input from 16 to 18 leads improve predictions for the HMS brain activity classification task?
instance.context: The standard pipeline used 16 derived EEG leads (bipolar montage). The author added a use_18_lead flag and reshaped the model input from 16 to 18 channels, submitting with the hgnet model.
instance.action: Added two extra leads and updated the model's reshape dimensions. The score improved from 0.26249 to 0.23945 (within this exploratory branch), suggesting the extra leads helped that particular model, but the overall configuration still couldn't beat the prior best of 0.22478. The 18-lead idea was not carried forward in subsequent versions.

general.goal: Does adding more input channels (derived features from the same raw signal) improve a model that processes multi-channel time-series data?
general.context: A fixed set of derived channels is used as model input. Additional channels can be computed from the same raw signals at low cost, but the model architecture dimensions must be updated to accept them.
general.action: Add the extra channels, update the model's input reshape/dimension accordingly, and evaluate. If the gain is visible in isolation but the overall ensemble doesn't improve, the extra channels may help only specific model variants; test them selectively rather than applying globally.

episode.objective: Optimize final ensemble composition and blend weights across all available models, toggling members and switching between mean/weighted aggregation.
episode.lever: ensemble blend weights and member selection
episode.outcome: v229 achieved LB 0.22428 (NEW BEST), v231 at 0.22474; final best 0.22428.

instance.goal: What is the best combination of ensemble members and blend weights across ~7 available model predictions (r21d, x3d, hgnet, double-head, raw EEG, butter-filtered EEG, one-image, spec) to minimize KL divergence?
instance.context: The author had a best LB of 0.22478 and ~7 diverse trained models. Over 13 submissions they toggled members on/off and switched between simple mean and hand-tuned weighted blends, achieving a new best of 0.22428.
instance.action: Systematically sweep ensemble composition: start with many members + weighted blend (v219: 0.22697), try removing one (v220: 0.22712), try fewer with mean (v221: 0.23710), re-add with weights (v222: 0.22627), continue alternating between adding/removing members and mean vs weighted blend. The best configuration (v229: 0.22428) used 6 models with weights [0.1,0.1,0.2,0.2,0.2,0.2]. Perturbing those weights (v230: 0.22550) or changing preprocessing/members (v231: 0.22474) did not beat it.

general.goal: How should multiple diverse model predictions be combined—which subset and what weighting—to minimize the ensemble's loss?
general.context: Several trained models of different architectures are available. No reliable offline validation exists, so the leaderboard is the primary signal. The search space is discrete (member inclusion) plus continuous (blend weights).
general.action: Alternate between two axes: (1) toggle individual members in/out, and (2) switch between equal-weight averaging and a hand-tuned weighted blend. Submit each variant. When adding members with a weighted blend beats the simple mean, keep the larger set; when a member's inclusion consistently hurts, drop it. Down-weight weaker members rather than excluding them entirely, since even weak models can help if given small weight. Stop when small weight perturbations no longer improve the score.

instance.goal: When reducing the ensemble to fewer members with simple averaging consistently scores worse than a larger weighted blend, what does that indicate about the aggregation strategy?
instance.context: Every time the author dropped to 2–3 members with simple mean (v221: 0.23710, v223: 0.23098, v225: 0.23748), the score degraded substantially compared to 6-member weighted blends (v219: 0.22697, v222: 0.22627, v224: 0.22673, v229: 0.22428). The pattern repeated across 6+ attempts.
instance.action: Prefer keeping more diverse ensemble members with down-weighted contributions over pruning to a small subset with equal weights. The best result (v229) used all 6 models with unequal weights rather than any smaller equal-weight subset.

general.goal: Is it better to use fewer high-quality models with equal weights or more models with unequal weights in an ensemble?
general.context: Repeated experiments show that pruning to a small subset with equal averaging consistently underperforms a larger set with hand-tuned weights, even when some members are individually weaker.
general.action: Keep a larger, more diverse ensemble and assign lower weights to weaker members rather than removing them. Even models that hurt when given equal weight can improve the ensemble when down-weighted, because they contribute orthogonal information. Only remove a member if it degrades the score at every tested weight.
